### Solver tolerance

Numerical stopping criterion of the selected solver.

Exact residual/change rule is solver-specific.

Tighter tolerances may take longer; they do not directly regularize data fitting.

Interactions: max_iterations; feature scaling.

A converged solver can still fit the wrong objective or overfit.

Maximum solver iterations, not neural training epochs.

Count depends on algorithm implementation.

Interactions: solver_tolerance; optimizer.

reading.definition: Linear regression predicts a number by adding weighted feature contributions and, usually, a constant intercept. reading.example: Here one feature predicts three targets: x = [1, 2, 3], y = [1, 2, 2]. To keep the solution visible we omit the intercept. Changing the ridge penalty changes the fitted coefficient, predictions and training error.

steps.title: Training values and sums
steps.prose: With one coefficient and no intercept, every prediction is x × w. The least-squares solution can be calculated from two sums: squared inputs and input–target products. With many features these become matrix operations rather than scalar sums.
steps.terms: The design matrix X stacks input rows. Transpose, written T, swaps its axes; XᵀX and Xᵀy collect the needed products.
steps.next: Use the two training sums to solve for the fitted coefficient.

steps.title: Fit the regression coefficient
steps.prose: Choose the coefficient that minimizes summed squared error plus lambda times its square. A larger lambda shrinks this coefficient towards zero in this example. Setting lambda to zero gives ordinary least squares.
steps.terms: Ridge is linear regression with an L2 penalty. Lambda is the chosen penalty strength, not a learned feature weight.
steps.next: Use the resulting coefficient to calculate predictions; this does not fit it again.

steps.title: Predictions and training error
steps.prose: Multiply each input by the fitted coefficient, then compare these predictions with the targets used to fit it. A larger penalty can make these training errors worse while potentially helping performance on new cases. The training numbers alone cannot tell us whether it helped generalization.
steps.terms: A prediction uses a fitted model. Squared training error is not a held-out evaluation score.
steps.next: The final section explains how to judge this fitted model on separate cases.

steps.title: Evaluate on new cases
steps.prose: After selecting the fitting procedure using validation data, measure its error on held-out cases in the target's units. Compare against a simple numerical baseline and inspect where errors occur. This section is an evaluation step, not another input to the closed-form coefficient.
steps.terms: MAE and RMSE measure numerical error in different ways; their definitions are in Evaluation metrics.
steps.next: Compare this regression objective with classification in the logistic regression lesson and regularization choices in the regularization lesson.

links: The training sums and selected penalty determine the fitted coefficient.
The fitted coefficient multiplies each input to produce a prediction.

reading.lesson_markdown:
Linear regression predicts a numerical target using a weighted sum, $\hat y=w_1x_1+\cdots+w_dx_d+b$. A weight describes a slope while the other features remain fixed. Its magnitude depends on feature units; a large coefficient is not automatically a large real-world effect.

Two points, $(0,1)$ and $(2,5)$, define the line $\hat y=2x+1$. Add $(1,4)$: that same line predicts 3 and misses by 1. Least squares fits a compromise across all rows by minimising summed or averaged squared residuals. These reductions have the same unregularised minimiser, but their scale matters when a penalty or a learning rate is introduced.

For many features, matrix notation writes predictions as $Xw+b$. Least-squares solvers do not require explicitly computing a matrix inverse. If columns are dependent, multiple coefficient vectors may make identical predictions; regularisation can make the solution more stable. A linear model can also use nonlinear input features such as $x^2$: “linear” refers to how coefficients enter the model.

Inspect held-out residuals, not only training fit. Curved residual patterns suggest missing structure; unusually large errors deserve investigation. Neither a good fit nor a coefficient alone establishes causation.

Sources: [D2L: linear regression](https://d2l.ai/chapter_linear-regression/linear-regression.html), [scikit-learn: ordinary least squares](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/linear_model.html#ordinary-least-squares).

# ML04. Logistic regression and classification

Classification predicts a category rather than a numerical measurement. Binary logistic regression first calculates a weighted score, then maps it to a probability for one of two classes. A separate decision threshold turns that probability into a yes/no prediction.

Features [1, 2] and weights [0.2, 0.1] give score 0.4 and positive-class probability about 0.60. A threshold of 0.5 predicts positive; a threshold of 0.7 predicts negative, without changing the model.

Linear regression in the linear regression lesson predicts a number directly. Logistic regression adds a probability mapping and a classification loss. The threshold controls the action, while the loss can be used to fit the probabilities.

[course map](../COURSE_MAP.md). Required background: ML03, P3.

## 1. Binary, multiclass and multilabel tasks

**Key terms.** A **logit** is a raw score; **sigmoid** converts one score into a binary probability; **softmax** normalizes several class scores; a **threshold** turns a probability into a decision. **Multilabel** permits several simultaneous labels.

**Process.** Transform features into logits, calculate target log loss and fit weights. At prediction, output probabilities first and apply the chosen decision rule afterwards. Changing the threshold alone does not retrain the model.

Logistic regression has a linear boundary in its supplied feature space, not a linear probability. Binary and mutually exclusive multiclass predictions need different output shapes; multilabel tasks commonly use independent binary outputs. Stable loss functions take logits directly rather than rounded probabilities. In PyTorch, standard CrossEntropyLoss expects logits and class indices for the common hard-label case.

Positive class labels and metric averaging must be stated. A threshold chosen to catch more spam can also increase legitimate-message false alarms. Class weights alter fitting, while threshold changes alter decisions from already fitted scores. They can interact but are not substitutes.

## 2. A worked calculation

**Symbols and assumptions.** z=x·w+b is a binary logit; p=sigmoid(z); y is 0 or 1. Natural logarithms make the loss unit a nat. C in a library's regularized estimator is an inverse-regularization control, not this probability.

\[
p=\frac1{1+e^{-z}},\qquad
\ell=-y\log p-(1-y)\log(1-p).
\]

At z=0, p=0.5. With y=1, loss is −ln(0.5)=0.6931 and the logit derivative p−y=−0.5. A positive target with predicted p=0.8 has loss 0.2231. Threshold 0.9 rejects it despite the good probability; threshold 0.5 accepts it. No weight changed between those decisions.

The numbers above are illustrative calculations, not measured benchmark results.

## 3. Choosing the probability model

A linear probability model fits a number directly to binary labels and may return values outside [0,1]. Logistic regression instead maps a linear score through sigmoid; a nonlinear classifier can learn a more complex boundary. Compare these as different probability models, not three steps in one model. Softmax models an exclusive choice; independent sigmoids need not sum to one. Well-ranked scores can be miscalibrated, so accuracy or AUROC alone is not probability validation.

The related settings are defined below this lesson in Model Lab, including their mathematical meaning, expected effects and interactions. The training lab exposes only controls that change an implemented operation; the broader [parameter catalogue](../metadata/parameters.json) also describes theory-only options.

## 4. Example: three-class prediction

For three Iris classes, fit multinomial logistic regression on scaled measurements and inspect a three-entry probability vector. Class order must match the saved label mapping. Do not train a binary sigmoid and quietly discard one species.

**Check.** A network outputs [batch,10] scores for a single-label ten-class task. Should you apply sigmoid and expect the outputs to sum to one?

**Answer.** No. Use the appropriate mutually exclusive classification objective and softmax for reported probabilities. Sigmoid is appropriate for separate binary labels under a different task definition.

## 5. Why cross-entropy gives a useful update

**Key terms.** A logit z is an unnormalized class score. Softmax turns K logits into K probabilities; a one-hot target has one entry equal to one.

**Process.** Compute logits, normalize with softmax, select the true-class probability and take its negative logarithm. Backpropagation passes the probability-minus-target error into each score's producing weights.

In this equation, K is the number of mutually exclusive classes, z_k is the score for class k, and y identifies the observed correct class. The indicator is 1 for that class and 0 for the others. Normalizing means dividing by the sum across classes so the probabilities add to one.

\[
p_k=\frac{\exp(z_k)}{\sum_j\exp(z_j)},\qquad
\ell=-\log p_y,\qquad
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial z_k}=p_k-\mathbf1[k=y].
\]

For probabilities [0.7,0.2,0.1] and true class two, the logit gradients are [0.7,−0.8,0.1]. A gradient-descent update tends to raise the true-class score and lower the others. Numerically stable implementations subtract the largest logit and combine log-softmax with the loss; computing exp on arbitrary large scores can overflow.

### Prediction is a separate decision

The default multiclass rule selects the largest probability. A binary decision threshold or cost matrix can change decisions without refitting weights; select it using development data, never the final test. The current runnable datasets are multiclass, so the lab does not pretend to offer a generic binary threshold control. Calibration is about whether probabilities agree with frequencies, not simply whether the winning class is correct.

## Sources

- [scikit-learn linear models](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html).
- [scikit-learn metrics](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html).
- [PyTorch 2.9 CrossEntropyLoss](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/generated/torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss.html).

\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial z_k}=p_k-\mathbf1[k=y].
\]

For probabilities [0.7,0.2,0.1] and true class two, the logit gradients are [0.7,−0.8,0.1]. A gradient-descent update tends to raise the true-class score and lower the others. Numerically stable implementations subtract the largest logit and combine log-softmax with the loss; computing exp on arbitrary large scores can overflow.

### Prediction is a separate decision

The default multiclass rule selects the largest probability. A binary decision threshold or cost matrix can change decisions without refitting weights; select it using development data, never the final test. The current runnable datasets are multiclass, so the lab does not pretend to offer a generic binary threshold control. Calibration is about whether probabilities agree with frequencies, not simply whether the winning class is correct.

notes.title: Binary, multiclass and multilabel tasks
notes.markdown:
Logistic regression has a linear boundary in its supplied feature space, not a linear probability. Binary and mutually exclusive multiclass predictions need different output shapes; multilabel tasks commonly use independent binary outputs. Stable loss functions take logits directly rather than rounded probabilities. In PyTorch, standard CrossEntropyLoss expects logits and class indices for the common hard-label case.

Positive class labels and metric averaging must be stated. A threshold chosen to catch more spam can also increase legitimate-message false alarms. Class weights alter fitting, while threshold changes alter decisions from already fitted scores. They can interact but are not substitutes.

notes.title: Choosing the probability model
notes.markdown: A linear probability model fits a number directly to binary labels and may return values outside [0,1]. Logistic regression instead maps a linear score through sigmoid; a nonlinear classifier can learn a more complex boundary. Compare these as different probability models, not three steps in one model. Softmax models an exclusive choice; independent sigmoids need not sum to one. Well-ranked scores can be miscalibrated, so accuracy or AUROC alone is not probability validation.

notes.title: Example: three-class prediction
notes.markdown: For three Iris classes, fit multinomial logistic regression on scaled measurements and inspect a three-entry probability vector. Class order must match the saved label mapping. Do not train a binary sigmoid and quietly discard one species.

notes.title: Why cross-entropy gives a useful update
notes.markdown:
**Key terms.** A logit z is an unnormalized class score. Softmax turns K logits into K probabilities; a one-hot target has one entry equal to one.

In this equation, K is the number of mutually exclusive classes, z_k is the score for class k, and y identifies the observed correct class. The indicator is 1 for that class and 0 for the others. Normalizing means dividing by the sum across classes so the probabilities add to one.

\[
p_k=\frac{\exp(z_k)}{\sum_j\exp(z_j)},\qquad
\ell=-\log p_y,\qquad
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial z_k}=p_k-\mathbf1[k=y].
\]

Numerically stable implementations subtract the largest logit and combine log-softmax with the loss; computing exp on arbitrary large scores can overflow.

A binary decision threshold or cost matrix can change decisions without refitting weights; select it using development data, never the final test. notes.title: Settings: Inverse regularization C, Class weighting
notes.markdown:
### Inverse regularization C

Estimator-specific inverse regularization scale.

For common conventions, larger C weakens relative regularization; exact objective scaling differs.

Larger C can fit training violations more aggressively and increase overfitting.

Interactions: scaling; kernel_gamma; sample/class weights.

C is not interchangeable with ridge alpha or lambda across sample counts/libraries.

### Class weighting

Relative fitting weight assigned to labels.

A weighted objective scales each sample/class contribution; reduction semantics vary.

Emphasizes selected classes but can change calibration and false alarms.

Interactions: sampling; loss denominator; threshold.

Do not silently apply both resampling and weighting as if they were one treatment.

reading.title: Logistic regression and classification
reading.definition: Classification predicts a category rather than a numerical measurement. Binary logistic regression first calculates a weighted score, then maps it to a probability for one of two classes. A separate decision threshold turns that probability into a yes/no prediction.
reading.example: Features [1, 2] and weights [0.2, 0.1] give score 0.4 and positive-class probability about 0.60. A threshold of 0.5 predicts positive; a threshold of 0.7 predicts negative, without changing the model.
reading.connection: Linear regression in the linear regression lesson predicts a number directly. Logistic regression adds a probability mapping and a classification loss. The threshold controls the action, while the loss can be used to fit the probabilities.

steps.title: Calculate the raw score
steps.prose: Multiply each feature by its learned weight, add the contributions and include a bias if the model has one. The raw score can be any real number; it is not yet a probability.
steps.terms: A logit is a raw score before the logistic probability mapping. The bias is a learned constant added to the weighted sum.
steps.next: Sigmoid converts this score into a binary-class probability.

steps.title: Convert score to probability
steps.prose: The sigmoid function maps the score to a value between zero and one. A score of zero maps to 0.5; larger positive scores favour the positive class. This estimated probability is useful, but it still needs checking for calibration.
steps.terms: Sigmoid is the function 1/(1 + exp(−z)). Its input z is the score, not a class label.
steps.next: This probability has two uses: make a thresholded decision, or score it against a known label during training.

steps.title: Choose a class using a threshold
steps.prose: Predict positive if the estimated probability is at least the chosen cutoff. Moving the cutoff changes which examples are called positive, not the fitted weights or their probabilities. Different error costs can justify different cutoffs.
steps.terms: The threshold is a decision setting chosen on validation data, not a learned weight.
steps.next: The loss section uses the probability directly; it is not calculated from this thresholded label.

steps.title: Training loss for a known label
steps.prose: Binary cross-entropy measures how much probability the model assigned to the observed answer. For a positive label it is −log(p); for a negative label it is −log(1−p). Changing only the decision threshold therefore leaves this loss unchanged.
steps.terms: Cross-entropy is a probabilistic training loss. Softmax extends the probability mapping to mutually exclusive classes, as explained in the deeper notes.
steps.next: The loss and optimization lesson shows gradient updates; Evaluation metrics compares the decisions after fitting.

links: Sigmoid converts the raw score into a positive-class probability.
Compare the probability with a chosen threshold to make a class decision.
Compare the probability directly with the known label to calculate cross-entropy.

reading.lesson_markdown:
A class decision is discrete, but training benefits from a smooth score. Binary logistic regression computes $s=w^Tx+b$ and maps it to a probability with $p=1/(1+e^{-s})$. At score 0, probability is 0.5; at score 2 it is about 0.881. The resulting decision boundary is still linear in the supplied features.

There are two branches after this probability. To make a decision, compare it with a chosen threshold. To train against a known label, calculate binary cross-entropy: $-y\ln p-(1-y)\ln(1-p)$. If the label is 1, changing p from 0.5 to 0.9 reduces the loss from about 0.693 to 0.105. Thresholding first would throw away this distinction.

A low threshold may catch more positives while increasing false alarms. Select it using validation data and relevant costs, not because 0.5 is universally right. Training weights and selecting a decision threshold solve different problems.

For one of K mutually exclusive classes, softmax normalises K logits into a categorical distribution. Independent sigmoid outputs instead allow multiple labels at once. Use the formulation matching the target, then check both discrimination and probability quality.

Sources: [SLP: logistic regression](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/4.pdf), [scikit-learn: logistic regression](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/linear_model.html#logistic-regression).

# ML05. Regularization and model selection

A model can fit its training examples closely but perform poorly on new data. Regularization discourages some kinds of overly flexible fit, for example by penalizing large coefficients. Model selection uses validation data to choose how much regularization or complexity to allow.

The example holds one candidate weight at 3 and its data loss at 0.4. Changing lambda shows how the L2 penalty contributes to the objective. It does not refit the candidate, so it is not evidence that one lambda trains a better model.

The linear regression lesson showed a coefficient actually changing when ridge strength changes. Here we separate the data-loss term, penalty term and validation choice so they are not confused.

[course map](../COURSE_MAP.md). Required background: ML04.

## 1. Why complexity can overfit

**Key terms.** **Bias** is systematic limitation; **variance** is sensitivity to the sampled training data; **regularization** restricts fitting; a **hyperparameter** is selected rather than learned by the inner fit. **Cross-validation** repeats fitting on held-out folds.

**Process.** Define a small configuration search, fit each complete pipeline on training folds and compare validation scores. Choose one recipe, refit on the allowed training data and evaluate the untouched final test only after selection.

A complex model can fit noise; too much shrinkage can erase useful signal. **L2** penalizes a sum of squared coefficients; **L1** penalizes their absolute magnitudes and can induce zeros; **elastic net** mixes both. Their effects depend on feature scaling and objective normalization. A fitted coefficient is a model parameter; the penalty strength is a hyperparameter. Do not equate similarly named alpha, lambda and C across libraries.

### Learning curves and validation curves

A learning curve asks whether more training data helps. Fit the same procedure on different training sizes, such as 100, 500 and 1,000 cases, and evaluate on a fixed held-out population. Keep the evaluation data outside each fit. A large gap between training and validation performance can suggest sensitivity to the available training data; it is not a complete diagnosis on its own.

A validation curve asks whether a setting helps at a fixed data size. For example, fit trees at depths 1, 3 and 8 and compare training and validation scores. Improving training fit while validation worsens suggests that the added complexity is not helping on these held-out cases. Neither curve is a universal rule about all deep networks.

Nested cross-validation uses an inner search to choose settings and an outer evaluation to test that selection procedure when no separate final holdout is available. The course's local comparison page does not run an automatic nested search.

## 2. A worked calculation

**Symbols and assumptions.** w contains coefficients, lambda is nonnegative penalty strength and L_data is a declared average loss. The simple objective here is L_data+lambda||w||²/2; it is not a claim about every library's exact scaling.

For a one-coefficient penalty with w=3 and lambda=0.2, added loss is 0.2×9/2=0.9 and added gradient is lambda×w=0.6. A polynomial expansion of d inputs through degree 2, including constant and cross terms, has (d+2)(d+1)/2 features: for d=3, that is 10, before any policy to drop the constant.

The numbers above are illustrative calculations, not measured benchmark results.

## 3. Ways to control model complexity

Limit polynomial degree, increase penalty, use early stopping or collect more independent data. These interventions act differently. A tree's depth limit is not numerically comparable to ridge lambda. Compare validation quality and cost rather than setting both controls to the same number.

The related settings are defined below this lesson in Model Lab, including their mathematical meaning, expected effects and interactions. The training lab exposes only controls that change an implemented operation; the broader [parameter catalogue](../metadata/parameters.json) also describes theory-only options.

## 4. Example: tune inside the training folds

On Wine Quality, compare linear and degree-2 ridge models using fixed inner folds and matched search counts. If a fitted scaler or feature selector saw outer test rows, the score is not a valid nested comparison.

**Check.** You test 100 settings and report the best test score. Why is a narrow bootstrap interval around that score insufficient?

**Answer.** The test set was used for model selection; uncertainty from resampling its cases does not undo selection bias. Use a new independent assessment or a design that nests selection inside evaluation.

## 5. Why choosing the best result is itself learning

**Key terms.** Model selection chooses an algorithm or setting; estimation fits its weights. Nested cross-validation separates the outer evaluation from inner selection.

**Process.** Reserve a final test first. Within the remaining data, fit every preprocessing operation and candidate model inside each training fold. Use inner validation to choose a candidate, refit only on the permitted data, then evaluate once at the outer boundary.

Trying 100 settings gives 100 chances to exploit validation noise. The smallest observed error is therefore an optimistic estimate of the chosen procedure's future error. More folds do not repair leakage: a scaler fitted on all rows before cross-validation still sees validation values.

### A numerical regularization check

The following small problem shows why L1 can remove a feature entirely. Think of a as the coefficient preferred by the unpenalized fit and w as the coefficient we will choose after adding a penalty. The sign function preserves whether a is positive or negative; max(…,0) prevents the remaining magnitude going below zero.

For the one-coefficient objective ½(w−a)²+λ|w|, the solution is sign(a)·max(|a|−λ,0). If a=0.6 and λ=0.8, the fitted coefficient is zero; if a=2 it becomes 1.2. L1 creates exact zeros. L2 shrinkage for ½(w−a)²+λw²/2 instead gives w=a/(1+λ), usually nonzero.

The interface uses fixed development/test partitions, not an automatic nested search. Its comparison screen is a learning instrument; repeatedly selecting from the displayed test scores does not become a valid nested experiment.

## Sources

- [scikit-learn linear models](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html).
- [scikit-learn cross-validation](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/cross_validation.html).
- [An Introduction to Statistical Learning, author site](https://www.statlearning.com/).

reading.definition: A model can fit its training examples closely but perform poorly on new data. Regularization discourages some kinds of overly flexible fit, for example by penalizing large coefficients. Model selection uses validation data to choose how much regularization or complexity to allow.
reading.example: The example holds one candidate weight at 3 and its data loss at 0.4. Changing lambda shows how the L2 penalty contributes to the objective. It does not refit the candidate, so it is not evidence that one lambda trains a better model.
reading.connection: The linear regression lesson showed a coefficient actually changing when ridge strength changes. Here we separate the data-loss term, penalty term and validation choice so they are not confused.

steps.title: Error on training examples
steps.prose: The data-loss term measures how well a candidate predicts the training answers. A very flexible model may reduce this term by capturing noise or accidental patterns, not only reusable relationships.
steps.terms: Overfitting means training performance is better than the model's performance on relevant unseen examples.
steps.next: Regularization adds a separate cost for selected properties of the fitted model.

steps.title: Cost for large coefficients
steps.prose: An L2 penalty adds lambda times the sum of squared coefficients. This makes large weights more expensive in the fitting objective. The control changes that cost while holding this demonstration's candidate weight fixed.
steps.terms: L2 means squared coefficient magnitude. L1 instead uses absolute magnitude and can produce exact zero coefficients.
steps.next: Add the penalty to the data loss to obtain the objective that fitting would minimize.

steps.title: The combined fitting objective
steps.prose: Training balances two costs: prediction error and coefficient magnitude. With a different penalty, a real fit usually chooses different coefficients. Comparing objective values across different lambdas is not itself a validation-based model comparison.
steps.terms: An objective is the quantity an optimizer minimizes; it is not necessarily the metric used to judge the final system.
steps.next: To choose lambda, actually fit candidates and compare their validation performance.

steps.title: Choose complexity using validation
steps.prose: Cross-validation repeatedly fits a full pipeline on part of the development data and scores it on the held-out part. Average these results to choose a setting, then follow the declared refitting and final-test procedure.
steps.terms: A fold is one partition in cross-validation. Regularization, tree depth and early stopping are different ways to control complexity.
steps.next: Subsequent method lessons use validation to choose their own settings; no single setting is best for every dataset.

reading.lesson_markdown:
A flexible model can fit accidental details of a sample. Regularisation restricts the fit so those details have less influence. Ridge penalises squared coefficient size; lasso penalises absolute size and can set coefficients exactly to zero; elastic net combines both. The penalty strength is a choice about fit, not an extra observation.

Suppose two nearly duplicate features receive large opposite coefficients. Their training predictions can look sensible while small input changes cause instability. Ridge discourages such large coefficients. Increasing its strength generally sacrifices some training fit; held-out performance can improve or worsen, so validation must decide.

Compare a training curve with a validation curve. Poor performance on both can suggest an unsuitable representation, too much restriction, or a fitting bug. A large training–validation gap suggests sensitivity to the fitted sample. These are diagnostic patterns, not infallible labels.

Select penalty, depth, and model family inside the validation procedure. Report the selected configuration and the untouched evaluation. Trying many settings also consumes statistical evidence: a winning validation score is partly a result of selection. Scaling matters because a penalty on coefficients depends on feature units.

Sources: [scikit-learn: ridge, lasso and elastic net](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/linear_model.html#ridge-regression-and-classification), [D2L: weight decay](https://d2l.ai/chapter_linear-regression/weight-decay.html).

/api/learning/document/ML06.goal: Nearest-neighbour prediction compares a new example with stored training examples and uses the answers of the closest ones. It is a local rule: the prediction depends on nearby cases rather than one fitted line. A support vector machine, or SVM, is a different method that learns a separating boundary with a margin.

# ML06. Nearest neighbours, kernels and SVMs

Nearest-neighbour prediction compares a new example with stored training examples and uses the answers of the closest ones. It is a local rule: the prediction depends on nearby cases rather than one fitted line. A support vector machine, or SVM, is a different method that learns a separating boundary with a margin.

For nearest neighbours we classify query x = 3 using labelled points at 0, 1, 2, 4 and 5. The control changes how many neighbours vote. A separate final section explains how a kernel-based SVM differs; it is not a later stage of nearest-neighbour prediction.

Feature scaling from the features and preprocessing lesson affects distances. This lesson compares two uses of similarity while keeping their prediction mechanisms distinct.

[course map](../COURSE_MAP.md). Required background: ML05.

## 1. Local voting versus margin classification

**Key terms.** **k-NN** predicts from nearby training examples; a **distance metric** defines nearby; a **support vector** constrains a margin solution; a **kernel** calculates an implicit feature similarity. **Hinge loss** penalizes insufficient signed margin.

**Process.** For k-NN, store training representations, measure query distances and aggregate neighbours. For an SVM, fit a margin-based decision function first, then apply it to queries. Scaling belongs before both fitting and distance/kernel computation.

Small k can follow local noise; larger k smooths decisions and can miss small classes. Distance weighting gives close neighbours more influence. In high dimensions, irrelevant coordinates and concentrated distances can make neighbourhoods less useful.

An RBF kernel can represent nonlinear boundaries without constructing all transformed features explicitly. Its gamma controls locality; C controls the trade-off between fitting violations and regularization under the estimator's objective. Kernel SVM training/storage can become expensive as the number of cases grows. An explicit-feature linear classifier is often the stronger operational baseline for sparse large text.

## 2. A worked calculation

**Symbols and assumptions.** For classification labels y∈{−1,+1}, f(x) is a real decision score. Hinge loss is max(0,1−y f(x)). The RBF kernel uses gamma≥0 and squared Euclidean distance.

With neighbour labels [A,A,B], an unweighted k=3 vote selects A. At distances [2,2,0.2], inverse-distance weights are [0.5,0.5,5], so B wins. For a positive example with f(x)=0.3, hinge loss is 0.7. For two points at squared distance 4 and gamma=0.5, RBF similarity is exp(−2)≈0.1353.

The numbers above are illustrative calculations, not measured benchmark results.

## 3. Choosing k, kernel and regularization

A linear kernel tests whether nonlinear geometry is needed. Increasing gamma and C together can create a highly local, overfit boundary; neither guarantees improvement. k-NN requires retained training data at prediction, while a linear model summarizes it in weights.

The related settings are defined below this lesson in Model Lab, including their mathematical meaning, expected effects and interactions. The training lab exposes only controls that change an implemented operation; the broader [parameter catalogue](../metadata/parameters.json) also describes theory-only options.

## 4. Example: compare nearest neighbours and SVMs

Compare standardized k-NN, linear SVM and RBF SVM on the same digits split with equal numbers of search candidates. Record prediction latency and fit time as well as macro-F1. Do not rank their speed using unmeasured complexity slogans.

**Check.** A feature measured in thousands dominates one measured in fractions. Can changing k alone repair this geometry?

**Answer.** Not reliably. Inspect units and fit a justified scaler on training data, then retune the distance method within the same validation design.

## 5. Margin, kernel and regularization work together

**Key terms.** A margin measures a labelled example's signed distance-related score. Hinge loss penalizes examples whose signed score is below one. A support vector influences the fitted margin boundary.

**Process.** Fit a preprocessing transform on training data, compute linear or kernel similarities and solve the regularized margin objective. A new row uses that same transform and similarities to the stored support vectors.

The equation balances two costs. The first term discourages large weights; the second adds a penalty whenever a training example is wrong or not far enough on the correct side of the boundary. The chosen constant C controls how much these violations count. Inputs are x_i, labels y_i are −1 or +1, w are learned weights and b is the bias.

\[
\min_{w,b}\ \frac12\|w\|^2+C\sum_i\max(0,1-y_i(w^\top x_i+b)).
\]

This binary formulation uses labels −1 and +1 and an unaveraged loss sum. Multiclass SVC uses a reduction to binary problems. C is not λ: its numerical meaning changes with the loss normalization and number of training rows.

### A similarity calculation

With RBF gamma=0.5, distance squared 2 gives similarity exp(−1)≈0.368. If one unscaled feature makes distance squared 200, similarity is exp(−100), effectively zero. Changing feature units can therefore overwhelm kernel behaviour before C has any useful interpretation.

In the lab, gamma affects RBF only and is disabled for a linear kernel. SVC does not automatically supply calibrated probabilities here, so the results show class metrics without inventing log loss or a confidence calibration score.

## Sources

- [scikit-learn nearest neighbours](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/neighbors.html).
- [scikit-learn SVM](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/svm.html).

steps.title: Measure distances to training cases
steps.prose: Compare the query with each training point using a chosen distance. With one numerical feature, absolute distance is enough. In several dimensions, a feature measured in large units can dominate unless scaling and distance choice are appropriate.
steps.terms: A neighbour is a nearby stored training example under the selected distance measure.
steps.next: Order the cases by distance, using a stated rule when distances tie.

steps.title: Select the k nearest cases
steps.prose: Keep the k closest training examples. Small k is very local and can react strongly to noise; larger k averages a wider neighbourhood. k is the number of neighbours, not the number of classes.
steps.terms: k is a chosen hyperparameter. A tie-breaking rule makes equal-distance choices reproducible.
steps.next: Use the selected cases' labels to form a vote.

steps.title: Vote on the class
steps.prose: Count positive labels among the selected neighbours. Their fraction is a local estimate, and a majority vote gives the class for these odd k choices. Distance-weighted voting would instead give closer cases more influence.
steps.terms: A vote fraction is not automatically a calibrated probability for the wider population.
steps.next: The next section is a comparison with another method, not a computation using this vote.

steps.title: A different method: SVM and kernels
steps.prose: An SVM learns a boundary that balances a wide margin against training violations. A kernel supplies pairwise similarities corresponding to an implicit feature space, which can support a nonlinear boundary. An RBF kernel gives high similarity to close points, but that value is not a class probability.
steps.terms: Margin is separation from the decision boundary; the RBF parameter gamma controls how quickly similarity falls with distance.
steps.next: The additional notes compare linear and kernel SVMs, scaling, regularization and prediction cost.
steps.node: A different method: SVM and kernels

reading.lesson_markdown:
Nearest-neighbour prediction asks which stored training cases resemble the new input. The similarity definition is part of the model. For a one-dimensional point 2.2 and training locations 1, 2, and 5, absolute distances are 1.2, 0.2, and 2.8. With k=1 the label at 2 decides; with k=3 all three labels vote. Increasing k smooths decisions but may mix distinct groups.

Euclidean distance sums squared numerical differences across features. Changing metres to millimetres multiplies a length difference by 1,000 and its squared contribution by a million. Training-fitted scaling can therefore change neighbours and predictions. It does not guarantee a higher score. Nearest-neighbour methods retain training examples and can be expensive at prediction time.

An **SVM** takes a different route: learn a separating decision surface with a margin. Support vectors are cases constraining this surface. A soft-margin penalty permits violations; the C parameter trades these penalties against the margin objective. A kernel computes a permitted inner-product similarity in an implicit feature space, enabling nonlinear boundaries. It is not an arbitrary similarity function with no mathematical restrictions.

Both methods depend on representation and scale, but “find nearby examples” and “fit a margin” are different learning rules. The worked view compares their mechanics rather than pretending one flows into the other.

Sources: [scikit-learn: nearest neighbours](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/neighbors.html), [scikit-learn: support vector machines](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/svm.html).

# ML07. Naive Bayes classification

Naive Bayes predicts a class by combining how common the class is with how likely the observed features are within that class. For example, a word can be more common in spam than ordinary email. With several features, the model simplifies the calculation by treating them as independent once the class is known; that is the 'naive' assumption.

We use eight training cases: four positive and four negative. A binary feature is present in three positive cases but only one negative case. We will use this evidence to calculate a class probability for a new case with that feature.

Unlike logistic regression, which directly fits a class probability from features, Naive Bayes models feature probabilities within each class. Both can classify; they make different modelling assumptions.

[course map](../COURSE_MAP.md). Required background: ML04.

## 1. Feature distributions and independence assumptions

**Key terms.** A **generative classifier** models class priors and feature distributions given class; a **discriminative classifier** models the class decision directly. **Naive Bayes** assumes conditional feature independence. **Covariance** describes joint feature variation. **Linear/quadratic discriminant analysis (LDA/QDA)** use Gaussian class models with shared/separate covariances.

**Process.** Estimate class priors and class-conditional feature statistics from training data. Score a new example under each class, combine with priors, normalize if probabilities are needed and choose a label or threshold.

The word generative here describes a statistical factorization; it does not mean a modern text-generation assistant. Multinomial naive Bayes suits nonnegative count-like features. Gaussian naive Bayes uses a per-feature Gaussian model. Bernoulli naive Bayes models presence/absence. Feature representation and likelihood must agree.

Conditional independence means features are independent given the class, not independent in all data. Repeated correlated words can make predicted confidence too strong. Smoothing avoids impossible unseen-event probabilities, but an arbitrary large smoothing value can wash out useful evidence. LDA shares covariance across classes; QDA estimates more flexible class-specific covariance and needs more data or regularization.

## 2. A worked calculation

**Symbols and assumptions.** P(c) is class prior and P(x_j|c) is a feature likelihood. The naive Bayes score is P(c) times the product of feature likelihoods. The normalization sums scores over classes.

For two classes spam/ham with priors 0.2/0.8, suppose two observed binary features have likelihoods [0.6,0.5] under spam and [0.1,0.2] under ham. Scores are 0.2×0.6×0.5=0.06 and 0.8×0.1×0.2=0.016. Normalized spam probability is 0.06/0.076≈0.7895 under these assumptions. This is not a calibrated guarantee.

The numbers above are illustrative calculations, not measured benchmark results.

## 3. Naive Bayes, LDA and QDA

Compare a naive Bayes model with logistic regression under the same vocabulary/split, or LDA with QDA on scaled numeric data. QDA can express curved boundaries but estimates more covariance terms. A simple model's small-data advantage is a hypothesis to measure, not a law.

The related settings are defined below this lesson in Model Lab, including their mathematical meaning, expected effects and interactions. The training lab exposes only controls that change an implemented operation; the broader [parameter catalogue](../metadata/parameters.json) also describes theory-only options.

## 4. Example: classification versus probability quality

Wine gives a bounded numeric comparison. SMS is only a conditional future dataset: audit privacy and duplicate groups before displaying examples. No real contact details should appear in a public screenshot or unrestricted log.

**Check.** Why can naive Bayes classify accurately while its probability estimates are poor?

**Answer.** Its independence and likelihood assumptions can preserve class ordering while overstating combined evidence. Evaluate calibration separately from classification accuracy.

## 5. Bayesian updating: keep a distribution over a probability

Bayesian updating combines an initial model of uncertainty with observed evidence. A **prior** describes an unknown parameter before these observations; a **likelihood** describes how observations arise for a proposed parameter; a **posterior** is the updated distribution. This differs from using Bayes' rule only to classify one row, as in the core Naive Bayes example.

Suppose a binary trial has one unknown success probability p. Assume trials are independent conditional on this fixed p. A Beta distribution is a convenient prior because updating it with successes and failures gives another Beta distribution. Its two positive parameters control the prior's shape; they are not observed data counts.

\[
p\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a,b),\qquad p\mid D\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a+s,b+f).
\]

Here s and f count observed successes and failures. Start with Beta(2,2), then observe three successes and one failure. The posterior is Beta(5,3). Its mean, 5/8=0.625, is also the model's predictive success probability for the next trial. The empirical success fraction is 3/4=0.75; these differ because the posterior still incorporates the prior. The posterior remains a distribution, not certainty that p equals 0.625.

Follow the information: specify the trial and prior → observe permitted training outcomes → update both parameters → calculate a predictive probability or a credible interval. A credible interval describes posterior uncertainty under the model. It is not the same construction as the bootstrap interval introduced in the statistics lesson.

**Practice.** Starting from Beta(1,1), observe two successes and no failures. What is the next-trial success probability? **Answer.** Beta(3,1) gives 3/4, not certainty of success. More observations narrow uncertainty only when the assumed fixed-probability model is appropriate. Repeated observations from correlated users or a changing environment require reconsidering that model.

Continue to graphical models below to see how several uncertain quantities can be connected. [Conjugate updating reference](https://stanford.edu/~ashlearn/RLForFinanceBook/appendix7.pdf).

## 6. Probabilistic graphical models: factor a joint distribution

A probabilistic graphical model expresses how a joint distribution can be assembled from smaller distributions. Its nodes represent **random variables**, unlike the data entities in the graph-neural-network lesson. A directed acyclic graph specifies one factorization; its arrows do not, by themselves, justify causal claims.

Consider hidden topic Z and two observed word indicators X and Y. The model assumes the indicators are independent once Z is known:

\[
p(z,x,y)=p(z)p(x\mid z)p(y\mid z).
\]

This is the same conditional-independence pattern underlying a Naive Bayes classifier, but the topic here is hidden. It is not a statement that words are independent in the complete population. Suppose P(Z=1)=0.5, and the probabilities of X=1 and Y=1 are 0.8 and 0.6 in topic 1, versus 0.2 and 0.1 in topic 0. After observing both words, the two unnormalized weights are 0.5×0.8×0.6=0.24 and 0.5×0.2×0.1=0.01. Normalizing gives P(Z=1|X=Y=1)=0.96.

**Inference** asks a probability query in a specified model, such as that posterior topic probability. **Learning** estimates model parameters from data. To obtain P(X,Y), sum the joint over hidden Z. In larger graphs, variable elimination reorders these sums and products to reuse intermediate factors; intermediate factor size can still make exact inference expensive. An undirected model instead specifies nonnegative factors with a global normalizer and needs its own independence interpretation.

**Practice.** If Y is unobserved, should its probability simply be set to zero? **Answer.** No. Sum over its possible values; because its conditional probabilities sum to one, the posterior topic query uses the remaining observed evidence. Missing is not the same event as Y=0.

The advanced uncertainty section in ML15 explains approximate inference when exact sums or integrals become impractical. [Graphical-model lecture](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~rsalakhu/10417/Lectures/Lecture_GM.pdf).

## Sources

- [scikit-learn naive Bayes](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/naive_bayes.html).
- [scikit-learn LDA/QDA](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/lda_qda.html).

**Process.** Estimate class priors and class-conditional feature statistics from training data. Score a new example under each class, combine with priors, normalize if probabilities are needed and choose a label or threshold.

The word generative here describes a statistical factorization; it does not mean a modern text-generation assistant. Multinomial naive Bayes suits nonnegative count-like features. Gaussian naive Bayes uses a per-feature Gaussian model. Bernoulli naive Bayes models presence/absence. Feature representation and likelihood must agree.

Conditional independence means features are independent given the class, not independent in all data. Repeated correlated words can make predicted confidence too strong. Smoothing avoids impossible unseen-event probabilities, but an arbitrary large smoothing value can wash out useful evidence. LDA shares covariance across classes; QDA estimates more flexible class-specific covariance and needs more data or regularization.

sections.title: A worked calculation
sections.markdown:
## 2. A worked calculation

**Symbols and assumptions.** P(c) is class prior and P(x_j|c) is a feature likelihood. The naive Bayes score is P(c) times the product of feature likelihoods. The normalization sums scores over classes.

For two classes spam/ham with priors 0.2/0.8, suppose two observed binary features have likelihoods [0.6,0.5] under spam and [0.1,0.2] under ham. Scores are 0.2×0.6×0.5=0.06 and 0.8×0.1×0.2=0.016. Normalized spam probability is 0.06/0.076≈0.7895 under these assumptions. This is not a calibrated guarantee.

The numbers above are illustrative calculations, not measured benchmark results.

sections.markdown:
## 4. Example: classification versus probability quality

Wine gives a bounded numeric comparison. SMS is only a conditional future dataset: audit privacy and duplicate groups before displaying examples. No real contact details should appear in a public screenshot or unrestricted log.

**Check.** Why can naive Bayes classify accurately while its probability estimates are poor?

**Answer.** Its independence and likelihood assumptions can preserve class ordering while overstating combined evidence. Evaluate calibration separately from classification accuracy.

sections.title: Bayesian updating: keep a distribution over a probability
sections.markdown:
## 5. Bayesian updating: keep a distribution over a probability

Bayesian updating combines an initial model of uncertainty with observed evidence. A **prior** describes an unknown parameter before these observations; a **likelihood** describes how observations arise for a proposed parameter; a **posterior** is the updated distribution. This differs from using Bayes' rule only to classify one row, as in the core Naive Bayes example.

Suppose a binary trial has one unknown success probability p. Assume trials are independent conditional on this fixed p. A Beta distribution is a convenient prior because updating it with successes and failures gives another Beta distribution. Its two positive parameters control the prior's shape; they are not observed data counts.

\[
p\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a,b),\qquad p\mid D\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a+s,b+f).
\]

Here s and f count observed successes and failures. Start with Beta(2,2), then observe three successes and one failure. The posterior is Beta(5,3). Its mean, 5/8=0.625, is also the model's predictive success probability for the next trial. The empirical success fraction is 3/4=0.75; these differ because the posterior still incorporates the prior. The posterior remains a distribution, not certainty that p equals 0.625.

Follow the information: specify the trial and prior → observe permitted training outcomes → update both parameters → calculate a predictive probability or a credible interval. A credible interval describes posterior uncertainty under the model. It is not the same construction as the bootstrap interval introduced in the statistics lesson.

**Practice.** Starting from Beta(1,1), observe two successes and no failures. What is the next-trial success probability? **Answer.** Beta(3,1) gives 3/4, not certainty of success. More observations narrow uncertainty only when the assumed fixed-probability model is appropriate. Repeated observations from correlated users or a changing environment require reconsidering that model.

Continue to graphical models below to see how several uncertain quantities can be connected. [Conjugate updating reference](https://stanford.edu/~ashlearn/RLForFinanceBook/appendix7.pdf).

sections.title: Probabilistic graphical models: factor a joint distribution
sections.markdown:
## 6. Probabilistic graphical models: factor a joint distribution

A probabilistic graphical model expresses how a joint distribution can be assembled from smaller distributions. Its nodes represent **random variables**, unlike the data entities in the graph-neural-network lesson. A directed acyclic graph specifies one factorization; its arrows do not, by themselves, justify causal claims.

Consider hidden topic Z and two observed word indicators X and Y. The model assumes the indicators are independent once Z is known:

\[
p(z,x,y)=p(z)p(x\mid z)p(y\mid z).
\]

This is the same conditional-independence pattern underlying a Naive Bayes classifier, but the topic here is hidden. It is not a statement that words are independent in the complete population. Suppose P(Z=1)=0.5, and the probabilities of X=1 and Y=1 are 0.8 and 0.6 in topic 1, versus 0.2 and 0.1 in topic 0. After observing both words, the two unnormalized weights are 0.5×0.8×0.6=0.24 and 0.5×0.2×0.1=0.01. Normalizing gives P(Z=1|X=Y=1)=0.96.

**Inference** asks a probability query in a specified model, such as that posterior topic probability. **Learning** estimates model parameters from data. To obtain P(X,Y), sum the joint over hidden Z. In larger graphs, variable elimination reorders these sums and products to reuse intermediate factors; intermediate factor size can still make exact inference expensive. An undirected model instead specifies nonnegative factors with a global normalizer and needs its own independence interpretation.

**Practice.** If Y is unobserved, should its probability simply be set to zero? **Answer.** No. Sum over its possible values; because its conditional probabilities sum to one, the posterior topic query uses the remaining observed evidence. Missing is not the same event as Y=0.

The advanced uncertainty section in ML15 explains approximate inference when exact sums or integrals become impractical. [Graphical-model lecture](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~rsalakhu/10417/Lectures/Lecture_GM.pdf).

notes.title: Settings: Count smoothing, Variance stabilizer
notes.markdown:
### Count smoothing

Adds positive pseudocounts to categorical/count likelihood estimates.

P(term|c)=(count+alpha)/(class_total+alpha×vocabulary).

Larger smoothing weakens rare-event evidence and avoids zero estimates.

Interactions: vocabulary size; count representation.

Do not apply a count likelihood to arbitrary negative standardized inputs.

### Variance stabilizer

Adds implementation-defined variance stabilization to Gaussian estimates.

A small positive quantity is added to estimated variances.

Can reduce division by tiny variance while changing fitted likelihoods.

Interactions: feature scale; small class sample counts.

It is not the same units/control as multinomial pseudocount smoothing.

reading.title: Naive Bayes classification
reading.definition: Naive Bayes predicts a class by combining how common the class is with how likely the observed features are within that class. For example, a word can be more common in spam than ordinary email. With several features, the model simplifies the calculation by treating them as independent once the class is known; that is the 'naive' assumption.
reading.example: We use eight training cases: four positive and four negative. A binary feature is present in three positive cases but only one negative case. We will use this evidence to calculate a class probability for a new case with that feature.
reading.connection: Unlike logistic regression, which directly fits a class probability from features, Naive Bayes models feature probabilities within each class. Both can classify; they make different modelling assumptions.

steps.title: Class frequencies: the priors
steps.prose: Count the classes before looking at the new case's feature. Here each class has four of eight training cases, giving equal starting probabilities. In another population, the class frequencies could be different.
steps.terms: A prior is the class probability before considering the new example's feature.
steps.next: Combine each prior with that class's feature likelihood after calculating the likelihood separately.

steps.title: Feature probabilities within classes
steps.prose: Estimate how often the observed feature occurs inside each class. Additive smoothing adds alpha to each possible feature count, reducing the chance that an unseen training combination receives probability zero. The denominator must include the added count for both feature values.
steps.terms: A likelihood is the probability of the observed feature given a class. Alpha is a smoothing setting.
steps.next: The class prior and this likelihood are separate inputs to the multiplication step.

steps.title: Multiply each prior by its likelihood
steps.prose: A class gets a larger unnormalized score when it is common and when the observed feature is likely within that class. Multiply those two factors separately for positive and negative. With several features, Naive Bayes multiplies their likelihood terms under its simplifying assumption.
steps.terms: An unnormalized score has not yet been divided so the class probabilities add to one.
steps.next: Add the two scores and divide each by their total.

steps.title: Normalize into class probabilities
steps.prose: Dividing each class score by the total produces a posterior distribution for the new case under this model. The positive probability can then be thresholded to choose a class. Correlated features can make Naive Bayes overconfident because the evidence may be counted more than once.
steps.terms: A posterior is the class probability after considering the observed evidence.
steps.next: Compare this model with logistic regression under the same data split; probability calibration needs its own evaluation.

links: The prior for each class is one factor in its class score.
The feature likelihood for each class is the other factor in its class score.
Divide each class score by the sum of all class scores.

reading.lesson_markdown:
Naive Bayes combines how common a class is with how likely the observed features are within that class. Its simplification is **conditional independence**: once the class is specified, the feature likelihood factors into separate contributions. Features need not be independent in the population. The assumption is often imperfect, especially for neighbouring words.

Consider 20 messages, ten spam and ten non-spam. “Prize” appears in eight spam and one non-spam message. Using only its presence as a binary feature, the two unnormalised class scores are $(10/20)(8/10)=0.4$ and $(10/20)(1/10)=0.05$. Divide each by their sum. The spam posterior is $0.4/0.45=8/9\approx0.889$, not 0.8. The larger score chooses a class; normalisation gives a probability distribution under the model.

With many features, log likelihoods avoid underflow from multiplying tiny numbers. Smoothing prevents an unseen training count from forcing an entire class score to zero, but requires a declared finite feature/vocabulary model.

Bernoulli naive Bayes models feature presence and absence. Multinomial naive Bayes models count contributions. Gaussian naive Bayes models continuous feature densities within classes; this is the variant available for numerical data in Model Lab. These are not interchangeable likelihoods, and a strong classifier can still have poorly calibrated probabilities.

Sources: [scikit-learn: naive Bayes](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/naive_bayes.html), [SLP: naive Bayes appendix](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/B.pdf).

/api/learning/document/ML08.markdown:
# ML08. Decision trees and random forests

A decision tree predicts by asking feature questions, such as whether a measurement is below a cutoff. Each answer sends an example down one branch until a leaf returns a prediction. A random forest trains many varied trees and combines their predictions, making the result less dependent on one particular tree.

The four training examples have feature values [1, 2, 3, 4] and labels [0, 0, 1, 1]. Change the cutoff to see which groups it creates and how mixed their labels are.

This diagram evaluates a candidate training split. Its two branches meet only to calculate split quality; a prediction for one new case would follow one branch, not average the two leaves. The forest note explains how multiple trees are combined.

[course map](../COURSE_MAP.md). Required background: ML05.

## 1. How trees differ from random forests

**Key terms.** A **decision tree** partitions features with tests; a **leaf** makes a prediction; **impurity** measures label mixing. **Bagging** fits models on resampled data; a **random forest** adds feature randomness to many trees.

**Process.** At each tree node, evaluate candidate splits using training labels, choose a permitted gain and repeat until stopping rules apply. Predict by following one path to a leaf; a forest combines the predictions of many fitted trees.

A deep tree can memorize small leaves and react strongly to training changes. Minimum leaf size, depth and pruning restrict this. Numeric scaling generally preserves order-based splits, unlike distance methods. Category encoding still matters: an arbitrary ordinal code may impose an unhelpful partition ordering.

A forest averages less-correlated errors. More trees can reduce Monte Carlo variation but do not create new independent training data. Out-of-bag observations can supply an internal estimate when bootstrap sampling is used; tuning repeatedly against that estimate still involves selection. Impurity-based feature importance can favour high-cardinality variables, and correlated features complicate interpretation.

## 2. A worked calculation

**Symbols and assumptions.** p_c is a node's class proportion, N is its sample count and G=1−Σp_c² is Gini impurity. Split gain is parent Gini minus the child-size-weighted Gini average.

A parent has 4 positives and 4 negatives, so G=0.5. Split into two four-case children with label counts 3/1 and 1/3. Each child has G=1−0.75²−0.25²=0.375. Weighted child impurity is 0.375 and gain is 0.125. A completely pure split would have larger training gain, but may depend on a leaked feature.

The numbers above are illustrative calculations, not measured benchmark results.

## 3. Tree depth, leaf size and forest size

Increase leaf size to reduce highly local fitting; cap depth or prune to restrict partitions. More forest trees chiefly change averaging cost/variation; increasing features per split changes tree correlation and strength. Compare a single constrained tree with the forest before attributing a gain to every ingredient.

The related settings are defined below this lesson in Model Lab, including their mathematical meaning, expected effects and interactions. The training lab exposes only controls that change an implemented operation; the broader [parameter catalogue](../metadata/parameters.json) also describes theory-only options.

## 4. Example: feature importance is not causality

On Wine Quality, inspect residuals and prediction stability across seeds. Do not identify an input as a causal driver just because it received high importance. Held-out permutation importance is another predictive diagnostic, with its own correlation caveats.

**Check.** Can growing 1,000 trees fix a target column accidentally included in X?

**Answer.** No. It can make the leaked result more stable. Remove forbidden features and rebuild a clean split/pipeline before comparing algorithms.

## Sources

- [scikit-learn ensembles](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/ensemble.html).
- [An Introduction to Statistical Learning, author site](https://www.statlearning.com/).

reading.lesson_markdown:
A decision tree asks a sequence of feature questions, such as whether a measurement is below a cutoff. Each split sends examples to smaller groups. A leaf stores a prediction based on the training labels that reached it. The model learns both the questions and their ordering.

For a group with half class A and half class B, Gini impurity is $1-(0.5^2+0.5^2)=0.5$. A split producing two pure groups has weighted child impurity 0. A pure but tiny leaf can fit noise, so maximum depth and minimum leaf size control how detailed the partition becomes. A greedy split is locally preferred; it is not guaranteed to produce the globally best tree.

A random forest fits many trees using resampled training cases and random feature subsets. Averaging reduces instability most effectively when trees do not make identical errors. This is why randomness helps an ensemble rather than merely making its individual trees stronger. More trees reduce Monte Carlo variability at increased cost; they do not fix shared bias or leakage.

Tree feature importance measures a particular use within a fitted model. Correlated features can share or distort this importance. It is not a causal attribution. Compare held-out performance, stability, and interpretation requirements before choosing one tree or a forest.

Sources: [scikit-learn: decision trees](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/tree.html), [scikit-learn: random forests](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/ensemble.html#forest).

# ML09. Gradient boosting

Gradient boosting builds a predictor in stages. Each new small model tries to correct errors made by the current combined model. For squared-error regression, the correction can be trained on the remaining differences between targets and predictions. This differs from a random forest, whose trees are trained without sequentially correcting a running prediction.

One example has target 3 and current prediction 1, leaving residual 2. We assume a small correction model returns 2 at this point. The learning-rate control changes how much of that correction is added; this demonstration does not fit the correction model.

A forest combines varied trees; boosting combines a sequence of corrections. Smaller corrections often need more stages, so learning rate and stage count should be considered together.

[course map](../COURSE_MAP.md). Required background: ML08.

## 1. How ensemble methods combine models

**Key terms.** **Boosting** adds models sequentially to improve an objective; a **weak learner** is one component; **shrinkage** scales its contribution. **Voting** combines predictions; **stacking** learns a combining model from out-of-fold predictions.

**Process.** Fit an initial prediction, calculate how current predictions fail, fit another learner to an appropriate correction signal and add a scaled contribution. Select the stopping point on development data, then assess the complete fitted ensemble.

For squared loss, fitting residuals gives an intuitive boosting example. Other losses use their own gradients and sometimes curvature; do not describe all boosting as literally predicting numeric residuals. Histogram methods bin feature values to reduce split-search cost. Missing-value handling, categorical support and constraints vary by implementation.

Random forests fit randomized trees largely independently; boosting uses a sequence whose later models depend on current errors. More boosting rounds can overfit or improve depending on rate and regularization. A small learning rate with many rounds is not the same computational budget as a large rate with few rounds.

## 2. A worked calculation

**Symbols and assumptions.** F_m is the ensemble after round m; h_m is a fitted correction; eta is shrinkage. The additive update is F_m(x)=F_(m−1)(x)+eta h_m(x).

For targets [3,7] and current predictions [2,5], residuals are [1,2]. Suppose a fitted correction predicts [1,2] and eta=0.1. New predictions are [2.1,5.2]; mean squared error drops from (1²+2²)/2=2.5 to (0.9²+1.8²)/2=2.025. This arithmetic assumes that particular correction; it is not a claim that every round helps validation.

The numbers above are illustrative calculations, not measured benchmark results.

## 3. Boosting settings and stacking

Control rounds together with learning rate, leaf count/depth, minimum leaf size and optional row subsampling. For stacking, train the combiner on predictions from base models that did not train on those same rows. Equal-weight averaging is a useful baseline before learning a complicated combiner.

The related settings are defined below this lesson in Model Lab, including their mathematical meaning, expected effects and interactions. The training lab exposes only controls that change an implemented operation; the broader [parameter catalogue](../metadata/parameters.json) also describes theory-only options.

## 4. Example: compare strong tabular baselines

Compare ridge, random forest and histogram gradient boosting on Wine Quality using the same splits and search budget. Save chosen configurations, not only a winner's score. If the boosted model wins tabular data, the later neural comparison must keep that baseline.

**Check.** Why is training a stacker on in-sample predictions optimistic?

**Answer.** Its inputs are unrealistically easy because base learners already saw those labels. Generate out-of-fold training predictions for the combiner; keep the final test separate.

## 5. A boosting update, not just a collection of trees

**Key terms.** A residual is observed minus predicted value in this squared-error example. A negative gradient is the correction direction for the chosen loss. Shrinkage scales the added learner.

**Process.** Start with a simple prediction. Compute the current loss gradient, fit a shallow learner to the correction and add a scaled version to the running prediction. Repeat, checking generalization rather than only reducing training loss.

For targets [1,3] and initial prediction [2,2], residuals are [−1,+1]. A tree reproducing these residuals, added at rate 0.1, produces [1.9,2.1]. Mean squared error falls from 1 to 0.81. This example is a squared-loss gradient step; logistic boosting uses a different gradient and second-order variants also use curvature.

### Distinguish the ensemble mechanisms

Bagging fits randomized models largely independently and averages them. Boosting is sequential. Stacking fits a combiner on out-of-fold base-model predictions; training that combiner on each model's in-sample predictions is a common leakage route.

The executable histogram booster uses a fixed round budget and disables its automatic internal early stopping. A smaller boosting rate may need more rounds; changing both is a budget-aware system comparison, not a one-variable ablation.

## Sources

- [scikit-learn ensembles](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/ensemble.html).
- [scikit-learn cross-validation](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/cross_validation.html).

steps.title: Current prediction and residual
steps.prose: Start from the ensemble's current prediction. Subtract it from the known target to obtain the remaining error. Across a real training set this produces a correction target for every case, not just this one number.

steps.next: Fit a new small model to these residuals, or to the appropriate loss gradients for another objective.

steps.title: A small correction model
steps.prose: For half squared error, the negative derivative with respect to a prediction equals its residual. A small model tries to predict those correction values. Here its output is assumed to be 2 so we can focus on how the ensemble update works.
steps.terms: A weak learner is the small model added at a stage. The factor one-half simplifies derivatives and does not change the squared-error minimizer.
steps.next: Scale the correction before adding it to the running prediction.

steps.title: Add a scaled correction
steps.prose: Multiply the correction by the learning rate and add it to the existing prediction. This is a change to the ensemble prediction, not a gradient update to a single linear coefficient. Later corrections must be based on the updated predictions.
steps.terms: Shrinkage is another name for scaling each new model's contribution by a learning rate.
steps.next: Compare the updated prediction with the target; recompute residuals before any later stage.

steps.title: Check the new error
steps.prose: Recalculate squared error for this same teaching point. An improvement here only shows that the assumed correction helped this point. In real boosting, validation performance and a stopping rule determine whether further stages are useful.
steps.terms: The displayed loss is ordinary squared error; the half-squared form above differs only by a constant factor.
steps.next: For another stage, start from the updated ensemble and recompute its residuals. Do not reuse a stale correction.

reading.lesson_markdown:
Boosting builds an additive model in stages. Rather than fitting many independent models and averaging them, it fits the next component to improve the current ensemble. For squared-error regression, the correction targets are residuals: target minus current prediction.

If the target is 10 and the current prediction is 6, the residual is 4. Suppose the next small tree predicts a correction of 3. With learning rate 0.1, the ensemble prediction becomes $6+0.1(3)=6.3$, not 9. The smaller step can make many-stage fitting less aggressive, at the cost of needing more stages. For other differentiable objectives, the corrections follow negative gradients rather than literal numerical residuals.

Tree depth controls the complexity of each correction. Learning rate, number of stages, and early stopping interact: more stages are not automatically better after validation performance stops improving. Histogram methods group feature values into bins to make split search more efficient; they are an implementation strategy, not a new definition of the target.

Compare boosting with a forest using the same split and meaningful budget. Forests primarily average variable fits; boosting sequentially corrects a fit. Neither method is universally preferable, and both can exploit a spurious feature.

Sources: [scikit-learn: gradient boosting](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/ensemble.html#gradient-boosting), [D2L: optimisation perspective](https://d2l.ai/chapter_optimization/optimization-intro.html).
