reading.example: The walkthrough uses a small supplied vocabulary and fixed weights: hidden width four, additive positions, LayerNorm and a 4→8→4 GELU feed-forward branch. Select a head, position or block to inspect the actual arithmetic. This is not the architecture or learned competence of the locally prepared pretrained model.
reading.connection: The data lesson produced aligned token inputs. This walkthrough follows their full computation while keeping tensor axes, residual paths and attention/vocabulary normalizations distinct. The deeper notes separately explain real grouped-query dimensions and other positional methods.

steps.title: Input token IDs and tensor axes
steps.prose: The input is a sequence of vocabulary identifiers, not vectors of word meanings yet. The example's authored IDs identify pieces such as How, to and predict. Adding a token changes the sequence axis, while the feature width is chosen separately.
steps.terms: B is batch size and T input length. An integer ID names a vocabulary row; a larger ID does not mean a larger or more meaningful token.
steps.next: Look up the corresponding row of the token embedding table for each input position.
steps.node: Input token IDs and tensor axes

steps.title: Token embedding lookup
steps.prose: Replace each input ID with its saved feature vector. Two occurrences of one ID start from the same embedding row before position and context are incorporated. This lookup preserves token order and creates the hidden feature axis.
steps.terms: D denotes hidden width, here four. An embedding is a computed lookup of learned parameters, not a probability distribution over possible answers.
steps.next: Add this teaching decoder's positional vectors to make location available to later calculations.

steps.title: Additive position information
steps.prose: Add corresponding entries of the token and position vectors. The shape stays the same, but the same token at another position can now have different input features. These fixed additive vectors are one convention, not how every modern decoder represents position.
steps.terms: Position is sequence location. RoPE instead transforms query/key coordinates inside attention and must not be confused with this embedding addition.
steps.next: Pass position-aware inputs through preceding blocks, if any, to obtain the selected block's input.

steps.title: Input of the selected decoder block
steps.prose: The selector opens one block from the configured stack. Earlier blocks have still been calculated, and their output feeds the selected one. Preserve this incoming representation for the first residual addition while transforming an attention branch.
steps.terms: A block is one parameterized attention/feed-forward stage. Selecting a block changes the inspected trace slice rather than removing other blocks from the model.
steps.next: Normalize the branch input before forming queries, keys and values.
steps.node: Input of the selected decoder block

steps.title: LayerNorm before attention
steps.prose: For each token independently, subtract its feature mean and divide by the square root of feature variance plus epsilon, then apply gain/bias. The example fixes gain one and bias zero. Token count and feature width do not change.
steps.terms: Mu and sigma-squared summarize features of one token; epsilon avoids an unstable denominator. LayerNorm differs from normalizing over examples or class labels.
steps.next: Project the normalized features into separate query, key and value representations.

steps.title: Query, key and value projections
steps.prose: Apply three learned matrix maps to the normalized features. Queries and keys determine matching scores; values supply content for the weighted mixture. The familiar matching analogy does not mean literal questions or factual statements are stored in these tensors.
steps.terms: Q, K and V name three projected tensors here; V is not the vocabulary-size symbol used elsewhere. Projection means a feature-space linear map.
steps.next: Reshape the projected coordinates into the selected attention-head layout.

steps.title: Attention head dimensions
steps.prose: Split the four projected features into the selected number of heads without creating extra entries. At two heads, each head has two features per token. Each head then computes its own position-by-position mixture.
steps.terms: H is head count and d_h=D/H head width in this example. Heads are learned subspaces, not guaranteed grammar, reasoning or truth specialists.
steps.next: Compare each query with the allowed candidate keys in its own head.

steps.title: Scaled query–key scores
steps.prose: For one query, multiply corresponding query/key coordinates, sum and divide by the square root of head width. Repeat over keys to form its score row. The full tensor has separate batch, head, query-position and key-position axes.
steps.terms: In S_ij, i indexes the query and j the key. The dot product contracts feature coordinates; the scores are not probabilities yet.
steps.next: Apply the causal visibility rule before normalizing these scores.

steps.title: Causal attention mask
steps.prose: For a query at position i, retain keys at or before i and forbid later ones. The example writes negative infinity before softmax so forbidden keys receive zero weight. Parallel processing of training positions must still respect this rule.
steps.terms: Causal means no reading future sequence positions. A loss mask separately chooses which targets teach the model; it cannot enforce attention visibility.
steps.next: Normalize each permitted score row over its key positions.

steps.title: Attention softmax over key positions
steps.prose: Convert a query's permitted scores into nonnegative weights summing to one over keys. Subtracting the maximum before exponentiation preserves the result and improves numerical stability. Each query and head receives its own normalization.
steps.terms: Attention softmax's axis is source/key positions. Its weights are mixing coefficients, not confidence that the final answer is correct.
steps.next: Use the normalized row to form a weighted sum of value vectors.

steps.title: Weighted value mixture
steps.prose: Multiply each allowed value vector by its weight and add corresponding feature entries. The resulting vector has one head's feature width, not one new position for every source token. A large coefficient does not alone explain the final model answer.
steps.terms: A weighted sum mixes compatible vectors. It is different from concatenating source tokens or selecting one token as a hard evidence decision.
steps.next: Join all head outputs and apply the attention output projection.

steps.title: Head concatenation and output projection
steps.prose: Join the heads along their feature axis, then multiply by the output projection. This can combine information from their different mixtures and returns the branch to hidden width. Neither operation changes the number of token positions.
steps.terms: Concatenation appends feature coordinates; addition combines matching coordinates. W_O is the projection back into residual-compatible feature space.
steps.next: Add the preserved original block input to the attention branch output.

steps.title: First residual addition
steps.prose: The shortcut brings the selected block input unchanged around normalization and attention. Add it elementwise to the same-shaped attention output. This is a forward information path; it is not a repetition of the whole model or backpropagation.
steps.terms: The residual stream is the evolving token representation. A direct path contributes to gradients during training but does not guarantee unchanged meaning.
steps.next: Normalize this residual result before the feed-forward branch while preserving it for the next bypass.

steps.title: LayerNorm before the feed-forward branch
steps.prose: Normalize the first residual result independently at each token. The example uses the same gain/bias convention as its first norm, but a trained model can have distinct parameters for these two modules. The original embedding is not the input at this stage.
steps.terms: A feed-forward MLP transforms features within one position. Attention was the component that mixed different sequence positions.
steps.next: Expand the normalized feature vector into the intermediate MLP width.

steps.title: Feed-forward expansion
steps.prose: The first matrix map changes each token's four features into eight intermediate features. It shares its weights across token positions but not across different decoder blocks in this example. A larger intermediate width changes parameters and compute, not the context length.
steps.terms: MLP means multilayer perceptron. The intermediate width is a feature dimension, not another group of tokens or attention heads.
steps.next: Apply a nonlinear activation to these intermediate coordinates.

steps.title: GELU nonlinearity
steps.prose: Apply the displayed approximate GELU separately to each intermediate feature. Unlike ReLU it does not simply replace every negative value with zero. Without a nonlinearity, an unrestricted composition of linear maps would still be equivalent to one linear map.
steps.terms: GELU means Gaussian error linear unit. The example uses its stated tanh approximation; gated feed-forward variants are different computations.
steps.next: Project the activated intermediate vector back to hidden width.

steps.title: Feed-forward output projection
steps.prose: The second matrix maps eight activated coordinates back to four so they can be added to the residual stream. It changes feature values, not token positions. This simple branch omits biases and dropout and is not a gated Llama-style MLP.
steps.terms: The branch output must match the shortcut's shape. Feature expansion/contraction is neither generation nor a guarantee of information compression.
steps.next: Add this feed-forward correction to the preserved first residual result.

steps.title: Second residual addition
steps.prose: Carry the representation from before the feed-forward branch along its shortcut and add the branch output. Both paths have matching token and feature axes. The new representation is the selected block's output for the next block or final stage.
steps.terms: Both residual bypasses are forward connections. Full-model training differentiates through contributing operations, rather than treating attention weights as gradients.
steps.next: Continue through any later decoder blocks using their own parameters.

steps.title: Remaining decoder blocks
steps.prose: Run the configured stack in order. Each block consumes the preceding block's output and preserves the boundary shape while changing values. Inspecting an earlier block does not mean vocabulary scores are calculated from that block alone.
steps.terms: Depth counts successive parameterized transformations. Unlike a simple shared RNN recurrence, these example blocks use different matrices.
steps.next: Normalize the last block's features before mapping them to vocabulary scores.

steps.title: Final LayerNorm
steps.prose: Apply the final per-token normalization to the output of the full stack. This is separate from norms inside the inspected block. Placement is part of the declared pre-norm architecture; other Transformer recipes can differ.
steps.terms: Final hidden features have incorporated the allowed prefix through all configured blocks. Shape alone does not indicate how much useful information was learned.
steps.next: Project the final features into one raw score per vocabulary item.

steps.title: Vocabulary projection
steps.prose: Multiply each token's four final features by the separate four-by-six output matrix. Each position receives six candidate successor scores. This example keeps input and output matrices untied so its limited head-update demonstration has an unambiguous boundary.
steps.terms: A logit is an unnormalized score, not a percentage or measured accuracy. Vocabulary size controls the output score axis.
steps.next: Normalize vocabulary logits at each position to obtain next-token probabilities.

steps.title: Vocabulary softmax
steps.prose: Normalize across candidate token identities, independently for each position. This is a different axis and purpose from attention's normalization over keys. The highest score becomes the highest probability, but that probability is not verified factual confidence.
steps.terms: Vocabulary softmax predicts token identity; attention softmax mixes value information. These distributions are not interchangeable.
steps.next: At use time choose a next token; during training separately compare a known next-token target.

steps.title: Generation with fixed parameters
steps.prose: Use the final input position's distribution to choose and append a token, then predict again. The teaching button uses a bounded greedy step and recomputes earlier states. It does not train the weights or promise coherent language from fixed tiny matrices.
steps.terms: Autoregressive generation grows the input sequence. A compatible KV cache can avoid repeated projections; it is temporary inference state, not learned knowledge.
steps.next: The outer return is generation only. The training branch instead starts from a known target and a loss.

steps.title: Training loss for a known successor
steps.prose: The selected position is compared with its known next-token target, not a sampled guess treated as truth. The last position uses a supplied teaching target. The displayed loss scores one selected position rather than averaging all training positions.
steps.terms: Cross-entropy here is minus the natural log of the target probability, measured in nats. Teacher-forced training can score many permitted positions together.
steps.next: Differentiate this loss and apply an optimizer under the explicitly limited teaching update.
steps.node: Training loss for a known successor

steps.title: Head-only gradient and optimizer update
steps.prose: Freeze upstream features and calculate one exact SGD update of the output matrix at rate 0.1. This changes the illustrative head, not a saved checkpoint. Real full-model training also differentiates through embeddings and all contributing blocks.
steps.terms: The gradient measures local loss sensitivity. SGD applies it to parameters; the one-position example is not the lab's full-model AdamW training procedure.
steps.next: A real training loop takes another batch after updating; fixed-weight generation follows its separate return path.

reading.legend: The architecture shows forward feature flow and residual shortcuts. The outer return appends a generated token with fixed weights. The training branch compares a known target and illustrates only an output-head SGD update; it does not replay or modify a saved training run.
reading.lesson_markdown:
A decoder Transformer converts a token prefix into a distribution over the next token at each position. Each block updates a vector for every position; the vector width is not the vocabulary size. The small diagram uses hidden width four so the intermediate numbers can be inspected. It is not a scale model of every detail in a pretrained checkpoint.

### What happens inside one pre-norm block

Token IDs select learned embeddings. Position information distinguishes order. Layer normalization rescales the features at each position before a branch. Learned query, key, and value projections let each position compare with earlier permitted positions. Attention scores are scaled, masked, and normalised over keys; their weighted values are combined and projected back to the residual-stream width.

The first residual addition combines that branch output with the block input. Another normalization feeds a position-wise MLP, which expands features, applies a nonlinearity, and contracts them. A second residual addition preserves a direct path around the MLP. Stacking blocks repeats these transformations with different parameters. Neither residual route is generation or backpropagation.

### From representations to a token

A final normalization and vocabulary projection produce logits. Softmax over the vocabulary yields probabilities. Training compares the known successor with these scores. Generation instead selects a token from the final prefix position, appends it, and repeats with fixed weights.

Attention heads divide the representation into projected subspaces; their outputs are concatenated and mixed, not averaged as class votes. The original Transformer paper used an encoder–decoder design; this lesson demonstrates a later causal pre-norm decoder. Pretrained models can use RMSNorm, rotary positions, gated MLPs, grouped-query attention, and tied embeddings. Follow their actual equations and dimensions rather than assuming the teaching diagram's choices apply universally.

Sources: [D2L: Transformer architecture](https://d2l.ai/chapter_attention-mechanisms-and-transformers/transformer.html), [Vaswani et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762), [SLP: decoder language models](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/7.pdf).

# T4. Language-model architecture families

An architecture defines which representations interact and what state is carried through a model. Encoders, causal decoders and encoder–decoders differ in information access and output interface; expert layers and state-space operations change other parts of the computation. These categories can overlap within one model, so architecture names are not an ordered quality ranking.

Select a family to inspect its structure. The encoder–decoder example has three source positions and two target-prefix positions. Separate supplied examples illustrate two weighted experts or a scalar recurrent state; none is a trained comparison between model families.

The detailed decoder provided one concrete architecture. This lesson varies the structure while keeping visibility, shape, state, active computation and cache costs distinct, with positional and multimodal extensions in the deeper notes.

## 1. Architecture design choices

**Key terms.** An **architecture** defines the computation graph; **dense** layers use the full relevant matrix; **sparse** computation activates only selected components.

**Process.** Classify what a design changes—visibility, state, computation or input modality—before comparing its scores. That classification determines which costs and controls the experiment must measure.

Do not memorise a list of model brands. Ask: which positions interact, what state is retained, how many parameters are active, and what objective trains the representation?

| Family | Main property | Main trade-off |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Encoder-only | Bidirectional input representation | Strong classification/retrieval interface, not ordinary left-to-right generation |
| Decoder-only | Causal continuation | Flexible generation; sequential output steps |
| Encoder–decoder | Separate source processing and target generation | Natural conditional-generation interface; two interacting stacks |
| Sparse/sliding attention | Restricted token interactions | Longer sequences cheaply; some global connections need special handling |
| Recurrent/state-space | Compress history into state | Efficient long sequences; different access to exact past content |
| Hybrid | Mix attention and other sequence operations | Balance benefits, but more complex implementation and evaluation |
| Diffusion/masked-generation language models | Iterative refinement rather than only left-to-right generation | Alternative parallel/refinement opportunities; objective and serving differ |

These categories overlap. A mixture-of-experts decoder can also use grouped-query and sliding-window attention.

## 2. Positional methods

**Key terms.** **Absolute positions** label locations; **relative positions** describe offsets; **RoPE** uses rotations; **extrapolation** uses lengths beyond the training regime.

**Process.** Encode position in the chosen way before attention computes interactions. Test changed lengths next, because a larger configured window does not guarantee reliable use of distant information.

For a 2D pair, a rotation is:

\[
R(\phi)\begin{bmatrix}a\\b\end{bmatrix}

## 3. MHA, MQA, GQA and latent attention

**Key terms.** **MHA** has separate keys/values per query head; **MQA** shares one set; **GQA** shares groups; **latent attention** stores a compressed representation.

**Process.** Project hidden states into the selected query/key/value layout, compute attention and retain the needed cache. The sharing choice changes projection and cache costs, not automatically the allowed token pairs.

**Calculation.** At head width 64, 15 query heads with 15 KV heads need 2×15×64=1,920 cached values per token per layer. Sharing 5 KV heads needs 2×5×64=640: one third as many before dtype and runtime overhead.

Multi-head attention uses distinct key/value projections per head. Multi-query attention shares keys/values across query heads. Grouped-query attention shares them within groups. This reduces KV-cache storage and bandwidth at possible quality/architecture trade-offs. Query-head count is not the KV-head count in the memory equation.

Latent-attention approaches compress stored information and reconstruct needed components. They change how cache memory is represented; do not apply a standard uncompressed KV formula blindly to them. Implementation compatibility matters as much as nominal architecture support.

### Separate three ways of reducing attention cost

They change different objects and cannot be compared using one headline memory ratio.

1. **GQA/MQA** reduce the number of stored key/value heads. The number of query positions and allowed token interactions can remain unchanged.
2. **Sliding-window or sparse attention** removes some query–key connections. A token may no longer directly access evidence outside its permitted window; special global paths or multiple layers change that access pattern.
3. **Latent KV representations** compress the cached information. Reconstructing or absorbing projections into other operations changes the runtime arithmetic; the ordinary uncompressed cache formula no longer describes the complete implementation.
4. **FlashAttention** reorganizes the same dense attention operation to reduce IO/materialization. It need not remove interactions or change head sharing.

For RoPE, the identity `(R_m q)ᵀ(R_n k)=qᵀR_(n−m)k` explains why a relative position offset enters the score: rotations preserve lengths and compose by angle differences. It does not prove that a model trained on short sequences can use arbitrarily long contexts.

Compare quality on long evidence retrieval as well as bytes, throughput and latency. ## 4. Mixture of experts

**Key terms.** A **mixture of experts (MoE)** has alternative learned sub-networks; a **router** selects them; **active parameters** are those used for a token.

**Process.** Each token reaches the router, which assigns selected expert computations. Combine their outputs and continue the block; measure routing balance and communication as well as total parameter count.

An MoE layer has several expert networks and a router. For input representation `x`, router scores select a subset; output combines selected expert outputs:

\[
y=\sum_{e\in TopK(g(x))}a_e(x)f_e(x).
\]

Routing adds communication, load imbalance and capacity decisions. Load-balancing losses discourage all tokens selecting the same expert; overflow policies may drop or reroute tokens.

**Routing distinction:** choosing one complete classifier per dataset is a system-level routing decision. Token-level MoE routes internal hidden states through expert sublayers. Shared terminology does not make them the same implementation.

## 5. State spaces and alternative sequence models

**Key terms.** A **state-space model** updates a compact sequence state; **recurrence** carries that state forward; an **attention cache** instead retains token-specific keys and values.

**Process.** A sequence model consumes earlier information through its chosen state mechanism. Compare how that state updates and scales before assuming attention's cache and cost formulas apply.

A simplified state-space recurrence is `h_t=A h_(t−1)+B x_t`, `y_t=C h_t`. Modern selective/state-space models make parts input-dependent and use efficient scans. The finite state summarises prior input differently from attention's explicit access to stored token keys/values. This can improve certain length/resource trade-offs but is not a universal replacement for exact retrieval.

Diffusion language models iteratively refine corrupted/masked tokens. They involve a corruption schedule, denoising objective and generation schedule. Distinguish discrete token diffusion from image diffusion; architecture and likelihood accounting vary. This course surveys the branch; deriving each diffusion estimator requires the specialist route in the resource guide.

## 6. Multimodal language systems

**Key terms.** A **modality** is an input type such as text or audio; an **encoder** turns it into features; a **projector** maps features into a compatible space.

**Process.** Encode the non-text input, align its representation with the language system and fuse it through the chosen architecture. Test whether answers use that input rather than a text-only shortcut.

A vision-language system may encode image patches, map them through a projector and combine them with text representations. Audio systems can use acoustic encoders, discrete audio tokens or streaming representations. Video introduces time, frame sampling and synchronization. OCR is not equivalent to complete image understanding.

**Contrastive alignment** learns matched text/image representations; **generative alignment** learns to produce text conditioned on another modality; **joint training** may update several components. A frozen encoder plus learned projector differs from end-to-end multimodal pretraining.

Real issues: unreadably small images, incorrect crop/resizing, missing frames, audio accents, hallucinated chart values, private biometric data and poor grounding. Evaluate whether the answer is supported by the modality, not merely plausible from text priors.

## Exercises and checks

1. An MoE has 64 experts and activates 2. Does it need storage only for 2 experts? **No**, unless a separately designed loading/offloading arrangement provides others when needed.
2. Does GQA reduce all model memory by the query/KV head ratio? **No:** it mainly changes affected attention components and cache, not every weight/activation.
3. Why might a long-context state model still fail an exact quotation query? Compressed state can lose exact content; test the task instead of inferring capability from complexity.

Primary examples: [Switch Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961), [Mamba](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.00752), [LLaMA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.13971), [Gemini technical report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.11805). These establish example families, not a current leaderboard.

# T4. Language-model architecture families

An architecture defines which representations interact and what state is carried through a model. Encoders, causal decoders and encoder–decoders differ in information access and output interface; expert layers and state-space operations change other parts of the computation. These categories can overlap within one model, so architecture names are not an ordered quality ranking.

Select a family to inspect its structure. The encoder–decoder example has three source positions and two target-prefix positions. Separate supplied examples illustrate two weighted experts or a scalar recurrent state; none is a trained comparison between model families.

The detailed decoder provided one concrete architecture. This lesson varies the structure while keeping visibility, shape, state, active computation and cache costs distinct, with positional and multimodal extensions in the deeper notes.

sections.title: Architecture design choices
sections.markdown:
## 1. Architecture design choices

**Key terms.** An **architecture** defines the computation graph; **dense** layers use the full relevant matrix; **sparse** computation activates only selected components.

**Process.** Classify what a design changes—visibility, state, computation or input modality—before comparing its scores. That classification determines which costs and controls the experiment must measure.

Do not memorise a list of model brands. Ask: which positions interact, what state is retained, how many parameters are active, and what objective trains the representation?

| Family | Main property | Main trade-off |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Encoder-only | Bidirectional input representation | Strong classification/retrieval interface, not ordinary left-to-right generation |
| Decoder-only | Causal continuation | Flexible generation; sequential output steps |
| Encoder–decoder | Separate source processing and target generation | Natural conditional-generation interface; two interacting stacks |
| Sparse/sliding attention | Restricted token interactions | Longer sequences cheaply; some global connections need special handling |
| Recurrent/state-space | Compress history into state | Efficient long sequences; different access to exact past content |
| Hybrid | Mix attention and other sequence operations | Balance benefits, but more complex implementation and evaluation |
| Diffusion/masked-generation language models | Iterative refinement rather than only left-to-right generation | Alternative parallel/refinement opportunities; objective and serving differ |

These categories overlap. A mixture-of-experts decoder can also use grouped-query and sliding-window attention.

steps.title: Identify source and target streams
steps.prose: Conditional generation reads an available source while predicting a separate target sequence. The target prefix must not contain unknown future target answers. Here source and current target lengths are three and two, not matching axes by default.
steps.terms: B is batch size, D hidden width, T_s source length and T_t target-prefix length. These axes have different roles.
steps.next: Encode the source and represent the permitted target prefix as separate branches.

steps.title: Encode the source
steps.prose: A source encoder can use bidirectional context within the supplied source. It creates three source-position vectors for the example. That permission does not extend to future target answers, which belong to a different sequence.
steps.terms: Encoder self-attention relates source positions. A source mask still distinguishes valid input from padding.
steps.next: Use source states as keys and values when a decoder later reads this memory.

steps.title: Represent the permitted target prefix
steps.prose: The target side reads earlier permitted target tokens under a causal rule. Its two-position hidden representation supplies decoder-side queries. Source length and target-prefix length are independent and need separate masks.
steps.terms: Target self-attention relates allowed target positions. It is not the same attention operation as reading source representations.
steps.next: Cross-attend from these target queries to the source keys and values.

steps.title: Connect target queries to source memory
steps.prose: Each target position compares with the three source positions, giving a two-by-three score matrix per head. Normalize over source keys and mix their values. Cross-attention changes available information, not which sequence is being predicted.
steps.terms: In the equation Q_t contains target queries while K_s contains source keys. The head width controls dot-product scaling, not source length.
steps.next: Project the resulting target features to scores for the next target token.

steps.title: Predict the next target token
steps.prose: The vocabulary head maps conditioned decoder features to output scores. A generation process can then extend the target prefix while reusing compatible source computation. The source stream need not grow with every generated target token.
steps.terms: Conditional generation models p(y_t | x,y_<t). Weight updates and a complete numerical encoder–decoder execution are not performed here.
steps.next: The optimization lesson next returns to training arithmetic shared across architectures.

steps.title: Calculate routing weights for a shared input
steps.prose: A router assigns gate scores to expert subnetworks. The example uses logits [1,0] and softmax to form two weights. Both experts read the same token features; the router does not split the input into different examples.
steps.terms: MoE means mixture of experts. An expert is a parameterized subnetwork, not a verified semantic specialist.
steps.next: Evaluate the declared expert branches and retain gate weights for their later combination.

steps.title: Evaluate expert A
steps.prose: The first expert is supplied to return scalar two for this input. Its own parameters define the transformation. This value illustrates combination arithmetic, not evidence that it has learned a particular topic or skill.
steps.terms: Expert outputs must have compatible feature shapes before weighted addition. Distinct expert parameters need not imply interpretable specialization.
steps.next: Combine this branch with the other selected expert under the router weights.

steps.title: Evaluate expert B
steps.prose: The second expert is supplied to return minus one for the same input. Evaluating both is deliberate in this tiny example. A sparse top-k implementation might activate a subset and specify another gate normalization policy.
steps.terms: Total expert count and active experts per token measure different things. Both stored capacity and executed work matter.
steps.next: Send this branch and the other selected output to the weighted merge.

steps.title: Merge weighted expert outputs
steps.prose: Multiply each supplied expert output by its gate weight and add matching features. The root's gate values determine the mixture. This example activates both experts; a top-one choice would be a different calculation rather than the same result for free.
steps.terms: A weighted sum combines compatible outputs without concatenation. Router weights describe this computation, not answer correctness probabilities.
steps.next: Assess load balance, storage and communication as separate system-level questions.

steps.title: Define a carried state and transition
steps.prose: The illustrative recurrence starts at h zero and reads [1,0,1] with input coefficient 0.5 and state coefficient 0.8. It compresses earlier information into a fixed-width state instead of storing one key/value pair per earlier token.

steps.next: Apply the transition to the first input and zero boundary state.

steps.title: Update state for the first input
steps.prose: The first input contributes 0.5 while the zero prior state contributes nothing. The new scalar state is 0.5. A later transition will reuse the same coefficients, not introduce a separate learned parameter set for each position.
steps.terms: Shared recurrence parameters are distinct from carried state values. A state value changes with input even during fixed-weight inference.
steps.next: Carry this state to the second position along with its current input.

steps.title: Carry state through a zero input
steps.prose: At the second position, multiplying 0.5 by 0.8 yields 0.4, and zero input adds no new contribution. Persistence here is a numeric state transition, not a claim about remembering arbitrary exact earlier text.
steps.terms: A transition can retain or attenuate state information. A compressed state is different from a full list of token-specific attention values.
steps.next: Combine the retained state with the third input.

steps.title: Incorporate the final input

steps.terms: Modern selective state-space models use richer, often input-dependent operations. This example is not a Mamba implementation.
steps.next: Map the resulting state to an output using the separate readout coefficient.

steps.terms: The readout produces output features from state. State width, exact recall and long-context quality are separate design/evaluation questions.

reading.lesson_markdown:
Architecture determines which input positions may influence an output. An encoder-only model usually builds bidirectional representations of a supplied sequence. A decoder-only language model predicts successors using a causal prefix. An encoder–decoder separately represents a source and generates a target that can cross-attend to it.

For translation, the whole source sentence can be visible while the next target token may use only the already supplied or generated target prefix. Cross-attention queries come from the decoder; keys and values come from the source representation. This differs from the decoder's causal self-attention. For complete-document classification, bidirectional access is often appropriate because the entire document exists at prediction time.

Changing modality changes the input representation and training task: a vision Transformer embeds image patches, while speech models may encode acoustic frames. Calling everything a token does not make patch, text, and audio boundaries semantically interchangeable.

Mixture-of-experts routes representations through selected learned expert branches, often replacing a feed-forward sublayer. Total parameters and active parameters per token then differ. This is not simply an ensemble of finished answers. Choose a family by permitted evidence, output requirements, and budget, then inspect the actual implementation; the name “Transformer” leaves many details unspecified.

Sources: [T5](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.10683), [Vision Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11929), [Switch Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961).

# T5. Gradient accumulation and stable LLM training

Gradient accumulation combines several small forward/backward calculations before one optimizer update. The loss weighting must match the intended objective, especially when microbatches contain different numbers of valid targets. Numerical stability, clipping, scheduling and diagnostics are additional training choices, not substitutes for correctly aligned data and targets.

Microbatch A has two scored tokens with mean loss one; B has a selectable token count with mean loss three. At six B tokens the combined token mean is 2.5, while averaging the two microbatch means gives 2.0. The control changes this accounting, not a live run.

The training loop identified where gradients are accumulated and applied. This lesson derives their weighting on one worker; the distributed lesson later adds the separate convention used to combine workers.

## 1. Minimal training loop

**Key terms.** An **optimizer** applies updates; **zero_grad** clears stored gradients; **backward** accumulates derivatives; **evaluation mode** controls behaviours such as dropout.

**Process.** Fetch a batch, clear gradients at the update boundary, compute loss, backpropagate and update parameters. Validation is a separate branch with no optimizer step; verify the smallest loop before extending it.

Before scaling, run a single process, one device and a tiny clean batch. For a causal model, confirm that the last input position predicts the next token, not the token already at that position. Decide whether the framework or your code shifts labels.

Pseudocode, not a copy-paste library recipe:

```text
load configuration, tokenizer and document-level splits
initialize model and optimizer; record all versions
repeat:
    fetch token batch and visibility/loss masks
    compute logits
    compute SUM of valid-token negative log probabilities
    divide by the intended token count for the update
    backpropagate
    at the update boundary: synchronize as required, clip, optimizer step
    periodically evaluate a fixed held-out set without weight updates
    save complete resumable state and inspect samples
```

## 2. Token-weighted gradient accumulation

**Key terms.** A **microbatch mean** averages its scored tokens; an **update mean** averages all scored tokens across accumulation; **K** is the number of microbatches.

**Process.** Count valid targets before scaling the losses. Accumulate token-weighted contributions, then unscale and clip once at the update boundary before changing weights. Equal microbatch weights only match equal target counts.

Accumulation processes several microbatches before an optimizer step. Effective batch size in examples is approximately `microbatch × accumulation × data-parallel workers`, assuming equal batch sizes and a standard synchronization convention. Token counts vary with length/masking.

If microbatch A contains 10 valid targets and B contains 90, averaging their two mean losses gives each microbatch half the influence. Averaging all 100 token losses gives weights 0.1 and 0.9. Neither is automatically the intended objective. For token-mean training, accumulate sums with the corresponding global valid-token denominator. Distributed reduction semantics can introduce another scale factor.

Accumulation is not always exactly equivalent to one large forward batch: dropout, normalization variants, clipping, optimizer scheduling and rounding can differ. Define learning-rate schedule units—optimizer updates versus microsteps versus tokens.

### A two-microbatch update, with the denominator made explicit

Suppose the next update uses two microbatches containing 10 and 90 valid targets. Their mean losses are 2 and 4.

1. Convert means to sums: `S₁=20`, `S₂=360`; total target count is 100.
2. Backward `S₁/100`, retaining its parameter gradients but freeing that forward graph. Backward `S₂/100` on the second graph. The accumulated gradient matches the derivative of `(S₁+S₂)/100` under the same deterministic objective.
3. The combined scalar loss for reporting is 3.8. Averaging the two means would report 3.0 and optimize a different weighting.
4. Unscale if required, check finite gradients, clip the accumulated norm, then call the optimizer once. Clear gradient buffers at the boundary so the next update does not include this one unintentionally.
5. For a final incomplete accumulation window, use its actual intended denominator. Dividing every microbatch by a fixed accumulation count can incorrectly shrink the last update.

Knowing the total count before the backward calls may require preparing the small group first or a carefully specified equivalent normalization strategy. Avoid retaining every microbatch's full computation graph just to normalize later. Distributed averaging adds a world-size convention; T7 derives it separately. Reference: [PyTorch AMP accumulation and clipping](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/notes/amp_examples.html).

## 3. Numerical stability

**Key terms.** **FP16/BF16/FP32** are floating-point formats; **loss scaling** protects small gradients in some mixed-precision recipes; **non-finite** means NaN or infinity.

**Process.** Compute in supported precision, inspect losses and gradients, then convert or unscale before clipping and updating. Invalid arithmetic must be diagnosed before it contaminates subsequent optimizer state.

Use stable log-softmax/cross-entropy implementations rather than taking logs of rounded probabilities. Compute sensitive reductions in suitable precision. FP16 may require loss scaling to preserve small gradients; BF16 has a wider exponent range but not FP32 precision. Hardware and kernels determine supported operations.

Initialize weights to avoid exploding or vanishing activation scales. Monitor gradient norm, activation norms, attention-logit scale and embedding/output norms. Warmup, normalization, clipping and cautious optimizer settings are tools, not replacements for finding data/label errors.

## 4. Diagnosing training failures

**Key terms.** **Divergence** is unstable worsening; **overfitting** improves training but harms held-out behaviour; a **bottleneck** limits throughput.

**Process.** Observe the failure pattern, check data and numerics, and change one plausible cause at a time. Re-run a controlled small case before committing another full training budget.

| Symptom | First checks | Do not immediately conclude |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Loss implausibly near zero | Target leakage, wrong shift, padding-only scoring | “The architecture is amazing” |
| Loss flat near random baseline | Gradients, learning rate, trainable parameters, targets | “Need a larger model” |
| NaNs after a few steps | Overflow, invalid inputs, normalization, rate, division by zero | “Mixed precision never works” |
| Train improves, validation worsens | Overfitting, duplicates, mixture and distribution | “Validation is broken” |
| Repetitive generation | Data repetition, decoding, EOS/template, model quality | “Temperature alone fixes it” |
| GPU underused | Data loader, transfers, small kernels, synchronization | “Need more GPUs” |
| Resume changes behaviour | Missing optimizer/scheduler/RNG/sampler state | “Seeds guarantee equivalence” |

## 5. Efficient experiments

**Key terms.** A **pilot** is a short feasibility run; an **ablation** isolates a component; **early stopping** ends a run under a declared validation rule.

**Process.** Establish a working baseline, run a small controlled change and inspect its evidence. Scale the promising comparison only after correctness and resource costs are understood.

Start with a reference implementation and inspect its assumptions. Establish a fixed baseline, then change one meaningful component. Keep a run manifest with model/tokenizer hashes, config, data version, code revision, seed, hardware, package versions and valid-token exposure.

Run a **smoke test** for execution and shapes; a **tiny overfit test** for learning; a **short validation run** for obvious instability; then the budgeted comparison. A short run's ranking may reverse at scale, so call it a screening result, not the final conclusion.

Checkpoint state includes model, optimizer, scheduler, mixed-precision scaler when relevant, random states, data position and configuration. Checkpoint writes can be interrupted: write to a temporary destination and publish a complete artifact atomically where the storage system supports it. Verify restoration on a small run.

## 6. Optimizer and schedule settings

**Key terms.** A **schedule** changes learning rate over training; **warmup** increases it initially; **weight decay** shrinks parameters under its own rule.

**Process.** Choose the objective and effective batch first, then set optimizer, rate schedule and stopping policy. Record schedule units so resume or accumulation changes do not silently alter the recipe.

Batch by similar length when it reduces wasted padding without introducing unwanted ordering effects. Cache deterministic preprocessing. Use streaming/sharded reads when corpus size exceeds RAM. Measure tokens/second, not only batches/second. Long sequences and short sequences can have very different compute per batch.

Use held-out diagnostics by domain/language/length, not just one average. If the training mixture changes, compare exposure as well as update counts. Interpret early stopping against a predefined criterion; repeated hand selection based on generated samples is another source of selection bias.

## Exercises and checks

1. Microbatch means are 2 and 4 with 10 and 90 valid tokens. Token-mean loss? **3.8**, not 3.
2. What is the first experiment when a model cannot learn? A tiny clean overfit test with audited labels and gradients.
3. List the exact state needed to resume your proposed toy experiment; distinguish “approximately continue” from “bitwise reproduce.”

References: [PyTorch training basics](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/basics/intro.html), [Stanford CS336](https://cs336.stanford.edu/), [OLMo 2 training recipe](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.00656). The diagnostic table is a general engineering checklist, not a guarantee of one-to-one causes.

steps.title: Count the scored targets in this update
steps.prose: Count valid labels after shifting and loss masking, not padded tensor slots. The two supplied microbatch means may summarize different amounts of evidence. Plan the total denominator before backward or use a specified equivalent normalization procedure.
steps.terms: A microbatch is one forward/backward unit. An optimizer update can aggregate several such units; valid targets are the included token labels.
steps.next: Recover each microbatch's summed loss using its mean and valid-target count.

steps.title: Recover loss sums from the means
steps.prose: Multiply each mean loss by the number of included targets it summarizes. A contributes two; B contributes three times its count. These fixed losses demonstrate reduction weights, not observations from a trained checkpoint.
steps.terms: A mean times its count recovers the corresponding sum. Comparing only means can conceal the unequal evidence weights.
steps.next: Add the sums and divide by the intended total target count.

steps.title: Normalize the intended token-average objective
steps.prose: Use the combined target count so each scored token has equal influence. With equal counts this agrees with a mean of microbatch means; with unequal counts it does not. Other objectives are allowed if declared rather than silently conflated.
steps.terms: N is total valid targets; n_b counts targets in microbatch b. Loss reduction defines the statistical weighting, not just a logging choice.
steps.next: Differentiate correctly weighted contributions, accumulate their gradients and update once.

steps.title: Accumulate gradients and update once
steps.prose: Backpropagate each appropriately scaled contribution, retaining parameter gradients rather than all forward graphs. At the boundary unscale if needed, check finite gradients, clip if configured and apply one optimizer step. Then clear gradients for the next update.
steps.terms: Clipping limits gradient norm; loss scaling protects numerical computation in some precision recipes. Neither repairs incorrect target weighting.
steps.next: The deeper notes cover instability, diagnostics and schedule units; the next topic accounts for the memory those operations require.

links: Combine each target count with its supplied microbatch mean.
Sum loss contributions and divide by total valid targets.
Use equivalent normalized contributions in backward before one optimizer step.

reading.lesson_markdown:
Gradient accumulation combines several forward/backward microbatches before one optimizer update. It helps when a desired batch does not fit in memory. It is equivalent to a larger-batch objective only when loss scaling, model behaviour, and update boundaries match; repeated optimizer steps on small batches are a different procedure.

Suppose three microbatches contain 1, 1, and 100 valid target tokens. Averaging their three mean losses gives the two tiny batches two-thirds of the vote. A token-average objective gives those two tokens only $2/102$ of the weight. Recover each summed token loss, add the sums, and divide by the total number of scored tokens. Padding and ignored prompt tokens must not enter that count.

Clip gradients after accumulating the intended update, and update the optimizer and scheduler at their defined boundary. A zero-target microbatch needs deliberate handling rather than division by zero. Compare against a single-batch reference on a small deterministic case when checking the implementation.

Mixed precision changes which numerical operations use lower precision. FP16 may need loss scaling; BF16 has a different range/precision trade-off. A master-weight copy is implementation-dependent, not a universal property of every autocast setup. # T6. LLM parameter counts, memory and compute

A model's parameter count, raw weight storage, training-state memory and compute budget measure different things. Training can require gradients, optimizer history, activations and temporary workspaces beyond the weights. Resource estimates are conditional accounting tools; measured peak memory and throughput must establish whether a real configuration fits and runs usefully.

Select one, ten or one hundred million hypothetical parameters. The simple convention stores FP32 weights, FP32 gradients and two FP32 Adam moments. Its static state uses sixteen bytes per parameter before activations or runtime overhead; other recipes need different accounting.

The training loop explains what values exist and when. This lesson counts their storage and work before scaling, while keeping the detailed prepared-model count, scaling laws and hardware bottlenecks in the deeper explanations.

## 1. Parameter counting

**Key terms.** **Parameters N** are learned numbers; **training tokens D** count exposures; **d** is hidden width; **d_ff** is MLP width; **V** is vocabulary size.

**Process.** Count each matrix from its dimensions before estimating storage or compute. Add shared parameters only once, then use the total in the separate memory and work calculations below.

Parameters, training tokens, context length, update count, hardware time and money are different quantities. A model with fewer parameters can cost more overall if trained on many more tokens or served millions of times. Total lifetime cost includes data preparation, experiments, training, evaluation and inference.

In a simple dense decoder block, attention projections contribute roughly `4d²` weights and a non-gated MLP roughly `2 d d_ff`, ignoring biases/norms. With `d_ff=4d`, that is about `12d²` per layer. Gated MLPs, GQA, tied embeddings and expert layers change the count. Add embeddings `Vd` and any untied output projection.

### Count the prepared model instead of guessing from its name

For the configured bias-free SmolLM2 model: vocabulary 49,152; width 960; 32 layers; KV projection width 320; gated intermediate width 2560; tied input/output embeddings.

1. The shared embedding/output matrix contains `49,152×960 = 47,185,920` parameters. Do not count it twice when weights are tied.
2. Each block's attention matrices contain `960×960 + 960×320 + 960×320 + 960×960 = 2,457,600` parameters: query, key, value and output projections.
3. Its three gated-MLP matrices contain `3×960×2560 = 7,372,800` parameters. A two-matrix GELU formula would undercount this model.
4. Two RMSNorm scale vectors add `2×960 = 1,920` per block. Across 32 blocks the subtotal is `32×9,832,320 = 314,634,240`.
5. Add the shared embedding and final 960-element RMSNorm: total **361,821,120**. This is a parameter count, not the peak-memory requirement.

The recipe follows the [model configuration](https://huggingface.co/HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-360M-Instruct/blob/main/config.json). Another architecture can have biases, untied heads or expert weights, so reuse the counting procedure, not the total. The compute-optimal scaling study in [Chinchilla](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556) addresses a separate question: how to allocate a training-compute budget between parameters and tokens.

## 2. Training memory

**Key terms.** **Bits per value** determine raw storage; **activations** are forward intermediates; **optimizer state** stores update history; **GiB** means 2³⁰ bytes.

**Process.** Calculate raw weight bytes first, then add gradients, optimizer state, activations and temporary buffers. Compare the complete peak estimate with available device and host memory before launching training.

For `N` parameters stored at `b` bits, raw weights need `Nb/8` bytes. A 7-billion-parameter model at 16 bits needs about 14 GB decimal, or 13.04 GiB. That is **not** a complete training or serving requirement.

An illustrative mixed-precision Adam setup might store:

| Component | Bytes/parameter in this example |
| --- | ---: |
| Low-precision parameter copy | 2 |
| Low-precision gradients | 2 |
| FP32 master weights | 4 |
| Two FP32 Adam moments | 8 |
| **Subtotal** | **16** |

For 7B parameters, subtotal is 112 GB before activations, workspace, communication buffers and allocator overhead. Other implementations use different gradient/master-state choices. Do not present “16 bytes” as a universal constant.

Activations depend on batch, sequence length, width, layers and kernels. Gradient checkpointing discards selected intermediate activations and recomputes them during backward, trading compute for memory. Optimizer sharding distributes state but adds communication. Offloading moves state to CPU/disk and can create a bandwidth bottleneck.

## 3. FLOPs and time estimates

**Key terms.** A **FLOP** is a floating-point operation; **throughput** is operations per second; **sustained throughput** is achieved rather than advertised speed.

**Process.** Estimate total arithmetic from model and token counts, divide by measured or explicitly assumed sustained speed, then add non-compute overhead. Treat the result as an estimate, not a benchmark.

A common rough estimate for dense Transformer training is `C≈6ND`, where `N` is parameter count and `D` is training-token count. It approximates forward/backward matrix operations; attention at long context, embeddings, architecture and implementation can change the total.

For `N=10^9`, `D=20×10^9`, estimate `C≈1.2×10²⁰` FLOPs. If an assumed **sustained**, not peak, throughput is `10^14` FLOPs/s, time is `1.2×10^6` seconds, about 13.9 days. This is an arithmetic illustration, not a hardware benchmark. Add evaluation, checkpoints, failures and orchestration overhead.

Model FLOPs utilization compares useful model compute with a stated hardware peak, but definitions and precision conventions vary. GPU “100% utilization” is not equivalent to peak useful model FLOPs.

## 4. Scaling laws

**Key terms.** A **scaling law** is an empirical fitted relation; **N/D** are parameter/token counts; **A/B/α/β/E** are fitted constants; **C** is compute budget.

**Process.** Fit loss against model and data sizes, impose a budget, then examine its preferred allocation. Check whether the new architecture, corpus and deployment regime match the fit before using its recommendation.

A stylized loss model is:

\[
L(N,D)\approx E+A N^{-\alpha}+B D^{-\beta}.
\]

`E` is an estimated irreducible term within this fit; other constants are fitted empirically. Holding compute `C≈kND` fixed gives `D=C/(kN)`. Differentiating the resulting two-term expression yields approximately:

\[
N^*\propto C^{\beta/(\alpha+\beta)},\qquad
D^*\propto C^{\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)}.
\]

This explains a trade-off: more parameters leave fewer training tokens under a fixed budget. The fitted exponents and constants depend on the regime and recipe. A popular tokens-per-parameter heuristic is not a law for every dataset, MoE, context length or inference-heavy product. A smaller model trained longer can be preferable when serving cost dominates.

## 5. Compute and bandwidth limits

**Key terms.** **Arithmetic intensity** is work per byte moved; **bandwidth** is bytes moved per second; a **roofline** bounds speed using compute and bandwidth limits.

**Process.** Estimate the operation's data movement and arithmetic, then identify the tighter hardware limit. Profile the real workload next to determine whether computation or memory traffic deserves optimization.

Compute-bound work waits for arithmetic throughput; memory-bound work waits for data movement. **Arithmetic intensity** is FLOPs per byte moved. A large matrix multiplication can reuse loaded values and achieve high intensity. A small-batch decode step may move many weights for relatively few new tokens.

If memory bandwidth doubles but compute stays fixed, a memory-bound task may improve substantially; a compute-bound task may not. These are useful limiting models, not labels permanently attached to all prefill/decode workloads.

## 6. Experiment budgeting

**Key terms.** A **comparison budget** includes all runs and checks; **accelerator hours** measure occupied devices over time; **energy** integrates power over time.

**Process.** Allocate resources to baselines, seeds, pilots, evaluation and failures before choosing run sizes. Report the same budget unit for competing methods so equal updates are not mistaken for equal cost.

Budget the entire comparison: pilot runs, seeds, baselines, failed runs, data generation and evaluation. State whether equal budget means equal tokens, optimizer steps, elapsed time, accelerator hours or money. Those equalities are not interchangeable.

Energy is power integrated over time; carbon estimates also need location/time-dependent factors and system boundaries. Parameter count alone does not establish sustainability. Report assumptions rather than inventing precise emissions.

## Exercises and checks

1. 1B parameters at 4 bits: raw weights about 0.5 GB. What is missing? Quantization metadata, selected higher-precision tensors, activations/cache and runtime overhead.
2. `N=2B,D=10B`: rough dense-training compute is `1.2×10²⁰` FLOPs, the same product as the earlier example but not necessarily the same quality or actual runtime.
3. Why can lowering weight precision fail to speed up inference? Hardware/kernel support, dequantization, launch overhead, cache or another bottleneck.

Primary reading: [compute-optimal scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556). Systems teaching: [CS336](https://cs336.stanford.edu/). Separate raw weights, optimizer state, activations and inference cache before estimating the complete resource budget.

steps.title: Count actual parameter entries
steps.prose: Add the entries of the model's unique parameter tensors. Tied weights are one shared parameter storage, not two independent learned matrices. The control declares a hypothetical count; it does not inspect an unknown model or infer a count from a product name.
steps.terms: A parameter is one learned scalar. Token exposure, layer count and hidden width affect resources but are not themselves parameter counts.

steps.prose: Under this example's FP32 convention each weight value needs four bytes. Multiply the parameter count accordingly and distinguish decimal MB from binary MiB. Metadata, temporary copies and allocations are outside this value-only estimate.
steps.terms: Precision defines a value representation. Raw storage is not a peak device-memory estimate or a guarantee that a model will fit.
steps.next: Add the state required by the selected training recipe separately from the weights.

steps.title: Account for gradients and optimizer history

steps.next: Include activations, workspaces and implementation overhead before interpreting the total.

reading.lesson_markdown:
Parameter count is the number of learned entries, not the memory footprint of an experiment. A dense matrix from d inputs to h outputs has dh weights, plus h biases if used. A conventional attention block with four d×d projections has approximately $4d^2$ weights; a d→4d→d MLP has approximately $8d^2$. Gated MLPs, grouped-query projections, and tied vocabulary tables change that count.

Raw storage is entries times bytes per entry. For 100 million parameters in two-byte storage, weights alone require 200 million bytes, about 191 MiB. Training additionally needs gradients, optimizer state, activations, and temporary buffers. Inference adds cache and workspace. A model file's size is therefore not the GPU memory needed for a chosen workload.

Batch size and sequence length change activation costs. Dense attention can create a quadratic position-pair object, though memory-efficient kernels avoid storing it in the ordinary way. A rough dense-model training estimate is about 6ND FLOPs for N parameters and D tokens, with simplifying assumptions; it is not a hardware runtime prediction and can miss attention or other costs.

Measure actual peak memory, throughput, and wall time on the intended device. More parameters with too little data or too little training can be a worse use of a fixed compute budget. The small lab teaches these accounting choices; it does not reproduce large-model scaling experiments.

Sources: [Hoffmann et al.: compute-optimal training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556), [PyTorch: CUDA memory accounting](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/notes/cuda.html#cuda-memory-management).

# T7. Distributed LLM training and gradient reduction

Distributed training divides data, arithmetic or stored state across cooperating processes. Data parallelism uses model replicas on different examples and combines gradients; tensor, pipeline and state-sharding schemes divide other objects. Correct loss normalization and communication are required before more devices can be treated as a performance improvement.

Two data-parallel workers have unequal valid-token counts and supplied scalar mean gradients one and three. We calculate the intended global token-weighted gradient, then the local scaling needed when a reducer averages across the two workers. This is not an executed cluster job.

Microbatch accumulation combined evidence on one worker. This lesson adds communication and a reducer convention across workers; multiplying device counts alone does not establish either a correct gradient or a speedup.

## 1. Parallel work and communication

**Key terms.** A **worker** is a training process; **communication** moves tensors between workers; **synchronization** makes processes wait for shared progress.

**Process.** Establish a correct one-worker run, measure its bottleneck and only then divide work. Additional devices help only when useful parallel work exceeds communication and coordination overhead.

Each accelerator has finite memory and compute. Distributing work creates communication, synchronization and scheduling costs. If one worker is late, others may wait. If interconnect bandwidth is poor, sharding can save memory while losing throughput.

First distinguish **scale up**—use faster/larger resources—from **scale out**—add workers. Strong scaling fixes total work and adds workers; weak scaling increases work with resources. Their efficiency numbers answer different questions.

## 2. Parallelism families

**Key terms.** **Data parallelism** splits examples; **tensor parallelism** splits tensor operations; **pipeline parallelism** splits layers; **sharding** partitions stored state.

**Process.** Choose what each device owns, execute its local computation and exchange the required tensors. Reconstruct the intended global update before judging whether the distributed run is faster.

```text
Data parallel:       GPU 1 = full model, batch A
                     GPU 2 = full model, batch B → combine gradients

Tensor parallel:     GPUs hold slices of a layer → exchange partial results

Pipeline parallel:   layers 1–k on GPU 1 → layers k+1–L on GPU 2

Expert parallel:     experts on different GPUs → route token states between them
```

**Data parallelism** replicates the model and aggregates gradients. An all-reduce combines a value across workers and distributes the result. An all-gather assembles shards; reduce-scatter reduces values while distributing result shards.

**ZeRO/FSDP-style sharding** partitions optimizer state, gradients and/or parameters depending on the scheme. Parameters may be gathered for computation then resharded. This is not identical to tensor parallelism, which splits the layer's arithmetic itself.

**Tensor parallelism** splits matrix operations; it usually needs frequent fast communication. **Pipeline parallelism** splits layers and moves activations; microbatches reduce idle “bubbles.” **Expert parallelism** distributes MoE experts; routing can require all-to-all traffic. **Sequence/context parallelism** partitions sequence-related work or state; exact strategies differ by framework.

Combine these only after specifying the mapping. “8 GPUs with TP=2 and DP=4” describes a different execution than “DP=8.” Do not multiply every advertised parallelism dimension without checking whether groups overlap or are nested.

## 3. Effective gradients and reproducibility

**Key terms.** **DDP** is distributed data parallelism; **W** counts workers; **Sᵣ** is worker r's summed loss; **N** is the global valid-target count.

**Process.** Each worker computes its local loss contribution. Scale for the framework's gradient reduction, synchronize and apply the same global update. Unequal token counts require more care than averaging local means.

**Calculation.** For two workers with 10 and 90 valid targets and local mean losses 2 and 4, the global token mean is (10×2+90×4)/100=3.8, not (2+4)/2=3.0. With DDP gradient averaging, local losses scaled as W×local loss sum/N have numerical values 0.4 and 7.2; their average is 3.8 and their averaged gradients match the intended objective.

Verify whether gradients are summed or averaged and over which workers. The loss denominator must match the intended global valid-token objective. Each worker needs a different data shard; otherwise eight workers may process eight copies of the same examples. Save sampler and RNG states; a seed alone does not describe the full run.

Distributed failures include mismatched collective calls, a worker exiting while others wait, network timeouts, CPU data-loading stalls and inconsistent checkpoints. Diagnose the first failing worker's log, not only the final timeout message.

### Derive the loss scale under ordinary DDP averaging

Let rank `r` own token-loss sum `S_r` and valid-target count `N_r`. The intended global loss is:

\[
L=\frac{\sum_r S_r}{N},\qquad N=\sum_r N_r.
\]

For `W` workers and the ordinary DDP convention that averages parameter gradients across workers:

1. All-reduce the target counts to obtain the same global denominator `N` on every worker.
2. Each worker differentiates `W S_r/N`. After DDP's averaging, the combined gradient is `(1/W)Σ_r∇(W S_r/N)=∇L`.
3. Differentiating only `S_r/N` and then averaging shrinks the gradient by `W`. Averaging each worker's mean loss instead can give unequal-sized workers the wrong relative influence.
4. With accumulation, count the full update's intended targets. Suppress synchronization for appropriate intermediate microbatches only using a correct framework-supported pattern, then synchronize at the boundary.

Communication hooks, uneven-input handling and other frameworks can use different reduction conventions. Confirm the installed implementation rather than copying the world-size factor blindly. Start with a one-worker versus two-worker toy equivalence test, fixed data and disabled dropout. References: [PyTorch DDP](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/generated/torch.nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel.html) and [ZeRO](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054).

## 4. Kernels, fusion and FlashAttention

**Key terms.** A **kernel** is a device computation; **fusion** combines operations; **FlashAttention** reorganizes exact attention to reduce memory traffic.

**Process.** A framework operation selects a compatible kernel, which moves data and computes outputs. Check output/gradient agreement before attributing a speedup to better execution rather than a changed calculation.

A high-level attention expression may create enormous intermediate tensors. A kernel implements the arithmetic on hardware. **Fusion** combines operations to avoid writing/reading temporary results and reduce launch overhead.

FlashAttention reorganizes exact attention with tiling and stable online softmax, reducing transfers to/from high-bandwidth memory and avoiding materialization of the full score matrix in the usual form. It is not the same as sparse or approximate attention. Exact refers to the mathematical operation, subject to floating-point differences. Pairwise arithmetic still has quadratic sequence-length dependence for ordinary dense attention.

The crucial distinction: **algorithmic complexity**, **memory footprint**, **memory traffic** and **wall-clock time** are separate. A kernel can substantially speed up the same mathematical operation.

## 5. Cluster workflow

**Key terms.** A **login node** is the cluster entry machine; an **allocation** grants resources; a **job script** describes scheduled work; **SLURM** manages the queue.

**Process.** Connect by SSH, prepare the environment, submit a resource request and run on the assigned compute node. Collect logs and checkpoints before the allocation ends; SSH alone does not reserve a GPU.

```text
laptop → SSH → login node → submit scheduler request
→ allocated compute node(s) → distributed launcher → worker processes
→ logs, checkpoints and metrics → evaluate → release allocation
```

Read your cluster's rules first. Commands such as `squeue`, `sacct`, `sinfo` and `nvidia-smi` are read-only diagnostics where installed. `sbatch` submits a job; it is not required for every GPU system. A scheduler allocation and the Python distributed process group are separate layers.

Never kill other users' processes or run network-wide scans to debug your experiment. Keep credentials out of job scripts and logs. Use authorised data storage and obey quotas.

## 6. Profile before optimization

**Key terms.** A **profile** records where time or memory goes; **warmup** removes startup effects; **synchronization** can be needed to time completed accelerator work.

**Process.** Measure a representative baseline, isolate costly operations, change one bottleneck and profile again. Confirm numerical correctness alongside time and memory rather than optimizing a misleading timer.

Measure data-loading time, forward/backward time, optimizer time, communication, checkpoint writing and memory peaks. Accelerator operations may be asynchronous: naive wall-clock timing without synchronization can measure launch time instead of completion. Include warmup and repeated measurements; state batch/context/dtype and hardware.

## Exercises and checks

1. Microbatch 2, accumulation 8, DP 4: nominal effective example batch is 64. TP workers do not multiply the count of distinct examples in the same way.
2. A model fits only after FSDP but becomes slower. Is FSDP broken? **Not necessarily:** communication or offload may dominate; fitting and speeding up are different goals.
3. Explain why FlashAttention and PagedAttention solve different problems. **Answer:** attention IO/computation organization versus inference KV-cache memory management; see R6.

Primary sources: [FlashAttention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135), [NVIDIA parallelisms guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/latest/parallelisms.html), [PyTorch FSDP documentation](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/fsdp.html). APIs are version-sensitive: use docs matching your installed build.
