I report hardware, precision, input sizes, batch size, warmup, and whether tokenization, transfers, and queuing are included. On accelerators with asynchronous execution, I synchronize appropriately when timing; otherwise I may measure only work submission. I inspect tail latency, such as the 95th percentile, not just an average. Larger batches can improve throughput while making an individual request wait longer.

**Follow-up: Does a two-times smaller model guarantee two-times lower latency?** No. Kernel efficiency, memory bandwidth, overhead, batching, and hardware support can dominate the result.

**Source links:** [PyTorch benchmark utilities](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/benchmark_utils.html), [PyTorch CUDA memory management](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/cuda.html#cuda-memory-management).

/api/learning/interview/IDL12.title: A better-scoring model used twice the training budget. What can you conclude?
/api/learning/interview/IDL12.markdown:
**Answer.** I state the claim before deciding which factors to hold fixed. A fair comparison isolates the change relevant to that claim; reproducibility records enough information to repeat the procedure and inspect the outcome. Matching everything is impossible when methods differ, so unmatched budgets and data access must be explicit.

Suppose model A trains for 10,000 updates and model B for 20,000, both at batch size 32. Their example exposure is about 320,000 versus 640,000 before incomplete batches or masking. A better B score does not isolate architecture quality. Equal updates also do not ensure equal tokens, wall-clock time, energy, or tuning effort. I choose the relevant budget and report the others where practical.

I save dataset versions, split identifiers, preprocessing, model and tokenizer revisions, effective batch sizes, seeds, optimizer state, selection rules, and per-example predictions. I compare seeds when affordable and select checkpoints using validation rather than test outcomes. Ablations change one meaningful component while keeping the comparison understandable. Deterministic settings can reduce variability, but do not guarantee bitwise equality across hardware or software versions.

**Follow-up: If one method gets more hyperparameter trials, is its win invalid?** Not automatically, but the result includes that search advantage. Report it and use a controlled search budget for claims about the method itself.

**Source link:** [PyTorch reproducibility guidance](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/randomness.html).

/api/learning/interview/F01.title: The package installed, but your script cannot import it. What would you check?
/api/learning/interview/F01.markdown:
I would first check whether installation and execution use the same Python interpreter. A successful installation in another environment does not make a package available to this script.

The shell starts a Python process. That interpreter loads your modules and dependencies, executes code and asks the operating system for files, memory or network access. A virtual environment selects an interpreter/package set; it is not a separate computer or a security sandbox. `pip` installs packages; imports use Python's module search rules. Use `python -m pip` to reduce interpreter/pip mismatch.

**Follow-up example.** Use the executable running the script with its -m pip command. Compare interpreter paths and the environment before reinstalling; installation elsewhere does not fix this process.

/api/learning/interview/F02.title: Why does calling this function twice append to the same list?
/api/learning/interview/F02.markdown:
The likely cause is a shared mutable object, such as a default list created once when the function was defined. A fresh per-call list prevents accidental accumulation.

A function transforms inputs or performs an operation; a class groups state and related behaviour. Abstraction exposes a clear contract while hiding irrelevant detail—not necessarily inheritance. A mutable list can change in place; assigning it to a second name does not copy its contents. Python passes object references by assignment; saying simply “pass by reference” can mislead about rebinding.

Use pure functions for budget maths/token shifts, a record/dataclass for a run manifest, and a small adapter interface for model backends. Prefer composition over a deep class tree without a reason.

**Follow-up example.** A mutable default list may be reused across calls. Default to None and create a fresh list when no list was supplied. A shallow copy still shares nested objects, so choose copying deliberately.

/api/learning/interview/F03.title: You need the highest-scoring k results. Would you sort everything?
/api/learning/interview/F03.markdown:
Lists are ordered dynamic arrays; dictionary/set lookup is expected average O(1), not a universal worst-case guarantee. A heap keeps the smallest/largest-priority item accessible in O(log k) update work; a deque supports efficient operations at both ends. Sorting n items usually costs O(n log n); binary search needs sorted data and costs O(log n) comparisons.

For top-k chunks among n scores, a size-k heap uses O(n log k) time and O(k) extra storage; full sort is simpler and often fine for small n. Complexity describes growth, not exact milliseconds.

**Follow-up example.** Define ties and boundary cases such as k=0 first. A size-k heap can save work for small k; full sorting is often clearer for a small list. Complexity is not a measured latency.

/api/learning/interview/F04.title: How would you follow document links without looping forever?
/api/learning/interview/F04.markdown:
A tree is a connected acyclic graph; a rooted tree can describe a hierarchy. General graphs represent relationships that can include cycles. BFS explores unweighted shortest paths using a queue; DFS explores depth-first using a stack/recursion. A visited set prevents repeated traversal/cycles. An LRU cache evicts the least recently used entry; a TTL expires old entries. Neither policy defines whether the cached answer remains authorized or true.

**Follow-up example.** Keep a visited set and a defined stopping rule. If you cache results, include access scope and source version: expiry alone does not establish that a cached answer is true or permitted.

/api/learning/interview/F05.title: A tensor operation runs but gives the wrong loss. What could be happening?
/api/learning/interview/F05.markdown:
I would check shapes and the meaning of each axis before trusting the scalar loss. A valid broadcast can produce the wrong comparison without raising an exception.

A tensor is an array with shape/dtype/device. Matrix multiplication combines aligned dimensions: `[B,T,d] @ [d,V] → [B,T,V]`. Broadcasting can expand compatible dimensions without your intending it; correct execution is not proof of correct maths. A gradient gives the local sensitivity of a scalar objective to each parameter.

For `L=½(wx−y)²`, `dL/dw=(wx−y)x`. At `w=1,x=2,y=1`, gradient=2; learning rate .1 gives new w=.8. The chain rule connects such local derivatives through layers.

**Follow-up example.** Subtracting [B,1] and [B] can broadcast into [B,B]. Inspect the intended axes and unreduced values on two known cases; averaging a wrong-shaped loss can hide the bug.

/api/learning/interview/F06.title: Can you average two microbatch losses with unequal valid-token counts?
/api/learning/interview/F06.markdown:
Gradients add until cleared. Accumulation approximates a larger batch only if loss weighting and optimizer-step timing are correct; stochastic layers and other details can still differ. Ten valid tokens with mean loss 2 and ninety with mean loss 4 give `(10×2+90×4)/100=3.8`, not 3. Masked/padding tokens must not inflate the denominator.

**Follow-up example.** Accumulate correctly weighted gradients, then clip under the declared update rule and step once. Compare with a deterministic full-batch reference; dropout or batch-dependent layers can still differ.

/api/learning/interview/F07.title: Why is next-token cross-entropy not confidence that an answer is true?
/api/learning/interview/F07.markdown:
Cross-entropy punishes assigning low probability to the observed target. For one correct token with p=.25, loss is `−ln(.25)≈1.386` nats. KL compares distributions: `Σ p log(p/q)`; it is directional, generally not symmetric, and can diverge when q gives zero probability to p-supported events.

Calibration asks whether predicted confidence matches frequency for a defined event. A .9 token probability is not a .9 probability that a full answer is factually correct. Define the event, labels and sample population before making a confidence claim.

**Follow-up example.** A token probability of 0.9 concerns that token under its context, not verified factual correctness of the full answer. Calibration needs reviewed labels for the actual event.

/api/learning/interview/F08.title: A new system gains a few points on the same questions. Is that convincing?
/api/learning/interview/F08.markdown:
Bootstrap resampling builds many alternative evaluation lists by sampling the original units with replacement. For two systems on the same cases, resample the cases **as pairs**, recompute the score difference many times, and use an interval procedure such as percentile bounds. If questions share a document/scenario, resample that cluster where appropriate rather than pretending all questions are independent. The interval estimates uncertainty under the resampling assumptions. A 95% confidence procedure aims for repeated-sampling coverage; it is not a posterior probability assigned to this particular fixed population difference.

Example: an estimated gain .03 with interval [−.01,.07] does not clearly distinguish a gain from no gain under that procedure. Holm adjusts a declared family of p-value tests to control family-wise error: sort p-values and compare successively to `α/(m−i+1)`, stopping at the first failure. It cannot rescue leaked data or uncontrolled post-hoc searching.

**Follow-up example.** A bootstrap of fixed predictions estimates case-sampling uncertainty, not variation across retrained models. Repeat seeds separately when that source of variation matters.

/api/learning/interview/F09.title: How would you know which dataset produced a checkpoint?
/api/learning/interview/F09.markdown:
An ID names a record; a content hash fingerprints bytes under a defined hash/serialization rule. Different line endings or JSON ordering can change bytes, so canonicalize deliberately. Hashes help identify exact artifacts and detect changes; they do not establish truth, license permission or trust in the publisher.

**Follow-up example.** Record stable source IDs, raw and processed hashes, and configuration revisions. Row numbers can change after sorting; hashes detect changes but do not establish data rights or publisher trust.

/api/learning/interview/F10.title: A request timed out. Is it safe to retry?
/api/learning/interview/F10.markdown:
Not automatically: the server might have completed the work before its response was lost. The retry decision depends on whether the operation is safe to repeat or has reliable idempotency/status handling.

DNS resolves a hostname; transport establishes communication; TLS can protect data in transit and authenticate the server; HTTP carries the request/response. None alone authorizes a user to see a tenant's job. Your backend validates inputs, authenticates identity, checks permission, calls bounded services and returns a defined status/body.

Streaming delivers partial response events, not automatic durable completion. A timeout means the caller stopped waiting, not proof the server did nothing. Distinguish retryable rate/temporary failures from invalid requests and authorization denials; respect provider retry guidance within your budget/deadline.

**Follow-up example.** A remote write may already have completed. Use supported idempotency or status lookup and reconcile uncertain outcomes. Do not treat an authorization failure as a transient error.

/api/learning/interview/F11.title: Why does an async API stall during preprocessing?
/api/learning/interview/F11.markdown:
Async lets a task yield while waiting on I/O; it does not make CPU-heavy Python or model inference free. Blocking work inside the event loop can stall unrelated requests. Threads can help I/O and some native operations; Python runtime/GIL details vary, so measure rather than assume arbitrary parallel Python speedup. Processes isolate interpreters/state but add memory and communication costs.

A durable worker queue persists jobs across API restarts. An in-process background task does not automatically survive a crash. Bound concurrency, propagate cancellation/deadlines, and lock/atomically update shared budget/state where races matter.

**Follow-up example.** A semaphore limits in-flight work but cannot make a blocking CPU loop nonblocking. Use a suitable worker boundary; durable job storage is separate from concurrency control.

/api/learning/interview/F12.title: Two reviewers click execute together. How do you prevent duplicate tickets?
/api/learning/interview/F12.markdown:
Two workers can both pass a preliminary check before either writes. Enforce the allowed local execution with a transaction and unique key, rather than relying on the UI or a check-then-write sequence. Tables model proposals/approvals/executions; primary/foreign keys and uniqueness enforce relationships. An index speeds some reads at storage/write cost; it is not automatically useful for every query. A transaction groups operations under a chosen isolation model. ACID means atomicity, consistency constraints, isolation and durability—not that arbitrary business logic is correct.

For a synthetic ticket, a unique execution key plus a transaction prevents duplicate local writes. A remote API write cannot be made atomic merely by starting your local SQL transaction. Use provider idempotency, an outbox/reconciliation strategy and explicit uncertain outcomes where needed.

**Follow-up example.** Use a tested transaction and unique execution key for local state. A remote API is outside that transaction and needs compatible idempotency or reconciliation.

/api/learning/interview/F13.title: How would you run an experiment on a cluster and collect its logs?
/api/learning/interview/F13.markdown:
The terminal displays a shell; the shell launches commands. macOS and Linux have related Unix tooling but are not identical. SSH opens an authenticated encrypted connection to another machine. On a cluster, the login node is usually for light work; SLURM requests scheduled resources on compute nodes. Git versions source history, not running processes or hidden datasets.

Know `pwd`, `ls`, `cd`, `less`, `rg`, `head`, `tail`, `ps`, `df`, safe permissions, `ssh`, `scp/rsync` with reviewed paths, `tmux`, and cluster-approved `sbatch/squeue/sacct/scancel`. For Git: status/diff/add/commit/branch/switch/log, merge/rebase conflicts and safe pushing. Never practice destructive shell commands on your real thesis; use a disposable fixture directory.

**Follow-up example.** Test and version locally, connect with SSH, prepare the remote environment and submit a bounded scheduler job. Inspect status/logs and cancel only your own job; a login node is not a free training machine.

/api/learning/interview/F14.title: Your classifier finds more positives but its F1 falls. How is that possible?
/api/learning/interview/F14.markdown:
More true positives can improve recall while extra false alarms reduce precision enough to lower F1. I would compare both error types, not just recovered positives.

Linear regression predicts continuous values; logistic regression models class probabilities. Trees split feature space; random forests average/vote across randomized trees to reduce variance, without universally eliminating overfitting. Neural networks learn representations through differentiable layers. A strong lexical/logistic/tree baseline can beat a complicated model for the task and data at hand.

Precision asks how many predicted positives are correct; recall asks how many actual positives were found. F1 trades them off; macro averaging gives classes equal weight, not instances equal weight. Thresholds, prevalence and error costs matter. Use validation for choices and a held-out test for final reporting.

**Follow-up example.** TP=8, FP=2, FN=2 gives binary F1=16/20=0.80. TP=9, FP=9, FN=1 gives 18/28=0.6429: more recovered positives, but many more false alarms. Macro-F1 additionally averages class-level scores.

/api/learning/interview/F15.title: Why might lexical search beat embeddings on a support query?
/api/learning/interview/F15.markdown:
An exact product identifier or error code can be better served by lexical matching than broad learned similarity. I would inspect those queries before switching retrieval methods.

Classification, sequence labelling, retrieval, extraction, generation and entailment ask different questions. Words/tokens are not interchangeable. Negation, references, discourse, pragmatic intent and annotation guidelines can change a label even when vocabulary is similar. TF-IDF/BM25 use lexical matching/weighting; embeddings represent learned similarity; a cross-encoder jointly reads a query-document pair to score it.

RNN/LSTM models maintain sequential state; Transformers use attention with positional information. Bidirectional encoders suit many representation/classification tasks; causal decoders generate next tokens. This does not make one universally best.

**Follow-up example.** Exact error codes can favor lexical matching; paraphrases can favor learned similarity. Compare the actual relevance cases. Similarity does not prove entailment or source support.

/api/learning/interview/F16.title: Which parts of this project did you implement yourself?
/api/learning/interview/F16.markdown:
Explain your contribution using concrete decisions, code changes, tests and results. Distinguish original work from adapted components, name relevant tools or sources honestly, and be ready to explain and modify a small part of the implementation. Research design and independent coding are different kinds of evidence; do not claim either without an example.

For an unfamiliar question: clarify the task, state assumptions, derive a small case, propose a simple baseline, identify uncertainty and describe how you would test it. Avoid guessing a framework API as if certain.

**Follow-up example.** Separate research decisions, adapted/generated code, testing and unaided implementation. If a follow-up is unfamiliar, state assumptions and reason through a small case rather than invent experience.

/api/learning/interview/M01.title: Where do next-token training labels come from?
/api/learning/interview/M01.markdown:
In causal pretraining, the text supplies the target. For `[BOS,A,B,EOS]`, an explicit shifted convention uses inputs `[BOS,A,B]` and targets `[A,B,EOS]`. The objective averages negative log probability over included target positions. Some libraries accept unshifted labels and shift internally: check the implementation so you do not shift twice.

This differs from supervised classification, where annotators/dataset rules supply an external class label. A generated SFT answer is also not automatically a gold answer; it needs the chosen quality/provenance review.

**Follow-up example.** Some libraries shift labels internally. Check one explicit input/label pair so your own shift does not shift the target twice.

/api/learning/interview/M02.title: Why did changing the tokenizer or chat template break the model?
/api/learning/interview/M02.markdown:
A tokenizer converts text to IDs that the model's embeddings understand. BPE repeatedly merges frequent pairs under a learned rule; byte-based choices help represent arbitrary input but may fragment languages unevenly. Vocabulary size trades longer sequences against larger embedding/output tables. The exact tokenizer is part of the checkpoint contract.

A chat template turns roles/messages/tool results into the token sequence expected by an instruction model. Wrong role delimiters, special tokens or thinking-mode settings can change behaviour without changing weights. Do not “fix” a mismatched tokenizer by substituting IDs from another model.

**Follow-up example.** Token IDs belong to a particular vocabulary and embedding table. Inspect the serialized roles, special tokens and response mask instead of copying another model's IDs.

/api/learning/interview/M03.title: How can a causal model train in parallel but generate one token at a time?
/api/learning/interview/M03.markdown:
Causal training predicts the next token from preceding tokens. Masked training predicts deliberately hidden tokens using permitted bidirectional context. Encoder–decoder models encode an input and generate a target using decoder self-attention and cross-attention to the encoded input. They differ in objective and information flow, not only model size.

Teacher forcing provides true preceding target tokens during training. At generation time, a causal decoder conditions on its own prior outputs, so mistakes can affect later tokens. The causal mask prevents future-token leakage while allowing many training positions in parallel.

**Follow-up example.** Training knows the correct prefix at each position; generation must wait for its own earlier choices. Test the causal mask by changing a future input and checking earlier logits in evaluation mode.

/api/learning/interview/M04.title: What do queries, keys and values actually do in attention?
/api/learning/interview/M04.markdown:
Input states X are projected into queries Q, keys K and values V. For one head, `softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k + mask)V` forms a weighted sum of value vectors. The query/key comparison determines weights; values supply the mixed content. Scaling stabilizes score magnitude as key dimension grows. Multi-head attention learns several such projections; heads are concatenated/projected.

Residual connections preserve an additive path for information/gradients; normalization controls activation scales; the position-wise MLP transforms features. Positions matter because content-only attention does not by itself distinguish arbitrary token order. Learned/sinusoidal positions and RoPE encode order differently.

**Follow-up example.** The largest attention coefficient is a mixing weight, not proof of why an answer is true. Other heads, layers and residual paths also affect the result.

/api/learning/interview/M05.title: What changes when you call backward and then the optimizer?
/api/learning/interview/M05.markdown:
Read a batch → forward pass → compute correctly masked loss → backward gradients → optional accumulation/clipping → optimizer update → schedule/record/checkpoint. AdamW keeps moving gradient statistics and decouples weight decay; its extra state costs memory. Dropout, weight decay and early stopping solve different problems.

Loss decreasing does not prove useful generalization. Compare a tiny overfit sanity check, held-out loss and task outcomes. Mixed precision can reduce cost but introduces backend/dtype/operator constraints; FP16/BF16 are not interchangeable guarantees of stability.

**Follow-up example.** Backward computes gradients; the optimizer applies its update. If learning fails, check finite gradients, parameter connectivity, optimizer membership and whether a step actually occurs.

/api/learning/interview/M06.title: Training loss becomes NaN after 200 steps. What would you inspect?
/api/learning/interview/M06.markdown:
NaN means “not a number,” often produced by an invalid numerical operation. For this failure, locate the first nonfinite input/activation/loss/gradient; inspect data, masks, log/softmax stability, dtype and learning rate before randomly changing everything. An all-masked target batch can cause an invalid reduction. For OOM: identify weights, optimizer, activations, cache and concurrent processes; then reduce the actual limiting component. Training KV cache is not necessarily an inference-style persistent cache.

A checkpoint needs model/optimizer/scheduler and, where applicable, scaler, RNG and sampler/data position. Weights alone do not reproduce the next update. Resume compatibility and deterministic tolerances must be stated.

**Follow-up example.** A memory failure needs allocation/workload checks, not the same response as a nonfinite loss. A bad restart needs model, optimizer, random and data-order state checks. Diagnose the observed failure first.

/api/learning/interview/M07.title: Why might training not fit when FP16 weights occupy only 2 GB?
/api/learning/interview/M07.markdown:
Raw FP16 weights for 1B parameters occupy about 2 GB decimal before overhead. Training also needs gradients, optimizer states and activations. A common rough dense-training FLOP estimate is `6×parameters×training tokens`, under simplifying assumptions; attention/context, architecture and implementation can make it inaccurate. It is an order-of-magnitude budget, not a timing prediction.

Replicated data-parallel training copies model state across devices and aggregates gradients; FSDP/ZeRO shard selected state; TP splits tensor operations; PP splits layers/stages. Communication bandwidth, synchronization and pipeline bubbles can dominate. Gradient checkpointing recomputes activations to save memory at compute cost.

**Follow-up example.** Choose a distributed strategy only after identifying whether replicated state, activations or an operation is limiting. Sharding and recomputation solve different problems and add communication or compute.

/api/learning/interview/M08.title: Why does grouped-query attention reduce serving memory?
/api/learning/interview/M08.markdown:
GQA shares key/value heads among query heads, reducing KV storage relative to standard MHA at fixed other dimensions; MQA uses a single KV head. MoE routes tokens to a subset of expert networks: active computation and total parameter/storage requirements are different, and routing/load balance/communication add costs. RoPE rotates query/key components with position; it is not unlimited reliable context extrapolation.

An efficient attention kernel can avoid materializing large intermediate matrices and improve memory movement without changing the mathematical dense-attention function, up to numerical differences. State-space/hybrid/diffusion-language approaches change other assumptions and need their own objective/context evaluation.

**Follow-up example.** GQA shares KV heads; MoE instead selects expert subnetworks. Efficient kernels change execution and memory movement. Compare the resource each mechanism actually changes.

/api/learning/interview/M09.title: An assistant gives outdated policy answers and inconsistent JSON. Would you fine-tune it?
/api/learning/interview/M09.markdown:
Prompting changes the input; RAG supplies selected external evidence without necessarily changing weights. Continued pretraining extends a language-model objective on new text. SFT trains on demonstrations of desired input/output behaviour. None substitutes for permission to execute an external action.

Changing service limits belong in versioned evidence, not solely in a weight update. Consistent response/tool format may benefit from SFT, but first test a well-prompted baseline. A model can learn behaviour without reliably memorising exact current facts, and can memorize private training content despite retrieval ACLs.

**Follow-up example.** Use current permitted evidence for changing facts and a schema/validation baseline for formatting. SFT may improve consistent behaviour but does not replace fresh policy or authorization.

/api/learning/interview/M10.title: Why can LoRA still run out of memory with few trainable parameters?
/api/learning/interview/M10.markdown:
Full tuning updates all selected base parameters. LoRA learns a low-rank update: `W' = W + sBA`, with A `[r,d_in]` and B `[d_out,r]`; parameter count is `r(d_in+d_out)` instead of `d_in×d_out` for that matrix. At 4096×4096,r=8, this is 65,536 adapter parameters. Low trainable-parameter count does not remove base-weight or activation memory.

QLoRA combines low-bit base storage with adapter learning and specific implementation choices; it is not simply “LoRA has quantized gradients.” Hardware/operator support matters, so CUDA-oriented tooling is not assumed to run natively on M4. The adapter needs its compatible base/template/config and evaluated conversion path.

**Follow-up example.** The frozen base and required activations still occupy memory. QLoRA adds a particular low-bit base/adaptation recipe; it is not simply quantized gradients and needs supported operators.

/api/learning/interview/M11.title: What changes during one LLM reinforcement-learning iteration?
/api/learning/interview/M11.markdown:
The policy generates a response/action sequence; an environment/verifier/reward model assigns feedback; an advantage/baseline helps evaluate choices; an objective updates policy parameters. Repeat with controlled sampling and evaluate independently. Yes, LLM RL updates weights and is a form of post-training, but its signal/objective differ from matching a fixed demonstrated answer in SFT.

Separate roles: policy generates; reward model scores preferences; critic estimates value; reference policy anchors behaviour. The old rollout policy used for a PPO probability ratio need not be the fixed reference used for KL. Some methods omit a learned critic/reward model.

**Follow-up example.** Policy, reward model, critic and reference have different roles. The old sampling policy in a probability ratio need not be the fixed regularization reference.

/api/learning/interview/M12.title: What does DPO encourage in a preferred versus rejected answer pair?
/api/learning/interview/M12.markdown:
DPO encourages the preferred completion to gain relative likelihood against the rejected one, compared with a reference model. It learns from preferred/rejected response pairs without running a separate on-policy rollout-and-critic loop for that objective. A standard form is `−log σ(β[(log π(y+|x)−log π_ref(y+|x))−(log π(y−|x)−log π_ref(y−|x))])`. Sequence log probabilities sum included response-token log probabilities; masking and the actual chosen objective variant matter.

The margin compares the policy's relative preference against a reference, not just whether the winner's raw probability is large. At margin zero the loss is ln2≈.693; at scaled margin 1 it is about .313. Lower training loss does not guarantee truthful answers if pairs reward confidence, length or sycophancy.

**Follow-up example.** Decreasing pair loss does not establish truthfulness. Labels may reward verbosity or confidence; check held-out task quality and response masking independently.

/api/learning/interview/M13.title: What does PPO clip, and why does advantage sign matter?
/api/learning/interview/M13.markdown:
An advantage estimates how much better or worse a sampled action was than a baseline. PPO's clipped policy surrogate uses ratio `r=π_new(a|s)/π_old(a|s)` and advantage A: maximize `min(rA, clip(r,1−ε,1+ε)A)`, with value/entropy/KL terms depending on the implementation. For A=1,r=1.5,ε=.2, the clipped surrogate is 1.2 rather than 1.5. Negative advantage changes which term limits the objective; calculate instead of saying “always clip rewards.”

GRPO-family implementations use multiple sampled responses to a prompt to form a group-relative advantage, often using group reward mean/std instead of a learned value critic. Equal rewards give no centred relative signal; standard deviation handling must avoid division by zero. Loss normalization, KL and importance weighting vary by implementation/version.

**Follow-up example.** For A=-1, ratio=0.5 and band [0.8,1.2], the surrogate is min(-0.5,-0.8)=-0.8. It is maximized; a loss commonly negates it. GRPO normalization is not clipping rewards.

/api/learning/interview/M14.title: Why does temperature zero not guarantee factual or identical answers?
/api/learning/interview/M14.markdown:
At each step the model produces logits. Temperature rescales them before softmax; top-k/top-p restrict candidates under defined rules; sampling chooses a token; stopping rules terminate. Greedy decoding selects a maximum rather than naively dividing by zero for temperature=0. Low temperature does not prove factuality or universal reproducibility.

Constrained generation can enforce a grammar/schema, but a valid structure can contain false facts or unauthorized actions. Free-form reasoning adds computation/text and may help some tasks; an explanation is not automatically a faithful account of internal causation.

**Follow-up example.** A schema can ensure output structure without ensuring true facts or authorized actions. Decoding, semantic validation and backend permissions solve different problems.

/api/learning/interview/M15.title: Why does a long prompt delay the first token and require more memory?
/api/learning/interview/M15.markdown:
Prefill processes prompt tokens; decode produces further tokens while reusing eligible cached keys/values. Approximate KV bytes are `2×layers×batch×tokens×kv_heads×head_dim×bytes_per_element`, excluding allocator/paging/other overhead. For 12 layers, one sequence,1024 tokens,4 KV heads,64 dimensions,2-byte elements, the cache is 12 MiB. Doubling sequence count roughly doubles that component.

Quantization reduces precision/storage, with metadata, kernel and quality trade-offs. Distillation trains a student using teacher signal; pruning removes selected structure/weights. None guarantees speedup on unsupported kernels. Prefix caching, batching and speculative decoding affect different portions of latency; exactness depends on the algorithm used.

**Follow-up example.** Time to first token, inter-token gaps and total latency measure different things. State prompt/output lengths, concurrency, cache warmth and runtime before comparing.

/api/learning/interview/M16.title: A new model scores better. How would you establish that the change helped?
/api/learning/interview/M16.markdown:
Define the task, baseline, selection data, final evaluation and primary metric before comparing. Keep model/input/evidence/budget fixed except the intended factor; where not possible, call it an operational comparison rather than isolated causality. Report support/coverage, failures, cost and uncertainty—not only a selected best score.

Generalization can fail because inputs changed, label definitions changed or a shortcut stopped working. Test those separately. A probe can reveal decodable information without proving the model used it; an activation intervention needs controls for collateral damage and distribution effects.

**Follow-up example.** A probe can reveal decodable information without proving it caused a gain. Mechanistic claims need controlled interventions and checks beyond a better task score.

/api/learning/interview/S01.title: An employee asks about an error code. How does a retrieval assistant answer?
/api/learning/interview/S01.markdown:
Documents first need permission review, parsing and versioned source spans. When an employee asks about an error code, the server identifies the allowed sources, searches them, selects relevant passages within the context budget and supplies them to the answer model. The response needs citations to accessible passages that actually support its claims. Retrieved content is evidence, not authority to change tool permissions.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can improve access to current evidence; it does not guarantee the retriever finds the right source or that the generator uses it correctly. Separate failures at each stage. A perfect answer given oracle evidence can help diagnose a retrieval bottleneck, but oracle performance is not deployable performance.

**Follow-up example.** If manual oracle evidence fixes the answer, investigate parsing/retrieval before retraining generation. Oracle quality diagnoses a bottleneck; it is not deployable performance.

/api/learning/interview/S02.title: When would you use lexical search, vector search or reranking?
/api/learning/interview/S02.markdown:
Lexical retrieval matches words/identifiers with weighting; it is strong on exact error codes. Dense retrieval compares learned vector representations and may match paraphrases. Hybrid combines complementary scores/ranks using an explicit rule rather than adding incomparable raw numbers blindly. A cross-encoder reranks a smaller candidate list by reading query/document together, at extra latency.

An ANN index trades resource use and approximate vector-neighbour recall; high vector recall is not proof of task relevance. Normalization and cosine/dot-product/Euclidean choices must match the embedding model and index settings.

**Follow-up example.** Fuse scores or ranks using an explicit validated rule. Raw scores can have incompatible scales; vector-neighbor recall is not the same as relevance to a user's task.

/api/learning/interview/S03.title: A policy exception is split from its rule. How would you fix chunks and citations?
/api/learning/interview/S03.markdown:
Preserve semantic units and important caveats: a condition/negation/table header separated from its value can invert meaning. Small chunks improve specificity but can lose context; large chunks add noise/cost. Overlap helps some boundaries but can multiply near-duplicates. Choose by labelled task outcomes, not a universal token count.

Store immutable source version and exact span; validate citation references against sources the caller may access. A real source ID can still be attached to a claim it does not support. A source update must affect index selection, caches and retained summaries—not just the raw file.

**Follow-up example.** A genuine source ID is insufficient if the cited span does not support the claim. Preserve applicable version, surrounding qualifications and the caller's access rights.

/api/learning/interview/S04.title: A user asks for another team's private document. Where must access be checked?
/api/learning/interview/S04.markdown:
A vector store supplies similarity search and metadata/index management. A relational store supplies durable structured state and constraints; some systems also support vectors. Start with the simplest adequate deployment. You do not need several databases to demonstrate breadth.

Server-derived identity determines source scope. Metadata filters help enforce that policy but are not a replacement for authentication or authorization. Never let the model choose tenant IDs or arbitrary search filters. Unauthorized content must not leak through hits, previews, counts, cache entries, traces or judge requests.

**Follow-up example.** The server's authenticated identity defines scope. A vector database or metadata filter alone does not secure results, counts, previews, caches and traces.

/api/learning/interview/S05.title: A request exceeds its context window. What would you change?
/api/learning/interview/S05.markdown:
Weights store learned parameters; context is the current serialized input; retrieval brings external evidence; persistent memory is application-owned stored state. A growing chat transcript is not unlimited reliable memory. Count system instructions, messages, evidence, tools, special tokens and reserved output against the actual model/template limit.

For example, a 4,096-token budget minus 600 for system/tools, 300 for the user, 400 for history, 800 reserved for output and a 200-token margin leaves 1,796 for evidence. Treat it as a planning calculation; tokenize the actual serialized request. Removing evidence to fit may change answerability, so ask/abstain when needed.

**Follow-up example.** Summarizing history can lose conditions or preserve stale/private text. Keep provenance and retention rules; clarify or abstain if necessary evidence cannot fit.

/api/learning/interview/S06.title: When would you choose a fixed workflow rather than an agent?
/api/learning/interview/S06.markdown:
A fixed workflow follows code-defined steps; an agent lets a model choose some next actions based on state. Use dynamic choice only where it solves meaningful branching; it adds error, cost and policy risk. Bound allowed tools, steps, deadlines and spend; define terminal states and escalation.

Multiple agents may provide complementary checks, or merely repeat correlated errors. Compare against one agent/fixed workflow at a fair total budget. Do not judge only whether the tool order matches one script: enforce required safety ordering and actual outcomes while permitting valid alternatives.

**Follow-up example.** Multiple agents can repeat correlated errors at extra cost. Compare outcomes and required safety ordering at a matched total budget, allowing valid alternative tool paths.

/api/learning/interview/S07.title: An approved action retries after a timeout. How do you avoid a duplicate?
/api/learning/interview/S07.markdown:
Persist a proposal's exact payload/hash, requester, required approver, expiry and resource versions. Authenticate/authorize the reviewer independently. At execution recheck the approval and current state; edited/expired/stale proposals need review again. Use a unique execution key and database transaction for the local side effect.

If the network times out after a remote write, you may not know whether it succeeded. Use provider-supported idempotency/status lookup or reconciliation before retrying; otherwise expose an uncertain outcome. A graph checkpoint alone does not guarantee exactly-once external action. An outbox records intended work with the local transaction, but consumers still need duplicate-safe handling.

**Follow-up example.** If its payload or resource state changed after approval, obtain approval again. A durable workflow checkpoint does not guarantee exactly-once remote effects.

/api/learning/interview/S08.title: A retrieved runbook asks the assistant to send credentials. What prevents it?
/api/learning/interview/S08.markdown:
A tool schema defines inputs/outputs; the backend enforces allowed functions and resource scope. MCP provides a protocol boundary for a host/client to discover/use server capabilities. It does not make a server trustworthy or grant its tools authority. Pin/review the actual protocol/SDK revision and discovered tool definitions.

Prompt injection occurs when untrusted text tries to redirect system behaviour. Treat retrieved/tool text as data, enforce least privilege outside the model, isolate secrets and constrain outbound destinations. Valid JSON or a regex that removes suspicious phrases cannot prove safety. SSRF occurs when server-side requests are manipulated toward unintended/internal destinations; validate hosts/schemes/redirects and network policy.

**Follow-up example.** Schemas constrain shape; MCP supplies a protocol boundary. Neither authorizes an action. Backend scope, destination and secret-handling controls must reject the harmful request.

/api/learning/interview/S09.title: A remembered preference is stale. How should persistent memory work?
/api/learning/interview/S09.markdown:
Stored summaries/preferences can be stale, wrong, sensitive or scoped to the wrong person/tenant. Give memory a purpose, ownership, provenance, expiry/deletion rule and version dependencies. Separate session state from durable user preference and approved knowledge. Revalidate before using a remembered authorization or current fact; do not treat text memory as permission.

Retrieval caches, prefix/KV caches and answer caches are different objects with different invalidation/security constraints. Cross-session reuse must not expose private content or silently ignore source withdrawal.

**Follow-up example.** Application memory, caches and model weights are separate stores. Deleting a vector cannot promise erasure of weight memorization; explain what deletion and retention actually cover.

/api/learning/interview/S10.title: How would you evaluate an assistant and its LLM judge?
/api/learning/interview/S10.markdown:
Use known fixture outcomes for facts/actions and an explicit human rubric for semantic support/usefulness. Track supported resolution, completeness, clarification/abstention coverage, forbidden actions, duplicate effects and latency/cost separately. A generator grading its own outputs is not independent evidence.

An LLM judge is optional: blind model identity, calibrate against reviewed cases, examine disagreement, order/verbosity bias and prompt injection in evaluated text. Keep development tuning distinct from final cases. A synthetic teacher answer is not gold merely because it sounds fluent.

**Follow-up example.** A correct clarification can be preferable to a confident unsupported answer. Review judge false positives/negatives and order, verbosity and injection biases against an explicit rubric.

/api/learning/interview/S11.title: p95 latency doubled but average tokens per second did not. What would you inspect?
/api/learning/interview/S11.markdown:
p95 latency is the latency at or below which 95% of the measured requests fall under a stated window/workload. A few slow requests can worsen it even when average throughput is stable. Measure queueing, retrieval, prefill, decode and tool time separately. Bound admission/concurrency and propagate deadlines. Use backpressure/load shedding rather than infinite retries. A timeout/cancellation may leave work or billed usage in flight, so reserve worst-case allowed cost before dispatch and settle actual usage afterward; atomic reservations prevent races.

Routing to a smaller/local model can reduce some cost but may harm quality; escalation/fallback needs evidence, data-region permission and remaining budget. A provider-compatible API can differ in templates, capabilities, rates and usage fields. Do not silently switch to a paid or privacy-incompatible backend.

**Follow-up example.** Queueing, long outputs, retries and tools can worsen tail latency while average throughput is stable. A cheaper fallback must also satisfy quality, data policy and remaining budget.

/api/learning/interview/S12.title: A new index produces wrong answers after release. How would you recover?
/api/learning/interview/S12.markdown:
Logs record events, metrics aggregate measurements, traces connect request steps. Capture relevant versions, latency, errors, queue saturation and usage without exporting secrets/private source text by default. Quality drift needs labelled review/evaluation, not just uptime. Define a service-level indicator/objective with a population/window; “99% reliable” without a denominator is incomplete.

Release compatible code/model/template/index/policy versions together when required. Keep a tested fallback; rehearse restore from backup on synthetic data. Rolling back code may not undo database migrations, external side effects or a poisoned source—plan those separately. Local Compose or Kubernetes exercise is not proof of multi-region high availability.

**Follow-up example.** Rolling back application code may not restore an old index, reverse a migration or undo an external action. Recover a compatible approved state and test the repair.

/api/learning/interview/D01.title: Design a support assistant that uses the current policy
/api/learning/interview/D01.markdown:
Suppose employees ask about support incidents, and policy limits change over time. The assistant must use the applicable version and show where its answer came from. I would first clarify who may access which incidents, whether the assistant only answers or also performs actions, and how quickly a policy update must appear.

I would start with permission-aware incident lookup and lexical search over versioned documents. The answer model receives selected evidence; the application validates source references and support. Current policies belong in externally managed evidence, not only in fine-tuned weights. Dense retrieval or reranking should address a measured baseline weakness rather than appear by default.

For a concrete failure, incident 104 concerns a 28 MiB attachment under policy version 2. Version 1 allowed 30 MiB; version 2 allows 20 MiB. An answer using the old limit is wrong for this case even if its citation is genuine. Missing version information should lead to clarification or an explicitly conditional answer.

Ten thousand 768-dimensional float32 vectors need 30.72 MB of raw values before text, metadata and index overhead. At two requests per second and eight seconds average response time, stable average in-flight work is 16 by Little's law; this does not prove a laptop can run 16 generations concurrently.

I would evaluate current-version correctness, supported answers, useful clarification, access violations and latency. The first release can be read-only. A good follow-up is what happens when an old source is withdrawn: index, cache and retained summaries all need a compatible policy.

/api/learning/interview/D02.title: Design a human-approved action that can survive a restart
/api/learning/interview/D02.markdown:
The assistant proposes a ticket, a person approves it, and execution may happen after an application restart. I would store the exact proposal, requester, required approval, expiry and resource version before acknowledging that the work is waiting. Approval must bind to the payload that will actually execute.

For a local database action, the execution transaction rechecks current authority and proposal state, then uses a unique execution key to prevent two concurrent attempts creating two tickets. “We check whether a ticket exists first” is insufficient if both attempts can pass the check before either writes.

A remote service changes the problem. The local transaction cannot atomically include an arbitrary remote API. Use a supported idempotency key and status lookup, record durable intent and reconcile an uncertain timeout. If the provider cannot establish whether an irreversible action completed, expose that uncertainty instead of blindly retrying.

I would test duplicate clicks, a changed proposal, expired approval, lost responses and crashes before and after dispatch. Success means the correct authorized final state without an unintended duplicate, not a prescribed sequence of tool calls. A workflow checkpoint helps resumption but is not an exactly-once guarantee for external effects.

/api/learning/interview/D03.title: Serve a language model on limited local hardware
/api/learning/interview/D03.markdown:
I would ask for actual available memory, supported runtimes, privacy constraints and representative prompt/output lengths before choosing a model. Nominal parameter storage is only a lower bound: 1.7 billion parameters at four bits represent 0.85 GB of raw bits, before scales, unquantized tensors, cache, temporary buffers and runtime overhead.

The design can begin with one compatible local runtime, bounded admission and explicit context/output caps. Queueing is preferable to launching unlimited simultaneous generations, but a full queue must have a defined rejection or timeout response. A cloud fallback is optional only if its cost and data policy are authorized.

I would measure first-token time, later token gaps, total latency, throughput, peak memory and task quality at the intended workload. Compare cold and warm runs explicitly. Native Metal/MLX support and CUDA on a Linux GPU are different execution profiles; a container does not automatically provide Metal acceleration.

If the workload fails, determine whether the bottleneck is memory, prompt processing, output generation or queueing. Quantization, batching, a smaller model or another replica can address different limits and must be checked for quality regressions. Neither a parameter-count estimate nor a cache formula is a measured speed claim.

/api/learning/interview/D04.title: Plan a training study before committing substantial compute
/api/learning/interview/D04.markdown:
The first question is whether we want to demonstrate a mechanism or produce a useful model. I would define the task, allowed corpus, evaluation split, reference model and success measure before selecting size. Unique training data and repeated token exposures are different quantities.

A rough dense-training estimate for five million parameters and one million token exposures is 6×5 million×1 million = 3×10^13 FLOPs. It omits important architecture/context details and does not predict elapsed time. A stated 16-byte-per-parameter state recipe would account for 80 MB before activations and other allocations; actual precision and optimizer choices can change it.

I would inspect a small batch, verify loss/masks and trainable parameters, overfit a tiny clean case, then run a bounded throughput pilot. Only that pilot can inform a realistic resource request. Record checkpoint/resumption behavior and selection rules before a longer run.

A lower validation text loss but worse support answers could indicate an objective mismatch, masking/template error or forgetting. The conclusion should follow the task evidence, not just the training curve. Distributed execution comes after a correct single-device reference and a reasoned state/communication budget.

/api/learning/interview/D05.title: Keep an assistant usable during outages without exceeding its budget
/api/learning/interview/D05.markdown:
Suppose a provider becomes slow during a traffic spike and there is a hard spending ceiling. I would clarify which features can degrade, what users should see, and which alternative backends are permitted. A visible unavailable response can be safer than an unauthorized fallback.

Use bounded queues, request deadlines, concurrency limits and a finite retry allowance for eligible failures. A circuit breaker temporarily avoids a failing dependency; a rate limiter controls traffic. They do not solve the same problem, and permission denials should not be retried as temporary model failures.

Concurrent requests need atomic budget reservation before dispatch, based on allowed input and maximum output cost under current approved rates. Settle actual usage afterward. A client cancellation does not guarantee upstream work or billing stopped, so release reservations under a documented reconciliation policy rather than assuming everything was free.

I would inspect queue age, latency distribution, errors, usage and supported task outcomes. Test slow responses, uncertain completion, throttling and failure during recovery with local fake services. If both primary and fallback depend on the same network or database, they share a failure risk; two backend names do not prove independent availability.

/api/learning/interview/D06.title: Release a new model and index without leaking another team's data
/api/learning/interview/D06.markdown:
A release must carry compatible code, model, tokenizer/template, index and policy versions. I would establish trusted artifact sources, permitted data use, identity and access rules before opening traffic. The first design question is which threats and mistakes the system must resist, not whether it can be called “secure.”

Server-derived identity should constrain retrieval and tools. Retrieved text, tool metadata and model output remain untrusted inputs. A malicious document asking for secrets must not expand network destinations, source access or execution authority. Trace data also needs redaction and retention rules.

Before release, test wrong-base adapters, mismatched tokenizers, stale indexes, cross-team searches and secret-like dummy values in logs. Keep a recoverable approved version and test restoration. A new code version may require a database migration; rolling it back may not undo that migration or an already completed external action.

If another team's content appears in search, contain the access path, preserve necessary evidence safely and review other exposure surfaces before reopening. Delete/restore actions alone do not prove that downstream summaries, caches or exported logs are clean. Add a regression test for the actual failure. Specialist security/privacy review is distinct from demonstrating a safe local prototype.

/api/learning/interview/P01.title: Return a permitted record without mutating the input
/api/learning/interview/P01.markdown:
Implement lookup(records, record_id, caller_team). The caller's team comes from trusted authentication, not a field supplied by the language model. For a record with id=t1, team=a and status=open, caller a may receive id and status. A caller outside the allowed team must not receive private fields or confirmation that distinguishes a forbidden record from an unknown one under this policy.

A good solution separates lookup from authorization and returns only allowed output fields. Decide how malformed and duplicate records are handled rather than silently selecting an arbitrary duplicate. Test that changing the returned object cannot unexpectedly mutate the input record. Dictionary lookup can be efficient, but building the index has a cost and duplicate policy.

A useful follow-up is adding a new optional field. Explain whether the function should expose it automatically; an explicit output contract normally should not.

/api/learning/interview/P02.title: Rank tied results and stay within a context budget
/api/learning/interview/P02.markdown:
Given scored IDs [(b,0.8),(a,0.8),(c,0.2)], return the top two using score descending and ID ascending for ties. The expected IDs are [a,b]. State the behavior for k=0, k larger than the list and duplicate IDs.

A full sort is straightforward; a size-k heap can reduce asymptotic work for large n and small k. Either solution needs deterministic final ordering. Ranking is not authorization, so candidates must already be within the allowed scope.

For a separate context-allocation task, a total budget of 4,096 minus 600 system/tool, 300 user, 400 history, 800 output reserve and 200 safety margin leaves 1,796 evidence tokens. Reject an impossible negative budget instead of dropping safeguards. Verify the real serialized token count later; the arithmetic is a plan, not exact tokenizer output.

/api/learning/interview/P03.title: Explain and implement a stable softmax
/api/learning/interview/P03.markdown:
For logits [1000,1001], subtract the maximum before exponentiating. The result is proportional to [exp(-1),1], giving probabilities approximately [0.2689,0.7311]. Direct exponentiation can overflow without changing the underlying intended probabilities.

Explain why subtracting a common constant cancels in the normalization. Test equal logits and very large magnitudes. State the policy for invalid inputs rather than silently producing NaN. Temperature scales logits before normalization; a greedy temperature-zero path should choose a maximum directly instead of dividing by zero.

A follow-up is deterministic tie-breaking or seeded sampling. Numerical stability and a reproducible random sequence do not make a generated answer factual.

/api/learning/interview/P04.title: Find a future-token leak in a small decoder
/api/learning/interview/P04.markdown:
Use a small supplied attention block in evaluation mode. Feed [A,B,C], change only input C to another token, and compare outputs at positions A and B. Under the intended causal mask, those earlier logits should not change beyond declared numerical tolerance.

If they change, inspect mask orientation, the softmax axis and any operation mixing future positions. Check positions and batch axes before blaming the tokenizer. Training-mode dropout can make this diagnostic noisy, so control stochastic behavior.

A pretrained wrapper can help inspect a model but is not evidence that you implemented a decoder from scratch. If asked to implement one, identify embeddings, positions, Q/K/V, masking, residual paths and the output head explicitly, using autograd where allowed.

/api/learning/interview/P05.title: Calculate the correct loss for unequal microbatches
/api/learning/interview/P05.markdown:
One microbatch contains 10 scored targets with mean loss 2; another has 90 with mean loss 4. The correct combined token mean is (10×2+90×4)/100=3.8, not the unweighted average 3.

Explain which tokens are scored before implementing the calculation. Padding and excluded user-prompt targets do not belong in that denominator. With input [A,B,C] and next-token labels [B,C,D], ensure the library does not apply a second unwanted shift.

A good gradient test compares weighted microbatch contributions against one concatenated deterministic batch, then performs one update. Define what happens when there are no valid targets; do not divide by zero. Correct weighting alone does not make stochastic or batch-normalized executions identical.

/api/learning/interview/P06.title: Diagnose a training failure and restore the right state
/api/learning/interview/P06.markdown:
Suppose loss becomes nonfinite after a checkpoint, and restarting from its weights changes the next update. Explain the two separate investigations.

For the failure, locate the first nonfinite input, activation, loss or gradient and inspect the relevant mask, operation, dtype and update scale. A small clean batch helps distinguish a broken implementation from a difficult dataset.

For resumption, weights are not enough: optimizer/scheduler, applicable scaler, random states and data/sampler position can affect the next update. Compare uninterrupted and restored runs on a small controlled case. Reject a partial save and document numerical tolerances and version compatibility. Do not promise exact replay across arbitrary hardware changes.

/api/learning/interview/P07.title: Compare two prediction lists without overstating the gain
/api/learning/interview/P07.markdown:
Gold labels are [1,0,0,1]. Model A predicts [1,0,1,0]; B predicts [1,0,0,0]. A gets 2/4 correct and B gets 3/4, an accuracy gain of 0.25. These four cases are a teaching fixture, not strong evidence of general superiority.

A paired bootstrap resamples case indices and carries both predictions for each chosen case together. If several cases share a source, use an appropriate group-level unit. This resamples fixed predictions; it does not include retraining variation.

For a multiple-testing follow-up, sorted p-values 0.01,0.03,0.04 with alpha=0.05 face Holm thresholds 0.05/3,0.05/2,0.05. The first passes and the second fails, so stop; do not independently accept the third. Corrections do not repair leaked or repeatedly tuned evaluation data.

/api/learning/interview/P08.title: Diagnose a stale citation instead of changing the prompt blindly
/api/learning/interview/P08.markdown:
A request concerns an attachment of 28 MiB under policy version 2. An answer cites a genuine version-1 rule allowing 30 MiB, but version 2 allows 20 MiB. The source exists, yet the answer uses the wrong applicable rule.

Trace where the mismatch arose: source metadata/parsing, candidate filtering, retrieval, evidence selection or generation. A correct response should identify that 28 exceeds the applicable limit, or clarify the version if it is unknown. It should not perform an external action merely because it found a source.

Build a small relevance/support fixture with exact codes, paraphrases, exceptions and withdrawn versions. An extractive baseline can reveal whether an LLM adds value. A real citation ID is not proof that its span supports the claim.

/api/learning/interview/P09.title: Handle a slow fake API without an infinite retry loop
/api/learning/interview/P09.markdown:
A local fake service produces one timeout, then a rate-limit response, then success. Another endpoint returns a permission denial. Describe a finite retry policy that respects deadlines and does not treat these failures identically.

Bound concurrency and total attempts. Honor relevant retry guidance within the remaining deadline; use backoff/jitter where suitable. A permission denial needs a policy or credential correction, not fallback to a more permissive backend. Validate response shape before passing it onward.

If a request could write remotely, a timeout may conceal successful completion. Use supported idempotency/status handling or surface uncertainty. Cancelling the waiting caller does not prove upstream work stopped. No paid provider is needed to demonstrate this reasoning.

/api/learning/interview/P10.title: Prevent two concurrent local executions
/api/learning/interview/P10.markdown:
Two workers both read an approved proposal as unexecuted before either writes a ticket. A check-then-write approach can create duplicates.

Use a transaction and a unique execution key, with an appropriate isolation/locking strategy. Recheck the exact approved payload, expiry, resource version and executing authority. Race both attempts in a disposable database and show one permitted local side effect, not merely one successful UI message.

For a remote service, explain the remaining boundary: a local SQL transaction cannot include arbitrary remote effects atomically. A durable intent/outbox, compatible provider idempotency and reconciliation address different parts of the problem. Unknown completion must remain visible where it cannot be resolved.

/api/learning/interview/P11.title: Reject a harmful action even when its JSON is valid
/api/learning/interview/P11.markdown:
A retrieved document tells the assistant to ignore approval and send a secret to an external URL. The model emits a schema-valid tool call. Explain where execution must be prevented.

The backend checks authenticated identity, action scope, approved destinations and current authorization independently of the model. Document text cannot grant permission. A schema validates structure, not whether an action is allowed. A hidden button or stronger prompt is not the enforcing control.

Use synthetic secret-like text and fake tools to test cross-team lookup, cached previews, malicious metadata and stale approval. Inspect traces too: rejecting execution does not help if logging already leaked private content. No real secret or external transmission is needed.

/api/learning/interview/P12.title: Distinguish a numerical preference example from actual RL training
/api/learning/interview/P12.markdown:
Start with a DPO scaled margin of zero. Its pair loss is -log(sigmoid(0))=log 2≈0.6931. At scaled margin one the loss is about 0.3133. Explain which answer is labelled preferred and which reference/policy log probabilities form that margin.

For PPO, calculate the clipped policy surrogate for both advantage signs; do not call it clipping rewards. For a group-relative example, equal rewards provide no within-group ranking, and division by zero must be avoided.

These arithmetic tasks are not a trained policy. A toy action-policy update and a real language-model adapter run are additional evidence levels with different data, compute and evaluation requirements. A good answer names what was actually calculated or run, including masks, reference roles and independent quality checks.

/api/learning/interview/P13.title: Interpret a serving measurement before optimizing it
/api/learning/interview/P13.markdown:
Run A has first-token time 100 ms and nine later token gaps of 20 ms. Run B has first-token time 50 ms and nine gaps of 40 ms. For ten output tokens, totals under this simplified timing boundary are 280 ms and 410 ms. B starts sooner but finishes later.

State whether measurements include queueing, retrieval and postprocessing. Match prompt/output lengths, concurrency, runtime, cache warmth and model version before attributing a difference to compression. Quantization can reduce storage without speeding unsupported kernels or preserving all task quality.

A memory estimate is useful before loading a model, but is not a measured peak. If hardware is unavailable, label the design unmeasured instead of inventing latency numbers.

/api/learning/interview/P14.title: Explain a capacity estimate and a budget race
/api/learning/interview/P14.markdown:
At a stable average arrival rate of two requests per second and mean end-to-end time eight seconds, Little's law gives average in-flight work 16. This does not describe peak traffic, p95 latency or prove that one GPU can support that concurrency.

For a budget race, two requests both see enough money before either reserves it. A non-atomic check can overspend. Reserve permitted worst-case usage atomically before dispatch, then settle actual usage under the documented policy. Include allowed retries/candidates in planning and account for uncertain in-flight work.

A local simulated workload can demonstrate queue saturation, rate limiting, cancellation and recovery. Review traffic, errors, latency, saturation and task quality together; high tokens per second alone can hide unacceptable waiting or wrong answers.

/api/learning/interview/P15.title: Adapt a system design when the interviewer changes a constraint
/api/learning/interview/P15.markdown:
Choose one design scenario, explain its user/task and simplest viable data flow, then respond to a changed condition: offline only, ten times the peak traffic, a revoked source, an outage or stricter privacy.

A good answer identifies which assumptions broke and what changes as a result. Offline operation may remove cloud fallback; source revocation affects retrieval and caches; more traffic may expose queueing rather than model-size limits. Do not add agents, Kubernetes or fine-tuning solely to sound sophisticated.

Calculate one relevant bound, walk a successful request and a failure, and name what you would measure before committing. Explain what you deliberately leave out and when specialist help is needed. There is no single architecture diagram correct for every version of the problem.

/api/learning/interview/P16.title: Reproduce a run when a required artifact is missing
/api/learning/interview/P16.markdown:
A colleague receives weights but no tokenizer, preprocessing configuration or dependency versions. Explain why loading the tensors is not the same as reproducing the prediction pipeline.

Identify the compatible base/template or feature map, input/output contract, code revision and permitted data. Reproduce a small non-sensitive fixture first, with known expected outputs and declared tolerance. A hash detects changed bytes but does not establish a publisher is trusted.

In a disposable repository, inspect the diff and make a small tested change on a branch. Do not rewrite shared history casually or practice destructive commands on real work. A release should exclude secrets/private data and document its limitations. Another reader should be able to locate the exact code, settings and result, not just see a successful screenshot.
