reading.lesson_markdown:
A recurrent encoder reads one token vector at a time and updates a hidden state. The same weights are reused at every position. In a forward RNN, the state after “not good” can depend on both words, while the state after “not” cannot depend on the next word yet.

For $h_t=\tanh(0.5x_t+0.8h_{t-1})$, start with zero state and inputs 1 then 0. The first state is about 0.462; the next is $\tanh(0.8(0.462))\approx0.354$. Earlier evidence persists through the recurrence but can shrink or be transformed. These are fixed illustrative weights, not a fitted language model.

A bidirectional RNN also reads from the end toward the beginning, then combines states at each position. That can help tag an ambiguous word using both sides of a complete sentence. It is not legal to expose the true future when testing an ordinary causal next-token predictor.

Backpropagation through time differentiates through the unrolled updates. Long chains can cause vanishing or exploding gradients. Gated cells change how state is retained; bidirectionality changes which context is available. They solve different problems.

Sources: [D2L: recurrent networks](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-neural-networks/rnn.html), [SLP: RNNs and LSTMs](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/14.pdf).

# N09. LSTMs and bidirectional LSTMs

A long short-term memory network, or LSTM, is a recurrent model with a cell state for carried memory and a hidden state exposed to other layers. Gates determine how much old memory to retain, new information to write and memory to expose. A bidirectional LSTM uses two independent such recurrences when both input directions are available.

The scalar cell uses inputs [1,0,−1], fixed input/output gates and a selectable forget gate. Inspect one position to see its previous memory, candidate, new cell and hidden output. A second direction changes the representation width, not the sequence length.

An ordinary RNN repeatedly transforms its carried state. LSTM adds an additive gated memory path to address some training difficulties; the earlier rules for bidirectional alignment, padding and terminal summaries still apply.

## 1. Cell state, gates and hidden output

An LSTM carries cell state c and hidden state h. The forget gate scales old memory; the input gate controls a candidate addition; the output gate controls how much transformed cell state is exposed as h. Sigmoid gates lie between zero and one, but the cell state itself is not constrained to that interval.

The browser uses constant gate biases and a candidate that depends on the current input and previous hidden state. Those deliberately small parameters permit a complete numerical trace. A real LSTM normally learns input/recurrent matrices for every gate. There are no peepholes or projections in this teaching cell.

The additive memory path can help gradients travel, but forget gates can still shrink information, other paths still matter and useful long-range behaviour is not guaranteed. Increasing a forget gate retains more previous cell value in this example; it is not a universal accuracy improvement.

## 2. Stacked and bidirectional LSTMs

A BiLSTM runs two separately parameterized LSTMs, then aligns and concatenates their hidden outputs. It does not make one cell run backwards during its forward recurrence. The same future-context restrictions as a BiRNN apply.

For a padded batch, tensor layout, valid lengths and directional terminal states must be checked before classification. PyTorch's gate order and weight layout should be read from the actual API when porting parameters. A stacked BiLSTM passes a 2H-width token representation to its next layer; layers are not the same axis as directions. A CRF can follow its token features, but the LSTM gates do not enforce a valid tag sequence by themselves.

## Sources

[PyTorch LSTM](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.LSTM.html) · [Speech and Language Processing — author-hosted draft](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/)

reading.lesson_markdown:
An LSTM introduces an additive memory path called the cell state. A forget gate scales the previous cell; an input gate scales a proposed addition. Their sum forms the new cell. An output gate determines how much of its transformed content becomes the exposed hidden state. The gates are learned functions of current input and prior hidden state.

For previous cell 0.8, forget gate 0.9, input gate 0.2, and candidate −0.5, the new cell is $0.9(0.8)+0.2(-0.5)=0.62$. With output gate 0.7, hidden state is $0.7\tanh(0.62)\approx0.386$. Cell and hidden state are therefore related but not identical. Retaining information does not mean copying every input without change.

A BiLSTM runs two LSTMs in opposite directions and usually concatenates their states. Each token representation can then use left and right context. This is useful for complete-sentence tagging, while autoregressive generation requires the permitted causal direction.

Gating helps gradients and memory but does not guarantee unlimited long-range recall. Sequence length, initialisation, training data, and optimisation still matter. Compare gate definitions carefully: a compact diagram must not hide which state is retained and which is newly written.

Sources: [D2L: LSTM](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-modern/lstm.html), [SLP: recurrent encoders](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/14.pdf).

document.markdown:
# N10. GRUs and recurrent training

A gated recurrent unit, or GRU, controls a recurrent hidden state without a separate LSTM memory cell. The reset gate controls old-state information used in the candidate; the update gate mixes the candidate with the old state. The exact gate convention and reset placement must be read from the equation, because implementations can differ.

The inputs are [1,0,−1]. We hold the old-state mixture weight z at 0.25 and change the reset value. The example uses PyTorch's reset-after-projection convention; a separate matrix-and-bias check demonstrates why placement matters.

LSTM introduced gated memory and exposed hidden state. GRU merges these into one carried state, while the same choices about directions, padding, gradient history and sequence summaries remain separate training decisions.

## 1. GRU equations and reset placement

This course uses PyTorch's GRU convention: \(n_t=\tanh(W_xx_t+b_x+r_t\odot(W_hh_{t-1}+b_h))\), followed by \(h_t=(1-z_t)\odot n_t+z_t\odot h_{t-1}\). Thus a large update gate z retains more old state. Some descriptions reverse which quantity is called the update gate; compare the equation rather than the name.

PyTorch applies the reset gate after the recurrent affine transform in the candidate. Multiplying the old hidden state before the matrix is a different operation in multiple dimensions, especially with biases. The scalar, zero-bias example agrees under both placements, so the independent test also includes a multidimensional nonzero-bias case.

A GRU has no separate LSTM-style cell state. A BiGRU adds another independent directional pass; it is not a GRU that reads both directions in a single recurrence.

## 2. Gradient history, parameter counts and packed batches

Teacher forcing, truncated BPTT, gradient clipping, recurrent-state resets and padding address different issues. Clipping controls a gradient norm; it does not restore lost supervision or repair a misaligned target. Detaching a carried hidden state cuts the graph at that boundary.

For a fair architecture comparison, match data, preprocessing, selection budget and evaluation. Hidden width alone does not match parameter count across RNN/LSTM/GRU or across directions. Use the actual framework's parameter shapes, including its biases, to count them. Shared optimizer/system lessons own general Adam, scheduling and batching details.

### Count the actual framework parameters

For a single PyTorch layer with input width D, hidden width H, biases enabled and no projection, each direction contains \(G H(D+H+2)\) parameters. G is 1 for RNN, 3 for GRU and 4 for LSTM; the +2 accounts for two framework bias vectors per gate. With D=3 and H=4, those counts are 36, 108 and 144 per direction. Bidirectionality doubles this one-layer count. For a later bidirectional layer, input width is normally 2H, so do not simply reuse the first-layer D for the entire stack.

A shape check you can run without downloading data:

```python
import torch
x = torch.zeros(2, 5, 3)  # batch, padded positions, input features
lengths = torch.tensor([5, 3])
packed = torch.nn.utils.rnn.pack_padded_sequence(
    x, lengths.cpu(), batch_first=True, enforce_sorted=False
)
model = torch.nn.LSTM(3, 4, batch_first=True, bidirectional=True)
packed_output, (h, c) = model(packed)
output, valid_lengths = torch.nn.utils.rnn.pad_packed_sequence(
    packed_output, batch_first=True, total_length=5
)
sentence = torch.cat([h[-2], h[-1]], dim=-1)
print(output.shape, sentence.shape)  # [2, 5, 8], [2, 8]
```

This runs an untrained forward pass to verify axes and valid lengths, not language competence or a quality benchmark.

## Sources

[PyTorch GRU](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.GRU.html) · [Speech and Language Processing — author-hosted draft](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/)

steps.prose: The GRU carries h but no separate cell c. In the displayed convention, update gate z weights the old hidden state; one minus z weights the candidate. The reset gate affects how the old state contributes to that candidate.

steps.next: Form a candidate from the current input and reset-controlled recurrent contribution.

steps.title: Calculate the reset-controlled candidate
steps.prose: Project the old hidden state, multiply that recurrent contribution by reset, add the input contribution and apply tanh. Reset zero removes the recurrent candidate contribution here, but does not remove the old-state bypass into the final mixture.
steps.terms: PyTorch applies reset after the recurrent affine transformation. With matrices and biases this need not equal resetting the raw state before projection.
steps.next: Mix the proposed candidate with the preserved old state under the displayed update equation.

steps.title: Mix the candidate and old state
steps.prose: Use 0.75 times the candidate plus 0.25 times the old state. Changing reset affects the candidate and therefore this new state; z remains fixed. A larger z would retain more old state under this convention, not write more candidate.
steps.terms: A complementary mixture uses weights z and one minus z. Both routes remain differentiable under the stated cell computation.

steps.title: Choose directions and gradient history
steps.prose: A second GRU direction supplies suffix context using another parameter set. Detaching carried state instead cuts how far a training gradient reaches into earlier steps; it does not create a reverse input pass. Resetting state between independent documents is another choice.
steps.terms: Backpropagation through time, or BPTT, differentiates through repeated state updates. Truncation limits its history; clipping limits gradient magnitude.

reading.lesson_markdown:
A GRU controls recurrent memory using reset and update gates, without an LSTM's separate cell-state output. The reset gate changes how previous information enters the candidate. The update gate mixes the old state with that candidate. It is a learned, feature-wise mixture, not a threshold applied to the final class probability.

Using the convention $h_t=z_th_{t-1}+(1-z_t)\tilde h_t$, an old state 0.2, candidate 0.8, and update gate 0.75 give $0.75(0.2)+0.25(0.8)=0.35$. A source using the complementary gate convention may write a different-looking formula; identify which coefficient multiplies the old state before comparing implementations.

During batching, mask padding and keep each sequence's state associated with the correct example. Truncated backpropagation detaches the state between windows, limiting how far gradients travel even when numerical state is carried forward. Gradient clipping limits exploding update signals; it does not recover information lost through vanishing gradients.

GRUs can be cheaper than comparable LSTMs, but cell choice alone does not determine task performance. Compare hidden widths, parameter counts, context access, and training conditions rather than treating a smaller gate diagram as proof of superiority.

Sources: [D2L: GRU](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-modern/gru.html), [Cho et al.: recurrent encoder–decoder](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.1078).

# N11. Encoder–decoder models, attention and beam search

An encoder–decoder model represents an input sequence and generates a separate output sequence. Attention lets a decoder read different source positions while producing each target token. Beam search is a decoding procedure that keeps several candidate target prefixes; it changes the search, not the learned model weights or the definition of attention.

First we mix source values [1,2,4] using supplied attention weights to obtain context value 2. Separately, a two-token search tree shows greedy choosing a x with probability 0.30 while beam width two can keep b y with probability 0.38.

Recurrent encoders supply sequence states; an encoder–decoder uses source states to support another sequence's predictions. Distinguish source conditioning from candidate search before considering translation and other generation tasks.

## 1. Source attention and teacher forcing

An encoder reads a source sequence. A decoder predicts a target sequence conditioned on that source and permitted earlier target tokens. A classical recurrent encoder–decoder may initialize its decoder from a terminal source state. Attention allows each decoder query to read source positions again, reducing reliance on one fixed vector.

Encoder source attention, causal decoder self-attention and decoder-to-source cross-attention have different axes and masks. With two target queries and three source positions, cross-attention scores have shape 2 × 3 per head. A recurrent additive-attention score and scaled dot-product attention use different scoring functions even though both normalize over source positions.

Teacher forcing provides known earlier target tokens during training. It must not expose the token currently being predicted as an allowed input. The mismatch between gold prefixes during training and generated prefixes at inference can matter.

## 2. Search rules and generation choices

Greedy decoding selects the current best next token. Beam search retains a bounded collection of candidate prefixes, expands them and ranks cumulative scores. It is an approximation, not proof of the globally best sequence or the most truthful answer. Length penalties, end-of-sequence handling and constraints change the search objective.

T5 and BART apply encoder–decoder architectures with different pretraining recipes. The shared architecture-family lesson owns the full Transformer structure; this view focuses on source/target alignment and the small prefix tree. Compare generation quality, output length and search cost rather than treating beam width as a free quality knob.

## Sources

[Original neural translation attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473) · [Speech and Language Processing — author-hosted draft](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/)

steps.title: Encode the source sequence
steps.prose: The encoder can read the complete supplied source while retaining its valid-position mask. Its states can remain available while target generation grows. The numerical example supplies three scalar source values rather than executing a trained encoder.
steps.terms: Source memory means representations available to the decoder, not persistent memory across unrelated user sessions.

steps.title: Read source memory with attention
steps.prose: The supplied weights sum to one and mix the three source values into context value 2. A learned decoder normally obtains weights from query–key scores. The example isolates the mixing step without pretending to run complete translation.
steps.terms: In the equation a_tj is the attention weight on source position j for target step t, and v_j is its value. The weighted sum supplies one context feature.
steps.next: The next two sections separately demonstrate how a search procedure selects target sequences.

steps.title: Keep candidate output prefixes
steps.prose: At the first output step the fixed tree assigns a probability of 0.6 to a and 0.4 to b. Greedy keeps only a; beam width two keeps both. These probabilities are supplied independently of the attention-mixing example above.
steps.terms: A hypothesis is a candidate output prefix. Beam width caps the retained set; it does not modify parameters or make outputs truthful.
steps.next: Extend only the retained prefixes and compare their full equal-length probabilities.

steps.title: Extend and compare complete candidates
steps.prose: Multiply each retained prefix probability by its continuation probability. Greedy resolves its a x/a y tie in favor of x, scoring 0.30; beam two can find b y at 0.38. There is no end-of-sequence rule or length penalty in this fixed-length fixture.

reading.diagramLabel: Source conditioning; the search example is separate
reading.legend: This diagram shows source/target information access. The separate tree below explains beam search using fixed probabilities; it is not a continuation of the attention arithmetic.
reading.lesson_markdown:
An encoder represents a source sequence; a decoder produces a target sequence conditional on that representation and its generated prefix. Translation is a clear example: the source sentence is available before the target is complete. Source and target lengths need not match.

Attention lets a decoder position choose a weighted mixture of encoder states instead of relying only on one compressed source vector. In cross-attention, queries come from the decoder and keys/values from the source representation. This is separate from causal self-attention over the target prefix.

Training often supplies the gold previous target tokens, called teacher forcing. Inference supplies previously generated tokens, so early errors can change later inputs. Beam search keeps several high-scoring partial sequences rather than only one greedy choice. Sequence log-probabilities add; length penalties and stopping rules alter which completed hypothesis wins.

A larger beam is a more extensive search under the chosen model and score, not a guarantee of better translation. If the model prefers short or unfaithful outputs, search can expose that preference more strongly. Evaluate generated sequences as well as token loss, and distinguish search changes from changes to trained weights.

Sources: [D2L: sequence-to-sequence learning](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-modern/seq2seq.html), [D2L: beam search](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-modern/beam-search.html).

document.markdown:
# N12. Sequence labelling with HMMs, CRFs and Viterbi

Sequence labelling assigns a tag to each position while allowing neighboring tags to influence one another. A hidden Markov model, or HMM, uses probabilities for hidden transitions and observed emissions; a conditional random field, or CRF, uses scores to model tag sequences given an input. Viterbi finds a best path, while summing paths supplies a different normalization calculation.

Three positions each permit tags A or B, creating eight possible sequences. The displayed emission, start and transition values determine all path scores. We compute the best sequence and, independently, the sum needed to normalize path probabilities.

An encoder can produce per-token evidence without deciding a complete output structure. This lesson adds dependencies between adjacent output tags and separates structured decoding from training and task-specific span evaluation.

## 1. Path scores, decoding and normalization

An HMM models a joint distribution over observations and hidden tags using transition and emission probabilities. A linear-chain CRF models a conditional distribution over tag sequences given an input, using emission/transition scores and one global normalizer. CRF emissions need not sum to one, and its transition matrix is not automatically a probability matrix.

Viterbi decoding keeps the best prefix score ending in each tag and stores backpointers. Its max operation differs from the forward algorithm's sum/log-sum-exp over paths. CRF training uses a log-partition function; replacing it with the Viterbi maximum is not the same objective.

The browser enumerates all eight paths of a three-position, two-tag example to independently check the dynamic program. HMM logZ is the observation log-likelihood; CRF logZ normalizes conditional path scores. The tiny tag names A/B are not a complete NER scheme.

### Reconstruct one Viterbi update

Start and transition values are shown in the live example. For the CRF, the first prefix scores are [2,1]. At the second position, ending in A gives `0+max(2+0.5, 1−0.5)=2.5`; ending in B gives `3+max(2−1, 1+0.8)=4.8`. Record the winning predecessor separately for each ending tag. At the third position the two final scores become 6.3 and 5.6. The winner is B→B→A, not the independently highest-emission path A→B→A.

For the HMM, first-position joint masses are `0.6×0.8=0.48` and `0.4×0.3=0.12`. At the second position they become `0.2×max(0.48×0.7,0.12×0.4)=0.0672` and `0.7×max(0.48×0.3,0.12×0.6)=0.1008`. The live recurrence takes logarithms to avoid tiny products; it makes the same maximum-path choice. Adding probabilities instead of maximizing would answer a different, path-sum question.

## 2. From tag sequences to exact entities

POS tagging assigns grammatical labels to tokens. NER additionally needs entity boundaries and types. BIO/IOB2/BILOU are different encoding conventions; a CRF does not guarantee legal BIO transitions unless those constraints are imposed.

A BiLSTM–CRF or encoder–CRF separates representation, emission projection and structured decoding. Subword alignment must be resolved before word/entity evaluation. Predicting the correct type for only half of a named entity can be a wrong span, even when most token labels are correct. Entity span/type F1 is demonstrated in the final evaluation lesson, not substituted with ordinary token accuracy.

### Training is not just best-path decoding

For a labelled CRF sequence, the negative conditional log-likelihood is
\[
L=\log Z(x)-s(x,y_{gold}).
\]
For the displayed CRF's gold path A→B→A, emissions sum to 7 and transitions contribute −1.5, so the gold score is 5.5. Its loss is the example's computed logZ minus 5.5, not logZ minus the Viterbi winner unless the gold sequence actually wins. Gradients compare model-expected sufficient statistics with the gold statistics; a neural emission network can receive those gradients.

For an HMM with known tags, count-based transition/emission estimation is supervised. With hidden tags, forward–backward computes posterior state/transition expectations; Baum–Welch uses them in an EM procedure. It sums uncertainty over paths rather than replacing all uncertain labels with one Viterbi path. These learning procedures are described here but are not new dashboard trainers.

## Sources

[CRF author tutorial](https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.4088) · [Speech and Language Processing — author-hosted draft](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/) · [BiLSTM-CNN-CRF](https://aclanthology.org/P16-1101/) · [HMM author chapter](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/A.pdf)

steps.title: Specify emissions, transitions and starts
steps.prose: Emissions describe the evidence at each position for each tag. Transitions connect a previous tag to a next tag, and start values score the first tag. The tables expose all inputs used by this fixed three-position calculation.
steps.terms: HMM emissions are P(observed token | tag), so a displayed row need not sum to one over tags. Recurrence uses log probabilities; CRF emissions/transitions are scores, not row-normalized probabilities.
steps.next: Use the same path evidence for either best-path decoding or path-sum normalization.

steps.title: Keep the best prefix for each ending tag
steps.prose: For each possible current tag, compare predecessor prefix scores plus transition scores, keep the maximum and add this position's emission. Remember the winning predecessor. This dynamic program avoids enumerating all sequences in larger problems.
steps.terms: Viterbi keeps delta_t(j), the best prefix score ending in tag j. e_t(j) is that position's emission and A_ij the previous-i to next-j transition score.
steps.next: Follow the stored predecessor choices to reconstruct the best full sequence.

steps.title: Recover the best tag sequence
steps.prose: Choose the best ending tag and follow the stored pointers back through the sentence. Reversing those recovered indices yields the forward-order tag path. A best final score without these pointers does not identify the whole prediction.
steps.terms: A backpointer records which previous tag gave a stored prefix maximum. Independent token argmax can ignore valuable transition evidence.
steps.next: Span reconstruction and evaluation can now use this decoded path; normalization is a separate branch.

steps.title: Sum paths to obtain a normalizer
steps.prose: Independently combine all path scores with log-sum-exp rather than max. For a CRF this normalizes conditional sequence scores; for an HMM it gives the observation likelihood. The displayed conditional best-path probability uses the normalizer, but Viterbi itself does not require it.
steps.terms: Z sums exp(score) over paths and logZ is its natural logarithm. CRF loss is logZ minus the gold path score, not necessarily minus the best-path score.
steps.next: The deeper notes distinguish supervised CRF learning and HMM forward–backward from best-path decoding.

steps.title: Turn word tags into the required outputs
steps.prose: The example uses tags A/B, not a complete entity scheme. A real entity tagger must align word or subword predictions, apply any declared boundary constraints and reconstruct source spans before scoring them. A CRF is not automatically BIO-valid.
steps.terms: BIO tags distinguish beginning, inside and outside positions. An exact entity match needs the required boundaries and entity type.
steps.next: The next lesson predicts grammatical trees, a different structure from a chain of output tags.

links: Maximize predecessor path scores using the supplied starts, emissions and transitions.
Follow stored predecessor indices from the winning ending tag.
Separately sum exp(path score) over paths to normalize probabilities.

reading.lesson_markdown:
Sequence labelling assigns a tag to each token, such as part of speech or an entity-boundary label. Independent tag predictions may produce an invalid sequence: an inside-person tag cannot normally begin a new person span under a BIO policy. Modelling transitions makes those relationships explicit.

An HMM models a joint distribution using state transitions and observation emissions. A linear-chain CRF instead scores tag sequences conditional on the observed input and normalises over permitted sequences. Neural emission scores can supply local evidence without changing this distinction.

Viterbi finds the highest-scoring path using dynamic programming. At each position and candidate tag, keep the best prefix score ending there and its backpointer. For two tags and three positions there are eight full paths, but we do not need to enumerate all of them for a long sequence. The recurrence reuses best prefixes. Viterbi's max operation finds one path; a forward log-sum-exp calculation sums probability mass and serves a different purpose.

State whether transitions are learned, constrained, or both. Evaluate exact typed spans as well as token tags when entity boundaries matter. A correct token majority can hide missed entities.

Sources: [SLP: sequence labelling](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/18.pdf), [SLP: hidden Markov models](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/A.pdf).

question.prompt: How does Viterbi differ from the forward/log-partition computation?

options.text: They always return the same scalar and tags.
options.feedback: A sum of path mass is not generally the largest individual path score, and normalization does not return one tag sequence.

options.text: Viterbi can ignore transition scores.
options.feedback: Transitions are part of the globally scored sequence under the declared model.

options.text: Viterbi maximizes predecessor path scores; the partition sums path mass.
options.feedback: Both can use dynamic programming, but changing max to sum/log-sum-exp changes the quantity being computed.

options.text: The forward algorithm is just greedy per-token argmax.
options.feedback: Forward recursion aggregates paths and is not independent greedy tagging.

question.prompt: Does adding a linear-chain CRF automatically make every predicted BIO sequence legal?

options.text: Yes, because CRF emission rows sum to one.
options.feedback: CRF emissions are arbitrary scores and row normalization is not what enforces BIO constraints.

options.text: Yes, because every HMM and CRF uses exactly the same tag inventory.
options.feedback: Inventories and encoding schemes are task/model choices, not a universal fixed set.

options.text: No sequence tagger can ever impose valid transitions.
options.feedback: A constrained decoder can forbid transitions under a documented scheme.

options.text: No; the scheme and transition constraints must be explicitly specified or enforced.

document.markdown:
# N13. Syntax: dependency and constituency parsing

Syntactic parsing predicts how words form a grammatical structure. A dependency parse connects words through head–dependent links; a constituency parse groups spans into nested phrases. These are alternative representations of a sentence, not successive processing stages or the same object as a list of word-class tags.

In 'cats chase mice', the example dependency tree makes chase the root, with cats as subject and mice as object. The deeper constituency example instead groups chase mice as a verb phrase and calculates a small grammar derivation.

Sequence labelling assigns tags along input order. Parsing adds a tree structure between or around those positions. Its constraints and evaluation must therefore match the chosen grammatical representation.

## 1. Dependency trees and constituent phrases

Constituency groups spans into nested phrases; dependency parsing links words through head–dependent relations. A POS tag sequence alone gives neither tree. Treebanks define tokenization, relation inventories and annotation conventions; an attachment can be debatable under different schemes.

A dependency parser scores arcs and often relation labels. Choosing each token's best incoming arc independently can create cycles or violate root constraints. Transition-based systems build a structure through actions; graph-based systems decode from arc scores under structural constraints. Projective and non-projective parsing permit different crossing structures.

The diagram uses “cats chase mice”: chase is the root, cats its subject and mice its object under the stated simple analysis. This is an authored illustration, not the output of a downloaded parser.

## 2. Parsing evaluation and constituency charts

Unlabelled attachment score measures correct heads; labelled attachment score also requires the relation label. Tokenization, punctuation inclusion and root conventions must match before comparing percentages. A parser can be useful while making errors on the structures important to a downstream task.

Dependency paths can connect candidate entities, and constituency spans can propose extraction units, but neither automatically proves a semantic relation. Neural parsers commonly use contextual token representations and biaffine scoring; a graph neural network is an optional additional representation, not another name for dependency parsing. Use a specified Universal Dependencies treebank and official scorer for an implementation study.

### A constituency chart is another structure

Consider a deliberately small probabilistic context-free grammar: S→NP VP with probability 1; VP→V NP with probability 1; V→chase with probability 1; NP→cats and NP→mice each with probability 0.5. For “cats chase mice”, the phrase derivation has probability 0.5×1×1×0.5=0.25.

A CKY-style chart first fills one-word spans, then combines smaller spans using compatible binary rules. The span “chase mice” becomes VP, then the full span becomes S. This illustrates a grammar already in binary form; general grammars need an appropriate transformation or another parsing algorithm. Constituent trees, dependency arcs and the sequence of POS tags are three different representations, even when all describe one sentence.

## Sources

[Universal Dependencies guidelines](https://universaldependencies.org/guidelines.html) · [Speech and Language Processing — author-hosted draft](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/)

steps.title: Choose a grammatical representation
steps.prose: Number the tokens before assigning links or phrase boundaries. Part-of-speech tags can describe word classes, but do not determine which word depends on which or which spans form phrases. A treebank's annotation scheme defines the desired structure.
steps.terms: A dependency head governs another word under a scheme. A constituent is a span grouped as a grammatical phrase.
steps.next: Inspect the authored dependency example while keeping constituency as an alternative representation.

steps.title: Read the example dependency tree
steps.prose: The artificial ROOT points to chase; chase points to cats and mice as subject and object. These arcs describe one simple grammatical analysis. They do not by themselves establish who supports an argument or whether the proposition is true.
steps.terms: An arc connects a head to a dependent. The root convention and relation inventory must come from the chosen annotation scheme.
steps.next: A real parser must choose a legal structure rather than simply maximize every independent arc.

steps.title: Decode under structural constraints
steps.prose: Independent highest-scoring heads can create cycles or invalid roots. Graph-based parsers optimize a tree under constraints; transition-based parsers construct one through actions. Constituency instead combines spans, illustrated by the grammar/chart notes.
steps.terms: Projectivity concerns whether dependency links cross in surface order. Grammatical constraints and semantic correctness are different requirements.
steps.next: Evaluate the chosen tree representation using its own matching convention.

steps.title: Measure the right structural errors
steps.prose: Unlabelled attachment checks heads; labelled attachment also requires the relation type. Tokenization, punctuation and root conventions affect these scores. A high average attachment score can still hide errors important for an extraction application.
steps.terms: UAS means unlabelled attachment score; LAS means labelled attachment score. Neither is a sentence classification accuracy.
steps.next: Contextual encoders next change how token evidence is represented without making any particular output tree automatic.

reading.lesson_markdown:
Parsing represents sentence structure beyond a list of words. A dependency tree links words through grammatical relations, typically with a head for each non-root token. A constituency tree groups words into nested phrases. The representations answer different structural questions and should not be mixed into one graph without defining the conversion.

In “The student read the paper,” a dependency analysis can link “student” as subject and “paper” as object of “read.” A constituency analysis groups “the paper” into a noun phrase. These descriptions help identify who did what, but syntax alone does not establish whether a claim is true or an argument is persuasive.

Unlabelled attachment score checks whether predicted heads match the reference; labelled attachment also requires the relation type. Span-based constituency evaluation compares predicted phrase spans under a declared policy. Tokenisation differences can invalidate otherwise plausible comparisons.

Parsers may fail on conversational ellipsis, unusual punctuation, and unfamiliar domains. If a downstream system consumes a predicted parse, those errors propagate. Compare against direct text representations before assuming an explicit tree is useful merely because it looks interpretable.

Sources: [SLP: dependency parsing](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/20.pdf), [SLP: constituency parsing](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/19.pdf).

# N14. Contextual token encoders: ELMo and BERT

A contextual encoder gives a token a representation that depends on its occurrence, not just its word identity. ELMo combines directional recurrent language-model features; BERT uses bidirectional Transformer context and masked-token pretraining. These methods produce token-level features that still need an appropriate head or pooling rule for a downstream task.

The illustration supplies a three-position input with a masked target and hidden width four. A target probability of 0.8 gives negative log-likelihood about 0.2231. The shapes and probability are supplied examples, not an actual downloaded BERT run.

Static word vectors reuse one lexical lookup, while recurrent and attention mechanisms can incorporate context. This lesson connects those mechanisms to pretraining objectives and explains why token encodings are not automatically good sentence-similarity embeddings.

## 1. Contextual pretraining objectives

ELMo builds contextual representations from directional LSTM language models and a task-specific weighted combination of layers. The forward and backward language-model states are combined, but this is not the same computation as a jointly bidirectional masked-attention encoder.

BERT uses context on both sides and predicts selected tokens from a corrupted input during masked-language pretraining. Original BERT sometimes keeps selected targets unchanged; the displayed all-masked example is a simplified corruption case. Original BERT used MLM and next-sentence prediction; RoBERTa does not simply repeat that recipe, ELECTRA uses replaced-token detection, and DeBERTa changes attention/position handling. These names identify different design choices, not an ordered universal ranking.

A bidirectional encoder can process a complete input sentence without being a causal next-token generator. Loss masking chooses which targets are scored; the attention mask chooses what positions can read. They cannot replace one another.

## 2. Token outputs, pooling and task heads

Token features have shape B × T × H. A token head returns B × T × C; a pooled classifier returns B × C. Special-token and subword policies determine which positions receive labels. For frozen encoders, put dropout in the intended mode and record the exact model/tokenizer revision.

The [CLS] vector is not automatically optimized for cosine sentence similarity. Fine-tuning a classifier, training a sentence embedding and extracting a frozen token representation are different uses. Existing Transformer lessons explain attention blocks; here the new material is contextual pretraining, pooling choices and task alignment.

## Sources

[BERT original paper](https://aclanthology.org/N19-1423/) · [Speech and Language Processing — author-hosted draft](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/) · [ELMo](https://aclanthology.org/N18-1202/)

steps.title: Construct a masked-token training example
steps.prose: Withhold selected original tokens under a declared corruption policy, then ask the model to predict those originals from the available input. The simplified view masks its selected target; original BERT's corruption recipe also included other cases.
steps.terms: Masked-language modelling, or MLM, supplies targets from observed text. It differs from predicting a successor using only a causal prefix.
steps.next: Encode the permitted input context while keeping padding visibility separate from target selection.

steps.title: Produce one contextual vector per position
steps.prose: An encoder transforms the input into a batch-by-token-by-feature tensor. Here [1,3,4] means one example, three positions and four features at each position. Context changes these features, but does not change which original position each row represents.
steps.terms: An attention mask restricts visible positions; a loss mask selects scored targets. Neither operation substitutes for the other.
steps.next: Project selected target-position states to vocabulary scores for the pretraining objective.

steps.title: Score the selected original token
steps.prose: The supplied gold-token probability is 0.8, so one target's loss is minus log 0.8. Unselected positions do not contribute MLM targets in this calculation. This objective measures prediction of withheld text, not sentence similarity or factual reliability.
steps.terms: A vocabulary head maps hidden features to scores over token IDs. A per-target negative log-probability is not a downstream task score.
steps.next: For downstream use, choose a head and representation suited to the required prediction unit.

steps.title: Choose a downstream representation and head
steps.prose: A token head can label each position; a pooled head can classify the whole input. Sentence similarity may require different training and pooling. The first special-token vector is not automatically optimized so that cosine distance reflects semantic similarity.
steps.terms: ELMo, BERT, RoBERTa and ELECTRA use distinct pretraining designs. A bidirectional encoder is not automatically a causal generator.
steps.next: The next lesson compares encoders trained or arranged for sentence and query–document comparison.

links: Encode the corrupted visible input, preserving token alignment and validity masks.
Score selected original token targets through a vocabulary head.

reading.lesson_markdown:
A contextual encoder gives a word occurrence a representation conditioned on surrounding text. “Bank” can therefore receive different vectors in a financial sentence and a river sentence. The output is usually one vector per input position, not automatically one useful vector for the whole sentence.

ELMo derives contextual representations from a bidirectional language-model architecture. BERT uses a bidirectional Transformer encoder trained partly by predicting selected masked tokens. The original BERT also used a next-sentence objective. This is not ordinary causal prediction of every next token: its attention visibility and target construction differ.

For a task such as tagging, attach a per-token classifier. For sentence classification, use an appropriate pooled representation and train the head; further fine-tuning can change the encoder. Merely averaging off-the-shelf token vectors is not guaranteed to produce strong sentence similarity embeddings.

Mask padded tokens, align subword pieces with word-level labels, and define how multiple pieces contribute to evaluation. A pretrained model can transfer useful language regularities while still carrying domain bias or missing specialised vocabulary. Contextualisation changes available information; it does not eliminate the need for task-specific evidence.

Sources: [Peters et al.: ELMo](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.05365), [Devlin et al.: BERT](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805), [SLP: masked language models](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/9.pdf).

document.markdown:
# N15. Sentence encoders and query–document interaction

A sentence encoder represents a larger text unit for comparison rather than assigning one static vector to each word. A bi-encoder computes query and document representations separately; a cross-encoder reads the pair jointly; late interaction keeps token vectors and compares them later. Where the texts first interact determines caching, computation and what information can be compared.

Compare a query with two documents using one of three architectures. Bi-encoder mode shows masked pooling and cosine scores; cross-encoder mode shows a joint pair structure without inventing a relevance score; late interaction calculates each query token's best document match.

A contextual token encoder supplies per-position vectors. Turning those into retrieval scores requires a deliberate pooling, training and interaction design, extending the earlier embedding geometry rather than treating every encoder as an interchangeable search model.

## 1. Independent, joint and token-level matching

A bi-encoder encodes the query and document separately, making document vectors cacheable. Query/document encoders may share weights or use separate towers and prompts. A cross-encoder jointly processes each pair, allowing token interactions before producing a score; it cannot reuse one final document vector to score every query.

Sentence-BERT adapts encoders for sentence-level comparison. Mean pooling must exclude padding; CLS, mean and last-token pooling are not interchangeable defaults across model families. Normalization turns a dot product of unit vectors into cosine similarity, but scalar rescaling lost under normalization can still affect another downstream head.

ColBERT-style late interaction retains multiple token vectors and aggregates token matches, often MaxSim. This is neither one pooled vector nor a full joint cross-encoder. Token storage and indexing costs are part of that choice.

## 2. Contrastive training and retrieval evaluation

The illustrative contrastive objective treats one document as positive and another as a negative: \(-\log(\exp(s_+/\tau)/\sum_j\exp(s_j/\tau))\). Temperature changes the loss and gradients without changing the already fixed score order. In-batch negatives can be false negatives when documents are actually equivalent or relevant.

Unsupervised SimCSE uses dropout views of the same sentence; supervised variants use labelled relations. Hard-negative mining must not accidentally choose true positives or use hidden evaluation labels. Compare bi-encoder candidate recall and cross-encoder reranking separately: a reranker cannot recover a relevant document absent from its candidate set. Record pooling, prompts, normalization, model revision and search configuration with every embedding index.

## Sources

[Sentence-BERT original paper](https://aclanthology.org/D19-1410/) · [Speech and Language Processing — author-hosted draft](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/) · [SimCSE](https://aclanthology.org/2021.emnlp-main.552/) · [ColBERT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.12832) · [Retrieve and rerank implementation](https://sbert.net/examples/sentence_transformer/applications/retrieve_rerank/README.html)

steps.title: Choose separate query and document encoding
steps.prose: In a bi-encoder the two texts meet only after each has been encoded. The towers may share weights or use distinct parameters and instructions. Independent document computation makes a reusable vector index possible.
steps.terms: A bi-encoder's document representation is query-independent under its saved encoding contract. Shared weights do not mean the inputs are jointly encoded.
steps.next: Pool the query's valid token states and prepare independent document vectors in parallel.

steps.title: Pool valid query states and normalize
steps.prose: Average only the two real token rows, then rescale to unit length. Including the nonzero padding row intentionally demonstrates a wrong pooling rule that changes the query. Validity masking and normalization perform different operations.
steps.terms: Masked mean pooling divides the sum of valid rows by their count. L2 normalization then changes vector length, not which rows were included.
steps.next: Use this exact pooled query in the downstream document comparison.

steps.title: Prepare reusable document vectors
steps.prose: The two supplied unit vectors represent independently encoded documents. They can be reused across queries only while model revision, instructions, pooling and normalization remain compatible. A changed encoder may require rebuilding the stored vectors.
steps.terms: Caching saves a reusable result. A compatible index must preserve the representation and score conventions used for the query side.
steps.next: Compare the query vector against each independently prepared document vector.

steps.title: Compare vectors and calculate a training loss
steps.prose: With unit vectors the dot product equals cosine. The fixed scores determine ranking; temperature rescales them only inside the displayed contrastive loss. A positive document competes with the supplied negative in that training objective.
steps.terms: In the contrastive equation s is a similarity, the positive is the designated matching document and tau>0 is temperature. Negatives are training contrasts, not guaranteed irrelevant text.
steps.next: Audit actual relevance judgements and candidate retrieval separately from this fixed-vector loss.

steps.title: Evaluate retrieval, negatives and reranking
steps.prose: Relevant items can be mistakenly used as negatives during training. At use time, a reranker can reorder only the candidates it receives. Check candidate recall, final ranking and resource cost instead of assuming a more interactive architecture wins.
steps.terms: A false negative is a relevant candidate treated as a negative label. Candidate recall and reranked quality describe different stages.
steps.next: The following task lessons attach encoders to classification and extraction with explicit output definitions.

links: Encode and pool the query independently, with the declared valid-token mask.
Encode documents independently so their representations can be cached.
The actual pooled query vector supplies one side of the score.
Compare each saved document vector with that same query vector.

steps.title: Prepare one joint query–document input
steps.prose: A cross-encoder reads the pair together before producing its relevance score. It cannot reuse one final query-independent document vector for every query, because each joint representation depends on the other input.
steps.terms: A joint encoder permits token interactions between both segments. Pair formatting and special tokens belong to the selected model.
steps.next: Prepare query and document segments under a shared pair-length budget.

steps.title: Supply the query segment
steps.prose: The query contributes two content tokens before the format's special markers. These are input tokens, not separately pooled query vectors. The joint encoding happens later when both segments are supplied together.
steps.terms: A segment identifies part of a paired input. The tokenizer/model contract determines separators and any segment IDs.
steps.next: Combine this segment with the candidate document in the joint encoder.

steps.title: Supply the document segment
steps.prose: The candidate contributes three content tokens. Its accessible text depends on the shared pair budget, so truncation can remove important evidence. Changing the query requires re-evaluating the pair rather than reusing a final document vector.
steps.terms: Content-token count excludes special markers. Pair-level truncation and independent document embedding are different operations.
steps.next: Encode both segments jointly before applying the relevance head.

steps.title: Jointly encode and score the pair
steps.prose: With the illustrative three special tokens, the pair has eight positions and 64 potential attention pairs per head. A task head would score its joint features. No trained relevance value is supplied here, and pair counts are not measured runtime.
steps.terms: Joint contextual features depend on both texts. A relevance score needs its training and calibration contract before being called a probability.
steps.next: Use joint scoring as a reranking stage and evaluate it on the candidate set it actually receives.

steps.title: Evaluate the reranked candidate set
steps.prose: A joint model can examine each candidate more closely, but cannot recover a relevant document missing from its input set. Measure the first-stage retrieval recall separately from reranking quality and the extra computation per pair.
steps.terms: Reranking reorders existing candidates. End-to-end retrieval can fail before the expensive scoring stage is reached.
steps.next: Compare caching and interaction trade-offs across the three architectures under a matched task.

links: Prepare the query segment without making an independent pooled query embedding.
Prepare the candidate segment under the joint input budget.
Both token streams enter the same encoder before relevance scoring.
Joint attention can connect document and query positions.

steps.title: Retain token vectors on both sides
steps.prose: Late interaction encodes query and documents independently but keeps several token vectors instead of immediately pooling each text to one vector. This permits document-side caching while preserving more local matching choices.
steps.terms: A multivector representation contains several feature vectors for one text. It is not the same as one vector with extra dimensions.
steps.next: Prepare query-token and document-token vectors independently before their late comparison.

steps.title: Keep query token vectors separate
steps.prose: The query has two supplied unit vectors, [1,0] and [0,1]. Each will select its own strongest document-token match. Averaging them first would change the scoring method and can change ranking behaviour.
steps.terms: Each valid query token contributes its own matching term. Padding positions must be excluded from the scoring contract.
steps.next: Keep document token vectors available for each query token's comparison.

steps.title: Cache document token vectors
steps.prose: Document A has vectors [1,0] and [0,1]; B has two copies of [0.8,0.6]. Each document can be encoded independently of the query. Multiple stored vectors cost more space than one pooled document vector.
steps.terms: A token index stores several features per document. Compression and approximate search introduce separate quality/cost trade-offs.
steps.next: For each query vector, find its strongest document-token match and then sum.

steps.title: Calculate best token matches and sum
steps.prose: For A the two query tokens each find a perfect dot-product match, giving 2. For B they contribute 0.8 and 0.6, giving 1.4. These MaxSim scores are neither probabilities nor interchangeable with single-vector cosine.
steps.terms: MaxSim sums the maximum token similarity for each query token. It differs from averaging all matches or using joint cross-attention.
steps.next: Evaluate a complete trained retrieval/indexing system separately from this supplied-vector example.

reading.lesson_markdown:
Retrieval needs to compare many candidates. A bi-encoder produces query and document vectors separately, so document vectors can be stored before the query arrives. A cross-encoder reads a query–document pair jointly and scores their interaction, usually at greater cost per candidate. The difference is where interaction occurs, not simply which model name is used.

The two towers of a bi-encoder may share weights, as in many sentence-embedding systems, or use different query and passage encoders. Their training objective must make the resulting spaces compatible. A contrastive objective rewards an intended pair relative to negatives; which negatives are sampled changes what distinctions the encoder learns.

For vectors `[1,0]` and `[1,1]`, cosine is about 0.707. That score has meaning only relative to the trained representation and candidate set; it is not a universal semantic percentage. A practical pipeline may retrieve many documents cheaply, then rerank a smaller set with a cross-encoder.

Measure candidate recall before final ranking quality. If the needed passage never reaches the reranker, better pair scoring cannot recover it. Also evaluate exact-name cases and paraphrases rather than assuming dense retrieval replaces lexical matching everywhere.

Sources: [Sentence-BERT](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10084), [Dense Passage Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.04906).

# N16. Text classification and paired-input inference

Text classification maps a document, token sequence or input pair to a defined label structure. Single-label classification chooses one mutually exclusive class; multilabel classification can assign several labels at once. The target structure determines the loss and decoding rule, not merely how many label names appear in a dataset.

The three supplied logits are [1,−1,0.2] for sports, politics and finance. Switch between one exclusive class and multiple allowed labels to compare softmax with independent sigmoids, then inspect the corresponding prediction rule.

Encoders and lexical pipelines create representations; a classifier turns them into task outputs. This lesson connects the output head to label semantics before the course moves to richer span and relation structures.

## 1. Output units, targets and losses

Single-label classification chooses one mutually exclusive class, usually with a softmax/cross-entropy objective. Multilabel classification permits several labels at once, often using independent sigmoid outputs and binary cross-entropy. A probability sum of one is not appropriate merely because the task has several possible labels.

Token classification predicts one output per token, while document classification pools or aggregates evidence for one output per document. Aspect-based sentiment may require identifying an aspect and judging sentiment toward it; a single document polarity can miss the task. Ordinal labels, hierarchies and severe imbalance may need additional modelling/evaluation choices.

For paired inputs, a cross-encoder can classify a premise–hypothesis or query–answer relation. Entailment is directional: swapping the pair can change the correct label. Similarity, paraphrase and entailment are not synonyms.

## 2. Threshold selection and error analysis

Choose decision thresholds on development data, per label only when the protocol and sample size support it. A sigmoid output is not automatically a calibrated probability; class weighting can change its interpretation. Shared metrics/calibration lessons own the general definitions.

Inspect negation, rare labels, document length and author/source leakage. Distinguish zero-shot label descriptions, frozen sentence-vector classifiers and supervised encoder fine-tuning. Their input access and training budgets differ. A larger encoder should earn its additional cost under a matched task, not by replacing a weak or incorrectly fitted baseline.

## Sources

[Hugging Face sequence classification guide](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/tasks/sequence_classification) · [Speech and Language Processing — author-hosted draft](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/)

steps.title: Define exclusive or overlapping labels
steps.prose: A single-label example needs one class index; a multilabel example needs a binary decision for each label. A document can concern both sports and finance even when a different dataset forces one choice. Specify the task before choosing the activation.

steps.title: Convert logits to task-compatible scores
steps.prose: Softmax creates one distribution summing to one across exclusive classes. Independent sigmoids give one score per label, without imposing that sum. Their numerical outputs alone do not show that probabilities are calibrated on real texts.
steps.terms: Cross-entropy suits an exclusive class target; binary cross-entropy can score per-label binary targets. Activation and training objective must agree.

steps.title: Decode labels with a declared decision rule
steps.prose: Argmax returns one highest-scoring class in single-label mode. The illustrative 0.5 threshold returns sports and finance in multilabel mode. Threshold tuning uses development evidence, not the test labels later used to report performance.

steps.terms: Natural-language inference, or NLI, concerns entailment, contradiction or unresolved relations under a premise. Paraphrase and similarity are different targets.

reading.lesson_markdown:
A document classifier maps one text to a label. A paired-input classifier conditions on two texts, for example a premise and a hypothesis. In natural-language inference, the label describes their relationship: entailment, contradiction, or insufficient support under the annotation policy. It is not simply the sentiment of either sentence.

For premise “All tickets were sold” and hypothesis “No tickets remain available,” the relationship may be supported. Change the premise to “Some tickets were sold,” and that conclusion no longer follows. A hypothesis-only model cannot see this difference. If it nevertheless scores well, dataset-specific wording may be predictive of labels.

Compare full-input, premise-only, and hypothesis-only conditions when investigating such shortcuts. Keep the same evaluation examples and define what each condition is permitted to read. A score difference can then identify reliance on information, without proving every successful prediction performs valid reasoning.

Calibration and thresholding depend on the task's class structure. Use error inspection for negation, quantifiers, entity swaps, and domain changes. A high aggregate score under one corpus's policy need not transfer to another definition of inference.

Sources: [Gururangan et al.: annotation artefacts in NLI](https://aclanthology.org/N18-2017/), [Poliak et al.: hypothesis-only baselines](https://aclanthology.org/S18-2023/).

document.markdown:
# N17. Information extraction: entities, relations and events

Information extraction converts text into structured records about mentions, entities, relations and events. A mention is a source span; coreference links mentions intended to refer to the same entity. Relation and event extraction add typed connections or roles. A valid output format does not by itself make these records supported by the text.

In 'Maya founded Acme. She leads it.', the intended reading links She to Maya and it to Acme. Founder and leader are different relations. Keeping these links and original mentions visible helps locate errors instead of hiding them inside a fluent generated record.

Classification assigns a label to a chosen unit. Extraction adds boundaries and links between units, so reliable source offsets and task-specific validation become essential in addition to a good encoder.

## 1. Mentions, links and typed records

An entity mention is a text span; an entity identifier links a mention to an external record. Coreference groups mentions referring to the same entity in a document. A relation connects arguments under a schema; an event may have a trigger and several typed roles. None of these objects follows automatically from a correct sentence-class label.

A pipeline can first detect mentions and then classify mention pairs. Joint models share representations or decode structures together, potentially changing error propagation. A generated JSON record is another output format, not proof that every field refers to real source text.

The authored example contains “Maya founded Acme. She leads it.” It links She to Maya and it to Acme under the intended reading, then distinguishes founded from leads. The explicit source anchors make a mistaken link visible.

## 2. Reference validation and semantic support

Check span boundaries, type inventories, legal argument roles, identifier resolution and source support. Nested or discontinuous mentions need richer representations than one BIO tag per token. Multiple plausible readings may need adjudication or abstention rather than an invented certainty.

Relation evaluation can assume gold mentions or require end-to-end extraction; those are different protocols. Coreference metrics also vary, so report the scorer/version and mention policy. Use deterministic schema/reference checks before semantic audit. Retain intermediate candidates to identify whether an error came from mention detection, linking, relation typing or generated unsupported content.

## Sources

[spaCy information-extraction pipeline concepts](https://spacy.io/usage/linguistic-features#named-entities) · [Speech and Language Processing — author-hosted draft](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/)

reading.lesson_markdown:
Information extraction turns text into structured records. Entity recognition finds typed mentions; relation extraction links mentions; event extraction identifies an event and its participants. Each extra stage introduces a question about what the source actually states.

In “Mira joined Acme in June,” an entity system may find Mira as a person and Acme as an organisation. A relation could represent employment; an event record could attach a person, organisation, and time to a joining event. The text does not specify Mira's later job title or whether she still works there. A plausible completion would be an unsupported addition.

Choose whether records use mention spans, canonical entities, or both. Two names can refer to one entity, and one name can refer to different entities. Relations may be directed; swapping participants can change the meaning. Define the schema and missing-value policy before evaluating generated JSON.

Measure exact spans, types, participant roles, and source support separately where useful. A schema-valid record can still be wrong. Pipeline errors accumulate, so compare end-to-end records as well as individual stage scores. Preserve source offsets to make every extracted claim inspectable.

Sources: [SLP: information extraction](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/21.pdf), [SLP: coreference and entity linking](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/24.pdf).

# N18. Machine translation and BLEU evaluation

Machine translation produces a target-language sequence intended to preserve a source's meaning. Automatic reference-based metrics compare a candidate with permitted reference translations, but they test different kinds of agreement. BLEU combines clipped n-gram precision with a brevity penalty; the simple example here isolates unigram BLEU-1 rather than implementing standard corpus BLEU.

The reference is 'the cat sat down'. Choose a short candidate, a repeated word or the exact reference. Clipping stops a repeated sat from gaining unlimited credit, and the brevity penalty reduces the score of an otherwise matching short fragment.

Encoder–decoder attention and search explain how a translation may be produced. This lesson asks how to evaluate the resulting text without confusing lexical overlap with preserved meaning or full translation quality.

## 1. Translation objectives and overlap metrics

Translation can use recurrent attention models, encoder–decoders or instructed generative models, but the source/target task must stay fixed. Segmentation, script, morphology, domain terminology and document context all affect what a correct translation means. Teacher forcing and beam search are explained in the sequence-to-sequence lesson rather than repeated here.

BLEU combines clipped n-gram precisions with a brevity penalty. The browser deliberately computes unigram BLEU-1 for transparency; it is not standard four-order corpus BLEU. Corpus BLEU aggregates counts before applying its formula, not by averaging sentence BLEU scores. Smoothing, effective order, reference count and tokenization affect the result.

chrF compares character n-gram overlap; COMET uses a learned evaluation model. A fluent or high-overlap output can still reverse a fact or omit a critical condition.

## 2. Scorer configuration and meaning preservation

Report the SacreBLEU signature or equivalent full configuration, corpus split, reference set, model/tokenizer revision and decoding settings. Learned metrics require their exact checkpoint and input configuration. Reference translations are not the only valid wording.

# N18. Machine translation and BLEU evaluation

Machine translation produces a target-language sequence intended to preserve a source's meaning. Automatic reference-based metrics compare a candidate with permitted reference translations, but they test different kinds of agreement. BLEU combines clipped n-gram precision with a brevity penalty; the simple example here isolates unigram BLEU-1 rather than implementing standard corpus BLEU.

The reference is 'the cat sat down'. Choose a short candidate, a repeated word or the exact reference. Clipping stops a repeated sat from gaining unlimited credit, and the brevity penalty reduces the score of an otherwise matching short fragment.

Encoder–decoder attention and search explain how a translation may be produced. This lesson asks how to evaluate the resulting text without confusing lexical overlap with preserved meaning or full translation quality.

sections.title: Translation objectives and overlap metrics
sections.markdown:
## 1. Translation objectives and overlap metrics

Translation can use recurrent attention models, encoder–decoders or instructed generative models, but the source/target task must stay fixed. Segmentation, script, morphology, domain terminology and document context all affect what a correct translation means. Teacher forcing and beam search are explained in the sequence-to-sequence lesson rather than repeated here.

BLEU combines clipped n-gram precisions with a brevity penalty. The browser deliberately computes unigram BLEU-1 for transparency; it is not standard four-order corpus BLEU. Corpus BLEU aggregates counts before applying its formula, not by averaging sentence BLEU scores. Smoothing, effective order, reference count and tokenization affect the result.

chrF compares character n-gram overlap; COMET uses a learned evaluation model. A fluent or high-overlap output can still reverse a fact or omit a critical condition.

steps.title: Fix the candidate, reference and token units
steps.prose: Use the same tokenizer to count both texts. The worked example uses whitespace-separated words and one reference. A real evaluation must specify tokenization, references and aggregation before comparing scores across systems or language pairs.

steps.title: Clip repeated word matches
steps.prose: Each candidate occurrence can match only an available occurrence in the reference. Repeating sat therefore cannot create another reference match. Divide the clipped count by candidate length to obtain this unigram precision.

steps.title: Apply the brevity penalty

reading.lesson_markdown:
Translation generates a target-language sequence preserving the source's meaning. Several target sentences may be valid, so exact string equality is often too strict. Encoder–decoder models condition generation on the source while the target decoder uses its permitted prefix.

BLEU counts modified n-gram precision against reference translations, combining different n-gram orders and a brevity penalty. Clipping prevents a repeated candidate word from earning more matched occurrences than the reference allows. The brevity penalty discourages a very short output that matches only easy words.

Corpus BLEU aggregates counts across a corpus; it is not generally the mean of sentence BLEU. Tokenisation, reference choice, smoothing, and implementation affect the number. A candidate with good overlap can still reverse a fact or omit a crucial negation, while a valid paraphrase can lose overlap.

Report the evaluation signature and inspect meaning, names, numbers, and omissions. Learned semantic metrics and human judgements offer additional evidence but also have assumptions and biases. Changing decoding or the reference set is not the same experiment as improving the model under a fixed evaluation protocol.

# N19. Question answering, answer spans and abstention

Question answering predicts an answer to a question under a defined information-access setting. An extractive reader chooses a span in supplied context; a generative system may produce new wording. Answer correctness, source support and deciding when no answer is available are separate requirements, with different evaluation rules.

The context tokens are 'The red car stopped .', and the gold answer is red car. Select car, red car or The red car to compare exact answer matching with partial token credit. All span coordinates here use inclusive token ends.

Translation metrics compare generated wording with references. Question answering additionally needs a question, a permissible evidence source and an answerability decision; it must not reuse an unrelated classification or entity-matching score.

## 1. Answer spans, generated answers and missing answers

An extractive reader assigns start/end scores to context positions. A valid decoder enforces start ≤ end, permitted context positions and any maximum answer length. Independently choosing the two highest logits can produce an illegal span. A retrieval step can fail before the reader ever sees useful context.

A generative QA model may return words not present verbatim in a passage. Correctness, answerability and evidence support then require separate tests. An explicit null/abstain decision should be selected using development data and a declared cost/metric, not hidden test labels.

The small diagram uses an exact context-token alignment and three candidate spans. Its answer-token F1 is not classification macro-F1 or entity span F1. A real SQuAD-style evaluator also specifies normalization and multiple-reference handling.

## 2. Exact match, token overlap and source support

Exact match asks whether the normalized answer matches a reference; token-overlap F1 rewards partial matches under that evaluator's tokenizer/normalizer. A partial entity name may receive answer-token credit while failing exact entity extraction. That is a metric definition, not a contradiction.

SQuAD 2 introduces unanswerable questions; closed-book factual QA and source-grounded QA test different information access. Evaluate retrieval recall, reader correctness, abstention and source support separately. A plausible span in a retrieved passage does not establish that the passage answers the actual question. Keep source offsets and truncated-context coverage visible.

## Sources

[SQuAD 2 original paper](https://aclanthology.org/P18-2124/) · [Speech and Language Processing — author-hosted draft](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/)

steps.title: Identify the supplied context and gold answer
steps.prose: Locate red car at token indices one through two, including both ends. This coordinate convention differs from the exclusive character-end offsets used in preprocessing. The reader sees a passage; it is not being tested on unaided factual recall.

steps.prose: The control chooses one of three supplied spans rather than running a trained start/end head. A real decoder must enforce start no later than end, valid context positions and any length restriction. Independent highest-scoring endpoints can violate these constraints.

reading.lesson_markdown:
Extractive question answering selects a span from a supplied passage. Open-domain QA first has to find a relevant passage; generative QA may produce an answer not present as one contiguous span. These settings provide different evidence and require different failure checks.

A span model scores start and end positions, then chooses a valid span under a stated decoding rule. Independent maximum start and end scores can produce an invalid order, so constraints matter. An unanswerable question should not force an arbitrary extraction.

Exact match checks equality after a defined normalisation. SQuAD token F1 compares token overlap as a multiset: “19 August” versus “August 19” has F1 1 but exact match 0 under its official evaluator. This reveals a limitation of overlap, not partial credit for word order. Boundary and normalisation policies must match before reproducing scores.

Abstention trades coverage against errors among answered questions. At zero coverage that conditional error is undefined, not zero. Choose an operating threshold on validation data and test it unchanged. A model can remain confidently wrong under domain shift, so confidence-based abstention is not proof that every answered question is supported.

Sources: [SQuAD project](https://rajpurkar.github.io/SQuAD-explorer/), [Official SQuAD evaluator](https://github.com/rajpurkar/SQuAD-explorer/blob/master/evaluate-v2.0.py).

document.markdown:
# N20. Summarization, dialogue and source faithfulness

Summarization selects and compresses source content, either by extracting passages or generating new wording. Source faithfulness asks whether the output preserves what the source supports; external truth asks a different question. Dialogue adds an interaction goal: helping a user may require clarification, correction or abstention rather than simply producing agreeable text.

The supplied source says 'trial improved symptoms'. Replacing improved with worsened leaves two of three reference words unchanged while reversing the main claim. The control reveals why lexical overlap alone cannot certify a faithful summary.

Generation scores and QA matching test limited forms of agreement. This lesson examines their blind spots and connects language-model outputs to source claims and actual interaction usefulness, without treating style as correctness.

## 1. Source faithfulness and summary evaluation

Extractive summarization selects source material; abstractive summarization generates new wording. Compression requires selecting what to omit, while faithfulness requires avoiding unsupported changes. A source-faithful summary may repeat a false source; a true external statement may still be unsupported by the supplied source.

ROUGE variants compare lexical or sequence overlap and use different matching/reduction rules. The example replaces “improved” with “worsened”: two of three unigrams still match even though the direction of the finding reverses. That toy recall is not a full implementation of every ROUGE variant and cannot certify factuality.

Evaluate claims, numbers, entities, scope, uncertainty and omitted qualifications. Do not turn a high overlap score or fluent style into proof that an answer is trustworthy.

## 2. Dialogue usefulness and correction

A dialogue system can manage intent/slots, retrieve a response, generate a response or combine those stages. Multi-turn state should reflect the actual user goal and evidence, not just the most recent wording. A satisfying response can agree with a false premise or avoid challenging an incorrect assumption.

Measure task completion, grounding, correction of false premises and appropriate uncertainty alongside preference judgements. LLM judges can inherit verbosity, order or agreement biases; the shared evaluation lesson covers judge auditing. Reducing unsupported content may require abstention or questions, not simply a longer reasoning trace. Keep evaluation examples independent from prompt iteration.

## Sources

[ROUGE original paper](https://aclanthology.org/W04-1013/) · [Speech and Language Processing — author-hosted draft](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/) · [Evaluation and interpretability](https://github.com/EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness)
