reading.title: Gradient accumulation and stable LLM training
reading.definition: Gradient accumulation combines several small forward/backward calculations before one optimizer update. The loss weighting must match the intended objective, especially when microbatches contain different numbers of valid targets. Numerical stability, clipping, scheduling and diagnostics are additional training choices, not substitutes for correctly aligned data and targets.
reading.example: Microbatch A has two scored tokens with mean loss one; B has a selectable token count with mean loss three. At six B tokens the combined token mean is 2.5, while averaging the two microbatch means gives 2.0. The control changes this accounting, not a live run.
reading.connection: The training loop identified where gradients are accumulated and applied. This lesson derives their weighting on one worker; the distributed lesson later adds the separate convention used to combine workers.

steps.title: Count the scored targets in this update
steps.prose: Count valid labels after shifting and loss masking, not padded tensor slots. The two supplied microbatch means may summarize different amounts of evidence. Plan the total denominator before backward or use a specified equivalent normalization procedure.
steps.terms: A microbatch is one forward/backward unit. An optimizer update can aggregate several such units; valid targets are the included token labels.
steps.next: Recover each microbatch's summed loss using its mean and valid-target count.

steps.title: Recover loss sums from the means
steps.prose: Multiply each mean loss by the number of included targets it summarizes. A contributes two; B contributes three times its count. These fixed losses demonstrate reduction weights, not observations from a trained checkpoint.
steps.terms: A mean times its count recovers the corresponding sum. Comparing only means can conceal the unequal evidence weights.
steps.next: Add the sums and divide by the intended total target count.

steps.title: Normalize the intended token-average objective
steps.prose: Use the combined target count so each scored token has equal influence. With equal counts this agrees with a mean of microbatch means; with unequal counts it does not. Other objectives are allowed if declared rather than silently conflated.
steps.terms: N is total valid targets; n_b counts targets in microbatch b. Loss reduction defines the statistical weighting, not just a logging choice.
steps.next: Differentiate correctly weighted contributions, accumulate their gradients and update once.

steps.title: Accumulate gradients and update once
steps.prose: Backpropagate each appropriately scaled contribution, retaining parameter gradients rather than all forward graphs. At the boundary unscale if needed, check finite gradients, clip if configured and apply one optimizer step. Then clear gradients for the next update.
steps.terms: Clipping limits gradient norm; loss scaling protects numerical computation in some precision recipes. Neither repairs incorrect target weighting.
steps.next: The deeper notes cover instability, diagnostics and schedule units; the next topic accounts for the memory those operations require.

reading.lesson_markdown:
Gradient accumulation combines several forward/backward microbatches before one optimizer update. It helps when a desired batch does not fit in memory. It is equivalent to a larger-batch objective only when loss scaling, model behaviour, and update boundaries match; repeated optimizer steps on small batches are a different procedure.

Suppose three microbatches contain 1, 1, and 100 valid target tokens. Averaging their three mean losses gives the two tiny batches two-thirds of the vote. A token-average objective gives those two tokens only $2/102$ of the weight. Recover each summed token loss, add the sums, and divide by the total number of scored tokens. Padding and ignored prompt tokens must not enter that count.

Clip gradients after accumulating the intended update, and update the optimizer and scheduler at their defined boundary. A zero-target microbatch needs deliberate handling rather than division by zero. Compare against a single-batch reference on a small deterministic case when checking the implementation.

Mixed precision changes which numerical operations use lower precision. FP16 may need loss scaling; BF16 has a different range/precision trade-off. A master-weight copy is implementation-dependent, not a universal property of every autocast setup. If loss becomes non-finite, inspect logits, masks, reduction, data, and update scale before launching a larger run. A correct small loop is the reference for debugging a large one.

Sources: [PyTorch: gradient accumulation with AMP](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/notes/amp_examples.html#gradient-accumulation), [Hugging Face: token-loss normalisation](https://huggingface.co/blog/gradient_accumulation).

document.markdown:
# T6. LLM parameter counts, memory and compute

A model's parameter count, raw weight storage, training-state memory and compute budget measure different things. Training can require gradients, optimizer history, activations and temporary workspaces beyond the weights. Resource estimates are conditional accounting tools; measured peak memory and throughput must establish whether a real configuration fits and runs usefully.

Select one, ten or one hundred million hypothetical parameters. The simple convention stores FP32 weights, FP32 gradients and two FP32 Adam moments. Its static state uses sixteen bytes per parameter before activations or runtime overhead; other recipes need different accounting.

The training loop explains what values exist and when. This lesson counts their storage and work before scaling, while keeping the detailed prepared-model count, scaling laws and hardware bottlenecks in the deeper explanations.

## 1. Parameter counting

**Key terms.** **Parameters N** are learned numbers; **training tokens D** count exposures; **d** is hidden width; **d_ff** is MLP width; **V** is vocabulary size.

**Process.** Count each matrix from its dimensions before estimating storage or compute. Add shared parameters only once, then use the total in the separate memory and work calculations below.

Parameters, training tokens, context length, update count, hardware time and money are different quantities. A model with fewer parameters can cost more overall if trained on many more tokens or served millions of times. Total lifetime cost includes data preparation, experiments, training, evaluation and inference.

In a simple dense decoder block, attention projections contribute roughly `4d²` weights and a non-gated MLP roughly `2 d d_ff`, ignoring biases/norms. With `d_ff=4d`, that is about `12d²` per layer. Gated MLPs, GQA, tied embeddings and expert layers change the count. Add embeddings `Vd` and any untied output projection.

### Count the prepared model instead of guessing from its name

For the configured bias-free SmolLM2 model: vocabulary 49,152; width 960; 32 layers; KV projection width 320; gated intermediate width 2560; tied input/output embeddings.

1. The shared embedding/output matrix contains `49,152×960 = 47,185,920` parameters. Do not count it twice when weights are tied.
2. Each block's attention matrices contain `960×960 + 960×320 + 960×320 + 960×960 = 2,457,600` parameters: query, key, value and output projections.
3. Its three gated-MLP matrices contain `3×960×2560 = 7,372,800` parameters. A two-matrix GELU formula would undercount this model.
4. Two RMSNorm scale vectors add `2×960 = 1,920` per block. Across 32 blocks the subtotal is `32×9,832,320 = 314,634,240`.
5. Add the shared embedding and final 960-element RMSNorm: total **361,821,120**. This is a parameter count, not the peak-memory requirement.

The recipe follows the [model configuration](https://huggingface.co/HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-360M-Instruct/blob/main/config.json). Another architecture can have biases, untied heads or expert weights, so reuse the counting procedure, not the total. The compute-optimal scaling study in [Chinchilla](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556) addresses a separate question: how to allocate a training-compute budget between parameters and tokens.

## 2. Training memory

**Key terms.** **Bits per value** determine raw storage; **activations** are forward intermediates; **optimizer state** stores update history; **GiB** means 2³⁰ bytes.

**Process.** Calculate raw weight bytes first, then add gradients, optimizer state, activations and temporary buffers. Compare the complete peak estimate with available device and host memory before launching training.

For `N` parameters stored at `b` bits, raw weights need `Nb/8` bytes. A 7-billion-parameter model at 16 bits needs about 14 GB decimal, or 13.04 GiB. That is **not** a complete training or serving requirement.

An illustrative mixed-precision Adam setup might store:

| Component | Bytes/parameter in this example |
| --- | ---: |
| Low-precision parameter copy | 2 |
| Low-precision gradients | 2 |
| FP32 master weights | 4 |
| Two FP32 Adam moments | 8 |
| **Subtotal** | **16** |

For 7B parameters, subtotal is 112 GB before activations, workspace, communication buffers and allocator overhead. Other implementations use different gradient/master-state choices. Do not present “16 bytes” as a universal constant.

Activations depend on batch, sequence length, width, layers and kernels. Gradient checkpointing discards selected intermediate activations and recomputes them during backward, trading compute for memory. Optimizer sharding distributes state but adds communication. Offloading moves state to CPU/disk and can create a bandwidth bottleneck.

## 3. FLOPs and time estimates

**Key terms.** A **FLOP** is a floating-point operation; **throughput** is operations per second; **sustained throughput** is achieved rather than advertised speed.

**Process.** Estimate total arithmetic from model and token counts, divide by measured or explicitly assumed sustained speed, then add non-compute overhead. Treat the result as an estimate, not a benchmark.

A common rough estimate for dense Transformer training is `C≈6ND`, where `N` is parameter count and `D` is training-token count. It approximates forward/backward matrix operations; attention at long context, embeddings, architecture and implementation can change the total.

For `N=10^9`, `D=20×10^9`, estimate `C≈1.2×10²⁰` FLOPs. If an assumed **sustained**, not peak, throughput is `10^14` FLOPs/s, time is `1.2×10^6` seconds, about 13.9 days. This is an arithmetic illustration, not a hardware benchmark. Add evaluation, checkpoints, failures and orchestration overhead.

Model FLOPs utilization compares useful model compute with a stated hardware peak, but definitions and precision conventions vary. GPU “100% utilization” is not equivalent to peak useful model FLOPs.

## 4. Scaling laws

**Key terms.** A **scaling law** is an empirical fitted relation; **N/D** are parameter/token counts; **A/B/α/β/E** are fitted constants; **C** is compute budget.

**Process.** Fit loss against model and data sizes, impose a budget, then examine its preferred allocation. Check whether the new architecture, corpus and deployment regime match the fit before using its recommendation.

A stylized loss model is:

\[
L(N,D)\approx E+A N^{-\alpha}+B D^{-\beta}.
\]

`E` is an estimated irreducible term within this fit; other constants are fitted empirically. Holding compute `C≈kND` fixed gives `D=C/(kN)`. Differentiating the resulting two-term expression yields approximately:

\[
N^*\propto C^{\beta/(\alpha+\beta)},\qquad
D^*\propto C^{\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)}.
\]

This explains a trade-off: more parameters leave fewer training tokens under a fixed budget. The fitted exponents and constants depend on the regime and recipe. A popular tokens-per-parameter heuristic is not a law for every dataset, MoE, context length or inference-heavy product. A smaller model trained longer can be preferable when serving cost dominates.

## 5. Compute and bandwidth limits

**Key terms.** **Arithmetic intensity** is work per byte moved; **bandwidth** is bytes moved per second; a **roofline** bounds speed using compute and bandwidth limits.

**Process.** Estimate the operation's data movement and arithmetic, then identify the tighter hardware limit. Profile the real workload next to determine whether computation or memory traffic deserves optimization.

Compute-bound work waits for arithmetic throughput; memory-bound work waits for data movement. **Arithmetic intensity** is FLOPs per byte moved. A large matrix multiplication can reuse loaded values and achieve high intensity. A small-batch decode step may move many weights for relatively few new tokens.

If memory bandwidth doubles but compute stays fixed, a memory-bound task may improve substantially; a compute-bound task may not. These are useful limiting models, not labels permanently attached to all prefill/decode workloads.

## 6. Experiment budgeting

**Key terms.** A **comparison budget** includes all runs and checks; **accelerator hours** measure occupied devices over time; **energy** integrates power over time.

**Process.** Allocate resources to baselines, seeds, pilots, evaluation and failures before choosing run sizes. Report the same budget unit for competing methods so equal updates are not mistaken for equal cost.

Budget the entire comparison: pilot runs, seeds, baselines, failed runs, data generation and evaluation. State whether equal budget means equal tokens, optimizer steps, elapsed time, accelerator hours or money. Those equalities are not interchangeable.

Energy is power integrated over time; carbon estimates also need location/time-dependent factors and system boundaries. Parameter count alone does not establish sustainability. Report assumptions rather than inventing precise emissions.

## Exercises and checks

1. 1B parameters at 4 bits: raw weights about 0.5 GB. What is missing? Quantization metadata, selected higher-precision tensors, activations/cache and runtime overhead.
2. `N=2B,D=10B`: rough dense-training compute is `1.2×10²⁰` FLOPs, the same product as the earlier example but not necessarily the same quality or actual runtime.
3. Why can lowering weight precision fail to speed up inference? Hardware/kernel support, dequantization, launch overhead, cache or another bottleneck.

Primary reading: [compute-optimal scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556). Systems teaching: [CS336](https://cs336.stanford.edu/). Separate raw weights, optimizer state, activations and inference cache before estimating the complete resource budget.

A common rough estimate for dense Transformer training is `C≈6ND`, where `N` is parameter count and `D` is training-token count. It approximates forward/backward matrix operations; attention at long context, embeddings, architecture and implementation can change the total.

For `N=10^9`, `D=20×10^9`, estimate `C≈1.2×10²⁰` FLOPs. If an assumed **sustained**, not peak, throughput is `10^14` FLOPs/s, time is `1.2×10^6` seconds, about 13.9 days. This is an arithmetic illustration, not a hardware benchmark. Add evaluation, checkpoints, failures and orchestration overhead.

Model FLOPs utilization compares useful model compute with a stated hardware peak, but definitions and precision conventions vary. GPU “100% utilization” is not equivalent to peak useful model FLOPs.

sections.title: Scaling laws
sections.markdown:
## 4. Scaling laws

**Key terms.** A **scaling law** is an empirical fitted relation; **N/D** are parameter/token counts; **A/B/α/β/E** are fitted constants; **C** is compute budget.

**Process.** Fit loss against model and data sizes, impose a budget, then examine its preferred allocation. Check whether the new architecture, corpus and deployment regime match the fit before using its recommendation.

A stylized loss model is:

\[
L(N,D)\approx E+A N^{-\alpha}+B D^{-\beta}.
\]

`E` is an estimated irreducible term within this fit; other constants are fitted empirically. Holding compute `C≈kND` fixed gives `D=C/(kN)`. Differentiating the resulting two-term expression yields approximately:

\[
N^*\propto C^{\beta/(\alpha+\beta)},\qquad
D^*\propto C^{\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)}.
\]

This explains a trade-off: more parameters leave fewer training tokens under a fixed budget. The fitted exponents and constants depend on the regime and recipe. A popular tokens-per-parameter heuristic is not a law for every dataset, MoE, context length or inference-heavy product. A smaller model trained longer can be preferable when serving cost dominates.

sections.title: Compute and bandwidth limits
sections.markdown:
## 5. Compute and bandwidth limits

**Key terms.** **Arithmetic intensity** is work per byte moved; **bandwidth** is bytes moved per second; a **roofline** bounds speed using compute and bandwidth limits.

**Process.** Estimate the operation's data movement and arithmetic, then identify the tighter hardware limit. Profile the real workload next to determine whether computation or memory traffic deserves optimization.

Compute-bound work waits for arithmetic throughput; memory-bound work waits for data movement. **Arithmetic intensity** is FLOPs per byte moved. A large matrix multiplication can reuse loaded values and achieve high intensity. A small-batch decode step may move many weights for relatively few new tokens.

If memory bandwidth doubles but compute stays fixed, a memory-bound task may improve substantially; a compute-bound task may not. These are useful limiting models, not labels permanently attached to all prefill/decode workloads.

sections.title: Experiment budgeting
sections.markdown:
## 6. Experiment budgeting

**Key terms.** A **comparison budget** includes all runs and checks; **accelerator hours** measure occupied devices over time; **energy** integrates power over time.

**Process.** Allocate resources to baselines, seeds, pilots, evaluation and failures before choosing run sizes. Report the same budget unit for competing methods so equal updates are not mistaken for equal cost.

Budget the entire comparison: pilot runs, seeds, baselines, failed runs, data generation and evaluation. State whether equal budget means equal tokens, optimizer steps, elapsed time, accelerator hours or money. Those equalities are not interchangeable.

Energy is power integrated over time; carbon estimates also need location/time-dependent factors and system boundaries. Parameter count alone does not establish sustainability. Report assumptions rather than inventing precise emissions.

sections.title: Exercises and checks
sections.markdown:
## Exercises and checks

1. 1B parameters at 4 bits: raw weights about 0.5 GB. What is missing? Quantization metadata, selected higher-precision tensors, activations/cache and runtime overhead.
2. `N=2B,D=10B`: rough dense-training compute is `1.2×10²⁰` FLOPs, the same product as the earlier example but not necessarily the same quality or actual runtime.
3. Why can lowering weight precision fail to speed up inference? Hardware/kernel support, dequantization, launch overhead, cache or another bottleneck.

Primary reading: [compute-optimal scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556). Systems teaching: [CS336](https://cs336.stanford.edu/). Separate raw weights, optimizer state, activations and inference cache before estimating the complete resource budget.

notes.title: Parameter counting
notes.markdown:
Parameters, training tokens, context length, update count, hardware time and money are different quantities. A model with fewer parameters can cost more overall if trained on many more tokens or served millions of times. Total lifetime cost includes data preparation, experiments, training, evaluation and inference.

In a simple dense decoder block, attention projections contribute roughly `4d²` weights and a non-gated MLP roughly `2 d d_ff`, ignoring biases/norms. With `d_ff=4d`, that is about `12d²` per layer. Gated MLPs, GQA, tied embeddings and expert layers change the count. Add embeddings `Vd` and any untied output projection.

### Count the prepared model instead of guessing from its name

For the configured bias-free SmolLM2 model: vocabulary 49,152; width 960; 32 layers; KV projection width 320; gated intermediate width 2560; tied input/output embeddings.

1. The shared embedding/output matrix contains `49,152×960 = 47,185,920` parameters. Do not count it twice when weights are tied.
2. Each block's attention matrices contain `960×960 + 960×320 + 960×320 + 960×960 = 2,457,600` parameters: query, key, value and output projections.
3. Its three gated-MLP matrices contain `3×960×2560 = 7,372,800` parameters. A two-matrix GELU formula would undercount this model.
4. Two RMSNorm scale vectors add `2×960 = 1,920` per block. Across 32 blocks the subtotal is `32×9,832,320 = 314,634,240`.
5. Add the shared embedding and final 960-element RMSNorm: total **361,821,120**. This is a parameter count, not the peak-memory requirement.

The recipe follows the [model configuration](https://huggingface.co/HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-360M-Instruct/blob/main/config.json). Another architecture can have biases, untied heads or expert weights, so reuse the counting procedure, not the total. The compute-optimal scaling study in [Chinchilla](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556) addresses a separate question: how to allocate a training-compute budget between parameters and tokens.

notes.title: Training memory
notes.markdown:
**Key terms.** **Bits per value** determine raw storage; **activations** are forward intermediates; **optimizer state** stores update history; **GiB** means 2³⁰ bytes.

For `N` parameters stored at `b` bits, raw weights need `Nb/8` bytes. A 7-billion-parameter model at 16 bits needs about 14 GB decimal, or 13.04 GiB. That is **not** a complete training or serving requirement.

An illustrative mixed-precision Adam setup might store:

| Component | Bytes/parameter in this example |
| --- | ---: |
| Low-precision parameter copy | 2 |
| Low-precision gradients | 2 |
| FP32 master weights | 4 |
| Two FP32 Adam moments | 8 |
| **Subtotal** | **16** |

For 7B parameters, subtotal is 112 GB before activations, workspace, communication buffers and allocator overhead. Other implementations use different gradient/master-state choices. Do not present “16 bytes” as a universal constant.

Activations depend on batch, sequence length, width, layers and kernels. Gradient checkpointing discards selected intermediate activations and recomputes them during backward, trading compute for memory. Optimizer sharding distributes state but adds communication. Offloading moves state to CPU/disk and can create a bandwidth bottleneck.

reading.title: LLM parameter counts, memory and compute
reading.definition: A model's parameter count, raw weight storage, training-state memory and compute budget measure different things. Training can require gradients, optimizer history, activations and temporary workspaces beyond the weights. Resource estimates are conditional accounting tools; measured peak memory and throughput must establish whether a real configuration fits and runs usefully.
reading.example: Select one, ten or one hundred million hypothetical parameters. The simple convention stores FP32 weights, FP32 gradients and two FP32 Adam moments. Its static state uses sixteen bytes per parameter before activations or runtime overhead; other recipes need different accounting.
reading.connection: The training loop explains what values exist and when. This lesson counts their storage and work before scaling, while keeping the detailed prepared-model count, scaling laws and hardware bottlenecks in the deeper explanations.

steps.title: Count actual parameter entries
steps.prose: Add the entries of the model's unique parameter tensors. Tied weights are one shared parameter storage, not two independent learned matrices. The control declares a hypothetical count; it does not inspect an unknown model or infer a count from a product name.
steps.terms: A parameter is one learned scalar. Token exposure, layer count and hidden width affect resources but are not themselves parameter counts.
steps.next: Use the parameter count with an explicit numerical format to calculate raw weight bytes.

steps.title: Calculate raw weight storage
steps.prose: Under this example's FP32 convention each weight value needs four bytes. Multiply the parameter count accordingly and distinguish decimal MB from binary MiB. Metadata, temporary copies and allocations are outside this value-only estimate.
steps.terms: Precision defines a value representation. Raw storage is not a peak device-memory estimate or a guarantee that a model will fit.
steps.next: Add the state required by the selected training recipe separately from the weights.

steps.title: Account for gradients and optimizer history
steps.prose: This FP32 Adam illustration adds four bytes per gradient and eight bytes for two moment arrays to four-byte weights. Its sixteen-byte subtotal is not a universal constant. Mixed precision, freezing, sharding and optimizer variants change the terms.
steps.terms: Optimizer state contains update history. Frozen parameters need different trainable-state accounting but still require their participating base computation.
steps.next: Include activations, workspaces and implementation overhead before interpreting the total.
steps.node: Account for gradients and optimizer history

steps.prose: Activations vary with context, batch, architecture and checkpointing. Profile a representative safe pilot rather than multiplying by an invented constant. Compute/time estimates also need achieved throughput and evaluation/checkpoint costs, not just advertised hardware peaks.

reading.lesson_markdown:
Parameter count is the number of learned entries, not the memory footprint of an experiment. A dense matrix from d inputs to h outputs has dh weights, plus h biases if used. A conventional attention block with four d×d projections has approximately $4d^2$ weights; a d→4d→d MLP has approximately $8d^2$. Gated MLPs, grouped-query projections, and tied vocabulary tables change that count.

Raw storage is entries times bytes per entry. For 100 million parameters in two-byte storage, weights alone require 200 million bytes, about 191 MiB. Training additionally needs gradients, optimizer state, activations, and temporary buffers. Inference adds cache and workspace. A model file's size is therefore not the GPU memory needed for a chosen workload.

Batch size and sequence length change activation costs. Dense attention can create a quadratic position-pair object, though memory-efficient kernels avoid storing it in the ordinary way. A rough dense-model training estimate is about 6ND FLOPs for N parameters and D tokens, with simplifying assumptions; it is not a hardware runtime prediction and can miss attention or other costs.

Measure actual peak memory, throughput, and wall time on the intended device. More parameters with too little data or too little training can be a worse use of a fixed compute budget. The small lab teaches these accounting choices; it does not reproduce large-model scaling experiments.

Sources: [Hoffmann et al.: compute-optimal training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556), [PyTorch: CUDA memory accounting](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/notes/cuda.html#cuda-memory-management).

document.markdown:
# T7. Distributed LLM training and gradient reduction

Distributed training divides data, arithmetic or stored state across cooperating processes. Data parallelism uses model replicas on different examples and combines gradients; tensor, pipeline and state-sharding schemes divide other objects. Correct loss normalization and communication are required before more devices can be treated as a performance improvement.

Two data-parallel workers have unequal valid-token counts and supplied scalar mean gradients one and three. We calculate the intended global token-weighted gradient, then the local scaling needed when a reducer averages across the two workers. This is not an executed cluster job.

Microbatch accumulation combined evidence on one worker. This lesson adds communication and a reducer convention across workers; multiplying device counts alone does not establish either a correct gradient or a speedup.

## 1. Parallel work and communication

**Key terms.** A **worker** is a training process; **communication** moves tensors between workers; **synchronization** makes processes wait for shared progress.

**Process.** Establish a correct one-worker run, measure its bottleneck and only then divide work. Additional devices help only when useful parallel work exceeds communication and coordination overhead.

Each accelerator has finite memory and compute. Distributing work creates communication, synchronization and scheduling costs. If one worker is late, others may wait. If interconnect bandwidth is poor, sharding can save memory while losing throughput.

First distinguish **scale up**—use faster/larger resources—from **scale out**—add workers. Strong scaling fixes total work and adds workers; weak scaling increases work with resources. Their efficiency numbers answer different questions.

## 2. Parallelism families

**Key terms.** **Data parallelism** splits examples; **tensor parallelism** splits tensor operations; **pipeline parallelism** splits layers; **sharding** partitions stored state.

**Process.** Choose what each device owns, execute its local computation and exchange the required tensors. Reconstruct the intended global update before judging whether the distributed run is faster.

```text
Data parallel:       GPU 1 = full model, batch A
                     GPU 2 = full model, batch B → combine gradients

Tensor parallel:     GPUs hold slices of a layer → exchange partial results

Pipeline parallel:   layers 1–k on GPU 1 → layers k+1–L on GPU 2

Expert parallel:     experts on different GPUs → route token states between them
```

**Data parallelism** replicates the model and aggregates gradients. An all-reduce combines a value across workers and distributes the result. An all-gather assembles shards; reduce-scatter reduces values while distributing result shards.

**ZeRO/FSDP-style sharding** partitions optimizer state, gradients and/or parameters depending on the scheme. Parameters may be gathered for computation then resharded. This is not identical to tensor parallelism, which splits the layer's arithmetic itself.

**Tensor parallelism** splits matrix operations; it usually needs frequent fast communication. **Pipeline parallelism** splits layers and moves activations; microbatches reduce idle “bubbles.” **Expert parallelism** distributes MoE experts; routing can require all-to-all traffic. **Sequence/context parallelism** partitions sequence-related work or state; exact strategies differ by framework.

Combine these only after specifying the mapping. “8 GPUs with TP=2 and DP=4” describes a different execution than “DP=8.” Do not multiply every advertised parallelism dimension without checking whether groups overlap or are nested.

## 3. Effective gradients and reproducibility

**Key terms.** **DDP** is distributed data parallelism; **W** counts workers; **Sᵣ** is worker r's summed loss; **N** is the global valid-target count.

**Process.** Each worker computes its local loss contribution. Scale for the framework's gradient reduction, synchronize and apply the same global update. Unequal token counts require more care than averaging local means.

**Calculation.** For two workers with 10 and 90 valid targets and local mean losses 2 and 4, the global token mean is (10×2+90×4)/100=3.8, not (2+4)/2=3.0. With DDP gradient averaging, local losses scaled as W×local loss sum/N have numerical values 0.4 and 7.2; their average is 3.8 and their averaged gradients match the intended objective.

Verify whether gradients are summed or averaged and over which workers. The loss denominator must match the intended global valid-token objective. Each worker needs a different data shard; otherwise eight workers may process eight copies of the same examples. Save sampler and RNG states; a seed alone does not describe the full run.

Distributed failures include mismatched collective calls, a worker exiting while others wait, network timeouts, CPU data-loading stalls and inconsistent checkpoints. Diagnose the first failing worker's log, not only the final timeout message.

### Derive the loss scale under ordinary DDP averaging

Let rank `r` own token-loss sum `S_r` and valid-target count `N_r`. The intended global loss is:

\[
L=\frac{\sum_r S_r}{N},\qquad N=\sum_r N_r.
\]

For `W` workers and the ordinary DDP convention that averages parameter gradients across workers:

1. All-reduce the target counts to obtain the same global denominator `N` on every worker.
2. Each worker differentiates `W S_r/N`. After DDP's averaging, the combined gradient is `(1/W)Σ_r∇(W S_r/N)=∇L`.
3. Differentiating only `S_r/N` and then averaging shrinks the gradient by `W`. Averaging each worker's mean loss instead can give unequal-sized workers the wrong relative influence.
4. With accumulation, count the full update's intended targets. Suppress synchronization for appropriate intermediate microbatches only using a correct framework-supported pattern, then synchronize at the boundary.

Communication hooks, uneven-input handling and other frameworks can use different reduction conventions. Confirm the installed implementation rather than copying the world-size factor blindly. Start with a one-worker versus two-worker toy equivalence test, fixed data and disabled dropout. References: [PyTorch DDP](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/generated/torch.nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel.html) and [ZeRO](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054).

## 4. Kernels, fusion and FlashAttention

**Key terms.** A **kernel** is a device computation; **fusion** combines operations; **FlashAttention** reorganizes exact attention to reduce memory traffic.

**Process.** A framework operation selects a compatible kernel, which moves data and computes outputs. Check output/gradient agreement before attributing a speedup to better execution rather than a changed calculation.

A high-level attention expression may create enormous intermediate tensors. A kernel implements the arithmetic on hardware. **Fusion** combines operations to avoid writing/reading temporary results and reduce launch overhead.

FlashAttention reorganizes exact attention with tiling and stable online softmax, reducing transfers to/from high-bandwidth memory and avoiding materialization of the full score matrix in the usual form. It is not the same as sparse or approximate attention. Exact refers to the mathematical operation, subject to floating-point differences. Pairwise arithmetic still has quadratic sequence-length dependence for ordinary dense attention.

The crucial distinction: **algorithmic complexity**, **memory footprint**, **memory traffic** and **wall-clock time** are separate. A kernel can substantially speed up the same mathematical operation.

## 5. Cluster workflow

**Key terms.** A **login node** is the cluster entry machine; an **allocation** grants resources; a **job script** describes scheduled work; **SLURM** manages the queue.

**Process.** Connect by SSH, prepare the environment, submit a resource request and run on the assigned compute node. Collect logs and checkpoints before the allocation ends; SSH alone does not reserve a GPU.

```text
laptop → SSH → login node → submit scheduler request
→ allocated compute node(s) → distributed launcher → worker processes
→ logs, checkpoints and metrics → evaluate → release allocation
```

Read your cluster's rules first. Commands such as `squeue`, `sacct`, `sinfo` and `nvidia-smi` are read-only diagnostics where installed. `sbatch` submits a job; it is not required for every GPU system. A scheduler allocation and the Python distributed process group are separate layers.

Never kill other users' processes or run network-wide scans to debug your experiment. Keep credentials out of job scripts and logs. Use authorised data storage and obey quotas.

## 6. Profile before optimization

**Key terms.** A **profile** records where time or memory goes; **warmup** removes startup effects; **synchronization** can be needed to time completed accelerator work.

**Process.** Measure a representative baseline, isolate costly operations, change one bottleneck and profile again. Confirm numerical correctness alongside time and memory rather than optimizing a misleading timer.

Measure data-loading time, forward/backward time, optimizer time, communication, checkpoint writing and memory peaks. Accelerator operations may be asynchronous: naive wall-clock timing without synchronization can measure launch time instead of completion. Include warmup and repeated measurements; state batch/context/dtype and hardware.

## Exercises and checks

1. Microbatch 2, accumulation 8, DP 4: nominal effective example batch is 64. TP workers do not multiply the count of distinct examples in the same way.
2. A model fits only after FSDP but becomes slower. Is FSDP broken? **Not necessarily:** communication or offload may dominate; fitting and speeding up are different goals.
3. Explain why FlashAttention and PagedAttention solve different problems. **Answer:** attention IO/computation organization versus inference KV-cache memory management; see R6.

Primary sources: [FlashAttention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135), [NVIDIA parallelisms guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/latest/parallelisms.html), [PyTorch FSDP documentation](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/fsdp.html). APIs are version-sensitive: use docs matching your installed build.

Let rank `r` own token-loss sum `S_r` and valid-target count `N_r`. The intended global loss is:

\[
L=\frac{\sum_r S_r}{N},\qquad N=\sum_r N_r.
\]

For `W` workers and the ordinary DDP convention that averages parameter gradients across workers:

1. All-reduce the target counts to obtain the same global denominator `N` on every worker.
2. Each worker differentiates `W S_r/N`. After DDP's averaging, the combined gradient is `(1/W)Σ_r∇(W S_r/N)=∇L`.
3. Differentiating only `S_r/N` and then averaging shrinks the gradient by `W`. Averaging each worker's mean loss instead can give unequal-sized workers the wrong relative influence.
4. With accumulation, count the full update's intended targets. Suppress synchronization for appropriate intermediate microbatches only using a correct framework-supported pattern, then synchronize at the boundary.

Communication hooks, uneven-input handling and other frameworks can use different reduction conventions. Confirm the installed implementation rather than copying the world-size factor blindly. Start with a one-worker versus two-worker toy equivalence test, fixed data and disabled dropout. References: [PyTorch DDP](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/generated/torch.nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel.html) and [ZeRO](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054).

sections.title: Kernels, fusion and FlashAttention
sections.markdown:
## 4. Kernels, fusion and FlashAttention

**Key terms.** A **kernel** is a device computation; **fusion** combines operations; **FlashAttention** reorganizes exact attention to reduce memory traffic.

**Process.** A framework operation selects a compatible kernel, which moves data and computes outputs. Check output/gradient agreement before attributing a speedup to better execution rather than a changed calculation.

A high-level attention expression may create enormous intermediate tensors. A kernel implements the arithmetic on hardware. **Fusion** combines operations to avoid writing/reading temporary results and reduce launch overhead.

FlashAttention reorganizes exact attention with tiling and stable online softmax, reducing transfers to/from high-bandwidth memory and avoiding materialization of the full score matrix in the usual form. It is not the same as sparse or approximate attention. Exact refers to the mathematical operation, subject to floating-point differences. Pairwise arithmetic still has quadratic sequence-length dependence for ordinary dense attention.

The crucial distinction: **algorithmic complexity**, **memory footprint**, **memory traffic** and **wall-clock time** are separate. A kernel can substantially speed up the same mathematical operation.

sections.title: Cluster workflow
sections.markdown:
## 5. Cluster workflow

**Key terms.** A **login node** is the cluster entry machine; an **allocation** grants resources; a **job script** describes scheduled work; **SLURM** manages the queue.

**Process.** Connect by SSH, prepare the environment, submit a resource request and run on the assigned compute node. Collect logs and checkpoints before the allocation ends; SSH alone does not reserve a GPU.

```text
laptop → SSH → login node → submit scheduler request
→ allocated compute node(s) → distributed launcher → worker processes
→ logs, checkpoints and metrics → evaluate → release allocation
```

Read your cluster's rules first. Commands such as `squeue`, `sacct`, `sinfo` and `nvidia-smi` are read-only diagnostics where installed. `sbatch` submits a job; it is not required for every GPU system. A scheduler allocation and the Python distributed process group are separate layers.

Never kill other users' processes or run network-wide scans to debug your experiment. Keep credentials out of job scripts and logs. Use authorised data storage and obey quotas.

sections.title: Profile before optimization
sections.markdown:
## 6. Profile before optimization

**Key terms.** A **profile** records where time or memory goes; **warmup** removes startup effects; **synchronization** can be needed to time completed accelerator work.

**Process.** Measure a representative baseline, isolate costly operations, change one bottleneck and profile again. Confirm numerical correctness alongside time and memory rather than optimizing a misleading timer.

Measure data-loading time, forward/backward time, optimizer time, communication, checkpoint writing and memory peaks. Accelerator operations may be asynchronous: naive wall-clock timing without synchronization can measure launch time instead of completion. Include warmup and repeated measurements; state batch/context/dtype and hardware.

sections.title: Exercises and checks
sections.markdown:
## Exercises and checks

1. Microbatch 2, accumulation 8, DP 4: nominal effective example batch is 64. TP workers do not multiply the count of distinct examples in the same way.
2. A model fits only after FSDP but becomes slower. Is FSDP broken? **Not necessarily:** communication or offload may dominate; fitting and speeding up are different goals.
3. Explain why FlashAttention and PagedAttention solve different problems. **Answer:** attention IO/computation organization versus inference KV-cache memory management; see R6.

Primary sources: [FlashAttention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135), [NVIDIA parallelisms guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/latest/parallelisms.html), [PyTorch FSDP documentation](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/fsdp.html). APIs are version-sensitive: use docs matching your installed build.

notes.title: Parallelism families
notes.markdown:
**Key terms.** **Data parallelism** splits examples; **tensor parallelism** splits tensor operations; **pipeline parallelism** splits layers; **sharding** partitions stored state.

```text
Data parallel:       GPU 1 = full model, batch A
                     GPU 2 = full model, batch B → combine gradients

Tensor parallel:     GPUs hold slices of a layer → exchange partial results

Pipeline parallel:   layers 1–k on GPU 1 → layers k+1–L on GPU 2

Expert parallel:     experts on different GPUs → route token states between them
```

**Data parallelism** replicates the model and aggregates gradients. An all-reduce combines a value across workers and distributes the result. An all-gather assembles shards; reduce-scatter reduces values while distributing result shards.

**ZeRO/FSDP-style sharding** partitions optimizer state, gradients and/or parameters depending on the scheme. Parameters may be gathered for computation then resharded. This is not identical to tensor parallelism, which splits the layer's arithmetic itself.

**Tensor parallelism** splits matrix operations; it usually needs frequent fast communication. **Pipeline parallelism** splits layers and moves activations; microbatches reduce idle “bubbles.” **Expert parallelism** distributes MoE experts; routing can require all-to-all traffic. **Sequence/context parallelism** partitions sequence-related work or state; exact strategies differ by framework.

Combine these only after specifying the mapping. “8 GPUs with TP=2 and DP=4” describes a different execution than “DP=8.” Do not multiply every advertised parallelism dimension without checking whether groups overlap or are nested.

notes.title: Effective gradients and reproducibility
notes.markdown:
**Key terms.** **DDP** is distributed data parallelism; **W** counts workers; **Sᵣ** is worker r's summed loss; **N** is the global valid-target count.

reading.title: Distributed LLM training and gradient reduction
reading.definition: Distributed training divides data, arithmetic or stored state across cooperating processes. Data parallelism uses model replicas on different examples and combines gradients; tensor, pipeline and state-sharding schemes divide other objects. Correct loss normalization and communication are required before more devices can be treated as a performance improvement.
reading.example: Two data-parallel workers have unequal valid-token counts and supplied scalar mean gradients one and three. We calculate the intended global token-weighted gradient, then the local scaling needed when a reducer averages across the two workers. This is not an executed cluster job.
reading.connection: Microbatch accumulation combined evidence on one worker. This lesson adds communication and a reducer convention across workers; multiplying device counts alone does not establish either a correct gradient or a speedup.

steps.title: Define replica ownership and local evidence
steps.prose: Each worker holds matching model parameters and receives different permitted examples. The example uses two valid tokens on A and a selectable count on B. Model replication is not layer sharding or multiplying the hidden width.
steps.terms: Data-parallel workers compute local gradients for a common objective. W is the number of participating replicas, here two.
steps.next: Use these counts both to define the desired global mean and to scale the executed local contributions.

steps.title: Calculate the reference global gradient
steps.prose: The desired gradient weights local mean gradients by their valid-token counts. This independent reference checks the distributed calculation; it is not a gradient magically fed back into each worker. The scalar values stand in for full parameter-gradient tensors.
steps.terms: n_A and n_B count valid targets, and g_A and g_B are supplied local means. A mean of local means weights workers rather than tokens.
steps.next: Compare this reference with the reducer result after applying its correct local scaling.

steps.title: Scale local losses for the reducer
steps.prose: Ordinary averaging reduction divides summed gradients by W. To recover the intended global token mean, scale each local mean loss by W times its local count divided by the global count. A sum reducer would require a different factor.
steps.terms: The global denominator must be known consistently. Reducer semantics and loss normalization are part of the algorithm, not interchangeable implementation trivia.
steps.next: Average the scaled local gradients and verify agreement with the reference objective.

steps.title: Synchronize and apply matching updates
steps.prose: Combining the two scaled contributions with the stated average reproduces the target gradient. Replicas then need the same optimizer update and consistent state. Communication failures, unequal participation and stale state can break that equivalence.
steps.terms: All-reduce aggregates values across workers. It does not pool model opinions or create another reasoning stage.
steps.next: The deeper notes compare sharding, kernels, cluster workflow and profiling before evaluation of the resulting model.

links: Independently calculate the intended token-weighted reference gradient.
Use valid counts and world size to scale the actual local losses.
Average scaled contributions under the stated reducer convention.

reading.legend: The left branch calculates scaled local contributions and their reduction. The right branch independently defines the desired result for checking. No distributed worker is launched by selecting the diagram.
reading.lesson_markdown:
Data parallelism gives each worker a model replica and different data, then combines gradients so replicas can apply a consistent update. Tensor or pipeline parallelism instead splits parts of the computation. Sharding optimizer or parameter state changes memory ownership. These are different reasons to use several devices.

The reference objective matters before choosing a reduction. If worker A sees one token with loss 2 and worker B sees three tokens with total loss 9, the global token mean is $(2+9)/4=2.75$. Averaging their local means gives $(2+3)/2=2.5$, which weights workers equally rather than tokens equally. Uneven token counts require scaling compatible with whether the reducer sums or averages gradients.

Synchronise at the intended accumulation boundary. All replicas must agree about the update; clipping and skipped non-finite updates need coherent handling. Also partition data so workers do not unintentionally repeat the same examples, and record how checkpoint state is assembled.

The local course illustrates these calculations but does not offer multi-GPU distributed training. Use a small deterministic single-process reference when validating a distributed implementation. A speedup claim requires measured communication, compute, and workload; doubling workers does not guarantee halving time.

Sources: [PyTorch: DistributedDataParallel](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.9/generated/torch.nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel.html), [PyTorch: fully sharded data parallel tutorial](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/intermediate/FSDP_tutorial.html).

question.prompt: A distributed setup averages each worker's mean loss, but workers have unequal valid-target counts. What should you check?

options.text: Whether the reduction implements the intended global target-weighted objective.
options.feedback: Equal averaging of unequal-target worker means can change the objective. Count valid targets and account for the distributed gradient reduction convention.

options.text: Only whether the workers use the same GPU model.
options.feedback: Matching hardware does not correct unequal statistical weighting.

options.text: Whether every worker reports the same file size.
options.feedback: File sizes are not necessarily the counts of valid prediction targets.

options.text: Whether test performance can choose the reduction rule.
options.feedback: The objective should be specified from the task, not chosen by exploiting a final test score.

question.explanation: Equal averaging of unequal-target worker means can change the objective. Count valid targets and account for the distributed gradient reduction convention.

question.prompt: Four data-parallel workers each process microbatches of 8 examples and accumulate 2 microbatches per optimizer update. What is the effective example batch size?

options.text: 16 examples.
options.feedback: That is one worker's accumulated batch, before combining four workers.

options.text: 64 examples.
options.feedback: 4 workers × 8 examples × 2 accumulation microbatches = 64 examples per synchronized update. Token counts can still vary across examples.

options.text: 32 examples.
options.feedback: That omits the accumulation factor of two.

options.text: 128 examples.
options.feedback: There are four workers, not an additional unexplained factor of two.

question.explanation: 4 workers × 8 examples × 2 accumulation microbatches = 64 examples per synchronized update. Token counts can still vary across examples.

document.markdown:
# T8. LLM evaluation and interpretability evidence

LLM evaluation tests a specified claim, such as better token prediction, task accuracy, source support, robustness or efficiency. Interpretability asks different questions about computation and mechanism. A score gain, an attention picture and a controlled intervention provide different evidence; none alone establishes every claim about useful or reliable behavior.

Two hypothetical task scores, 0.76 and 0.79, illustrate a difference of 0.03. A separate scalar intervention starts from 0.8 and subtracts a selected amount. These are interpretation exercises, not measured causal effects from a trained model.

After fitting and resource accounting, evaluate the artifact against its intended use. Shared metrics supply the formulas; this lesson connects matched protocols, uncertainty and mechanism claims without treating one as a substitute for another.

## 1. Evaluation protocols

**Key terms.** A **claim** states the proposed improvement; an **evaluation protocol** fixes how it is checked; a **held-out set** is excluded from fitting.

**Process.** Translate the claim into a measurable outcome before choosing a benchmark. Freeze the protocol, collect predictions and inspect failures before generalizing beyond that outcome.

Specify a claim before choosing a benchmark: next-token prediction, task success, source faithfulness, robustness, calibration, safety or efficiency. No single leaderboard measures all of them. Save model revision, tokenizer/template, prompts, examples, decoding, budgets and scoring code.

Likelihood-based multiple choice, free generation and constrained label generation are different protocols. A model can rank a correct choice highest but fail to emit it under a format constraint. Report the interface being tested.

## 2. Build an evaluation ladder

**Key terms.** A **sanity check** tests basic correctness; a **benchmark** measures a defined task; **robustness** tests changed conditions.

**Process.** Begin with small known cases, progress to matched held-out tasks and then test shifts or adversarial cases. Each level builds evidence for a stronger claim rather than replacing the earlier checks.

```text
unit checks → held-out language-model loss → task datasets
→ domain/length/language slices → adversarial and shift tests
→ human-reviewed cases → intended system evaluation
```

Benchmark contamination, reused development examples and repeated selection all weaken interpretation. Freeze a final set. Record unresolved samples rather than dropping malformed generations silently. Human annotation needs instructions, disagreement handling and safeguards for sensitive material.

## 3. Matched comparisons

**Key terms.** A **matched comparison** controls data and budgets; **paired evaluation** compares systems on the same cases; **seed variation** comes from training randomness.

**Process.** Freeze conditions, run comparable systems and save per-example predictions. Compute effects and uncertainty under the declared unit before deciding whether the change helped reliably.

Match available information and state resource budgets. Report uncertainty using appropriate independent units and training seeds where feasible. A confidence interval for one dataset does not establish universal superiority. If comparing many settings, distinguish exploratory screening from confirmatory comparisons.

For generative tasks, assess correctness, completeness, unsupported additions, contradictions and appropriate refusal. A factual statement can be unsupported by the supplied source; a source-faithful summary can repeat a false source. Those are different axes.

LLM judges can exhibit position, verbosity, self-preference and instruction-following biases. Blind system identities where feasible, randomize answer order and compare a sample with independent human judgements. Judge agreement with one annotator does not establish objective truth.

### Build an evaluation table that supports one clear conclusion

For a claimed robustness improvement, use one row per condition and columns for input access, training data, selection rule, token/compute budget and outcomes. A score without those columns can hide an unmatched comparison.

1. Freeze prompts, dataset groups and scoring rules before the confirmatory test. Mark exploratory results separately.
2. Save per-example labels, predictions and failure states. A malformed generation or abstention belongs in a declared denominator, not a silently filtered “successful outputs” subset.
3. Calculate paired differences on the same cases. Use document/group resampling when cases share a source, and report training-seed variation separately where feasible.
4. Evaluate an explicit transfer condition and important slices: domain, label policy, language, length, negation and rare entities. A global mean can improve while a critical slice fails.
5. For a proposed explanation, add a control that could refute it. For example, compare useful intermediate fields with shuffled or task-irrelevant fields under a matched budget; do not infer causality from an attention picture.

For generated answers, score correctness, support and coverage separately. A citation can identify a real source without supporting the claim attached to it. Use an independently reviewed subset to audit automatic judges. References: [LM Evaluation Harness](https://github.com/EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness) and [paired bootstrap implementation](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.bootstrap.html).

## 4. Inspection, attribution and intervention

**Key terms.** **Inspection** observes computation; **attribution** assigns relevance; an **intervention** changes computation to test an effect.

**Process.** Inspect model states to form a hypothesis, then use matched interventions where feasible. Report the difference between a useful visualization and evidence that a component caused behaviour.

**Behavioural analysis** studies inputs/outputs: change a guideline, remove context, vary a counterfactual. **Representational analysis** uses probes or similarities inside the network. **Mechanistic intervention** changes activations/components to test their role in computation.

A probe predicting a property shows it can be decoded under that probe setup, not that the model uses it for the task. A saliency map is local sensitivity, not a complete causal account. Activation patching replaces selected internal values from one run with values from another and measures an outcome change; matched controls and the choice of corruption matter.

A sparse autoencoder attempts to decompose activations using a sparsity-constrained dictionary. Features can be useful hypotheses, but names assigned by humans/models may be incomplete. Superposition means more concepts may be represented than there are clean one-concept-per-neuron axes.

Steering adds or modifies activation directions during inference. Test intended effect, unrelated capabilities, different prompts/languages and distribution shift. “A behaviour changed” does not prove the direction exclusively encodes that behaviour. R9 returns to the method/claim boundary.

## 5. Release as a reproducibility package

**Key terms.** A **model card** documents intended use and limits; a **manifest** lists artifacts; a **revision** fixes a version.

**Process.** Freeze the checkpoint, code, tokenizer and evaluation settings, then package the evidence and limitations. A separate reader should be able to reconstruct the reported comparison without private assumptions.

Include model/config/tokenizer versions, training objective, data provenance and known restrictions, evaluation protocol/results, intended uses, limitations and safety considerations. Release only data/weights you have rights to share. Remove secrets and private examples; prefer safe formats and inspect code before enabling remote execution.

**Open weights** means weights are available under stated terms. It does not necessarily mean open training data, reproducible training, unrestricted use or an open-source-compliant license. Model cards and dataset cards document a system; they do not certify its claims automatically.

## 6. Final evaluation exercise

**Key terms.** An **acceptance criterion** is a stated success condition; **reproducibility** means reconstructing results under declared conditions.

**Process.** Bring the trained artifact and its evidence together, test the declared criteria and document unresolved failures. Release or revise based on those checks, not merely a finished training progress bar.

You have a checkpoint with improved perplexity but worse scientific-summary fidelity. State five hypotheses: corpus shift, alignment loss, overfitting, decoding/template change, or a weak fidelity metric. Design a matched test for each rather than declaring that perplexity is useless or that the model has become “less intelligent.”

**Pass condition:** your report separates observations from explanations, gives exact inputs/budgets, includes failure examples and does not use an attention heatmap as proof of truthfulness.

References: [LM Evaluation Harness](https://github.com/EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness), [CS336 evaluation material](https://cs336.stanford.edu/), [NIST AI risk framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework). Interpretability is a specialist field: the mechanism overview here is not an exhaustive implementation course.

sections.markdown:
## 5. Release as a reproducibility package

**Key terms.** A **model card** documents intended use and limits; a **manifest** lists artifacts; a **revision** fixes a version.

**Process.** Freeze the checkpoint, code, tokenizer and evaluation settings, then package the evidence and limitations. A separate reader should be able to reconstruct the reported comparison without private assumptions.

Include model/config/tokenizer versions, training objective, data provenance and known restrictions, evaluation protocol/results, intended uses, limitations and safety considerations. Release only data/weights you have rights to share. Remove secrets and private examples; prefer safe formats and inspect code before enabling remote execution.

**Open weights** means weights are available under stated terms. It does not necessarily mean open training data, reproducible training, unrestricted use or an open-source-compliant license. Model cards and dataset cards document a system; they do not certify its claims automatically.

sections.title: Final evaluation exercise
sections.markdown:
## 6. Final evaluation exercise

**Key terms.** An **acceptance criterion** is a stated success condition; **reproducibility** means reconstructing results under declared conditions.

**Process.** Bring the trained artifact and its evidence together, test the declared criteria and document unresolved failures. Release or revise based on those checks, not merely a finished training progress bar.

You have a checkpoint with improved perplexity but worse scientific-summary fidelity. State five hypotheses: corpus shift, alignment loss, overfitting, decoding/template change, or a weak fidelity metric. Design a matched test for each rather than declaring that perplexity is useless or that the model has become “less intelligent.”

**Pass condition:** your report separates observations from explanations, gives exact inputs/budgets, includes failure examples and does not use an attention heatmap as proof of truthfulness.

References: [LM Evaluation Harness](https://github.com/EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness), [CS336 evaluation material](https://cs336.stanford.edu/), [NIST AI risk framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework). Interpretability is a specialist field: the mechanism overview here is not an exhaustive implementation course.

notes.title: Build an evaluation ladder
notes.markdown:
**Key terms.** A **sanity check** tests basic correctness; a **benchmark** measures a defined task; **robustness** tests changed conditions.

```text
unit checks → held-out language-model loss → task datasets
→ domain/length/language slices → adversarial and shift tests
→ human-reviewed cases → intended system evaluation
```

Benchmark contamination, reused development examples and repeated selection all weaken interpretation. Freeze a final set. Record unresolved samples rather than dropping malformed generations silently. Human annotation needs instructions, disagreement handling and safeguards for sensitive material.

notes.title: Matched comparisons
notes.markdown:
**Key terms.** A **matched comparison** controls data and budgets; **paired evaluation** compares systems on the same cases; **seed variation** comes from training randomness.

Match available information and state resource budgets. Report uncertainty using appropriate independent units and training seeds where feasible. A confidence interval for one dataset does not establish universal superiority. If comparing many settings, distinguish exploratory screening from confirmatory comparisons.

For generative tasks, assess correctness, completeness, unsupported additions, contradictions and appropriate refusal. A factual statement can be unsupported by the supplied source; a source-faithful summary can repeat a false source. Those are different axes.

LLM judges can exhibit position, verbosity, self-preference and instruction-following biases. Blind system identities where feasible, randomize answer order and compare a sample with independent human judgements. Judge agreement with one annotator does not establish objective truth.

### Build an evaluation table that supports one clear conclusion

For a claimed robustness improvement, use one row per condition and columns for input access, training data, selection rule, token/compute budget and outcomes. A score without those columns can hide an unmatched comparison.

1. Freeze prompts, dataset groups and scoring rules before the confirmatory test. Mark exploratory results separately.
2. Save per-example labels, predictions and failure states. A malformed generation or abstention belongs in a declared denominator, not a silently filtered “successful outputs” subset.
3. Calculate paired differences on the same cases. Use document/group resampling when cases share a source, and report training-seed variation separately where feasible.
4. Evaluate an explicit transfer condition and important slices: domain, label policy, language, length, negation and rare entities. A global mean can improve while a critical slice fails.

For generated answers, score correctness, support and coverage separately. A citation can identify a real source without supporting the claim attached to it. Use an independently reviewed subset to audit automatic judges. reading.title: LLM evaluation and interpretability evidence
reading.definition: LLM evaluation tests a specified claim, such as better token prediction, task accuracy, source support, robustness or efficiency. Interpretability asks different questions about computation and mechanism. A score gain, an attention picture and a controlled intervention provide different evidence; none alone establishes every claim about useful or reliable behavior.
reading.example: Two hypothetical task scores, 0.76 and 0.79, illustrate a difference of 0.03. A separate scalar intervention starts from 0.8 and subtracts a selected amount. These are interpretation exercises, not measured causal effects from a trained model.
reading.connection: After fitting and resource accounting, evaluate the artifact against its intended use. Shared metrics supply the formulas; this lesson connects matched protocols, uncertainty and mechanism claims without treating one as a substitute for another.

steps.title: Define the comparison before interpreting a gain
steps.prose: Specify the task, input access, model revision, training data and resource budget. The hypothetical 0.03 difference isolates a factor only if relevant alternatives are controlled. A different template or extra evidence can explain an apparent method gain.
steps.terms: A matched comparison holds declared conditions fixed except the intended factor. Held-out results concern a specified sample and protocol.
steps.next: Save per-case outcomes and use appropriate uncertainty and error analysis.
steps.node: Define the comparison before interpreting a gain

steps.title: Inspect disagreements and uncertainty
steps.prose: Use the same evaluation cases for a paired comparison and preserve document/group dependencies. Resampling fixed predictions estimates a conditional test-sample uncertainty; repeated training seeds measure another source of variation. Neither creates universal generalization.
steps.terms: Paired resampling keeps aligned cases for both systems. Malformed outputs, abstentions and failures need declared denominator rules.
steps.next: Distinguish these outcome measurements from inspecting or intervening on internal computations.

steps.title: Separate observation from intervention
steps.prose: An attention map or probe can motivate a hypothesis without proving a mechanism. The separate scalar intervention illustrates an effect calculation only. Real interventions need matched controls and preservation checks because unusual internal states can create broad disruption.
steps.terms: Inspection observes; an intervention changes a selected quantity. Decodability of a feature is not proof the model uses it for the task.
steps.next: State the narrow conclusion supported by the actual evidence and its controls.

steps.title: Report limitations and release evidence
steps.prose: Report which outcomes changed, what was held fixed and which alternatives remain plausible. Package compatible artifacts and reproducible settings only when permitted. Model cards document scope but do not certify truthfulness, causal explanation or safe deployment.
steps.terms: A causal claim needs a meaningful intervention design. Reproducibility requires the data/interface and selection protocol as well as final weights.
steps.next: Post-training begins by deciding whether a task needs changed weights, better evidence or a different system operation.

reading.lesson_markdown:
Begin with the comparison: what system changed, what data were fixed, and what outcome would support the claim? A prompt, tokenizer, generator version, label policy, or checkpoint change can alter the meaning of a result. A controlled ablation changes the relevant factor while preserving the intended comparison.

Token loss measures prediction of declared targets. Task accuracy, faithfulness, instruction following, latency, and security test different behaviours. Evaluate important cases and subgroups rather than treating one aggregate as general capability. Repeatedly choosing prompts using the test set makes it part of development, even when no weights are updated.

Interpretability adds a question about evidence. An attention pattern or probe can reveal an association. An intervention changes a component and measures an effect. A changed output after intervention is stronger evidence of causal influence in that setup, but does not automatically establish a unique mechanism or broad generalisation. Random-direction and location controls can help distinguish specificity from generic disruption.

Save versions, conditions, predictions, and limitations so another person can reconstruct the comparison. A fixed-prediction bootstrap addresses evaluation-sample sensitivity, not all model-training uncertainty. Model cards, introduced by Mitchell and colleagues, organise intended use and measured limitations; they do not certify safety or replace evidence.

Sources: [Mitchell et al.: model cards](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.03993), [CheckList behavioural evaluation](https://aclanthology.org/2020.acl-main.442/), [Attention is not Explanation](https://aclanthology.org/N19-1357/).

question.prompt: Two systems report lower token loss with different tokenizers. What can you conclude from those numbers alone?

options.text: The smaller number always identifies the better language model.
options.feedback: Different token units can change average loss without the intended quality improvement.

options.text: The larger vocabulary necessarily wins.
options.feedback: Vocabulary size alone does not determine text prediction quality or evaluation comparability.

options.text: They are not automatically comparable because the target units differ.
options.feedback: Loss per token depends on what a token is. Hold the protocol fixed or use a justified common unit before interpreting a ranking.

options.text: No common-unit comparison can ever be attempted.
options.feedback: Matched text and byte-based or task-level measures can help, with explicit context and budget caveats.

question.explanation: Loss per token depends on what a token is. Hold the protocol fixed or use a justified common unit before interpreting a ranking.

question.prompt: For a paired bootstrap comparison of two models on the same test examples, how should each resample be constructed?

options.text: Sample unrelated indices separately for the models.
options.feedback: That discards the pairing between their results on the same examples.

options.text: Pick whichever indices maximize the preferred model's score.
options.feedback: That is selective evaluation rather than uncertainty estimation.

options.text: Resample only the examples one model got right.
options.feedback: That changes the target evaluation population and biases the comparison.

options.text: Use the same sampled example indices for both models, then compute their metric difference.
options.feedback: Pairing retains example difficulty and shared error structure. Resample the correct independent unit; test-row bootstrap still omits training and selection variability.
